About half way up you come to the murals but unfortunately you are not allowed to take photos of them. Then the "mirror wall" before you get to the Lions Paw Terrace before the finl climb to the very top of Sigiriya. The view from the top is stunning and worth the effort to get there. Only the foundations of the royal place remaining,which later became a Buddhist shrine.Bizarrely the pop group Duran Duran filmed part of their hit song/video "Save a Prayer" there in 1982 (and other parts of Sri Lanka). They got a helicopter up to the top though!

I visited Sigiriya as a solo traveler. I arrived with a driver on a private tour. Not my choice, but it was what I could find to get there. I really did not want to climb to the top, especially as it was raining. You can visit the museum for free and see what is up there without climbing if you, like me, have a fear of falling. My driver advised me not to hire a guide, unfortunately post visit, as they tend to take advantage of visitors. Based on my experience, that would be true. Anyone who does the climb will have a richer experience than I did.

This is the thing to do in Sigiriya. It is expensive (4260 Srilanka rupees). However, it was well worth it. We took the first bus from Dambulla (it was scheduled to depart at 6:00 but did not leave till 6:30) and arrived at the gate shortly after it opened at 7:00. The climb was not that strenuous with many areas to stop and take pictures. The Sigiriya Damsels frescoes half way up were wonderful to look at. The climb would have been much harder later on with the heat and the crowds.

Very interesting place, with all the history. We found the museum and the layout of the water gardens quite sufficient to absorb all we needed. The 1200 or so steps to the top, in 33 degrees, with a queue of tourists all the way to the top did not appeal. The 3D fly- through computer imaging of how the place was in its heyday really brought it to life. (Museum / Visitors Centre) This is industrial tourism, the volume of tourists, particularly Chinese, possibly due to the New Year (year of the monkey) was phenomenal. I don't much like the huge gap between tourist/local ticket prices either - USD 30.00 or SLK 4200 for foreigners. Basic discrimination.

This is as beautiful from the bottom as it is at the top; tickets are not cheap but this is a not-be-missed site. I felt a real sense of achievement as I reached the windy but serene top; the views are, of course, amazing.

While being in the que to buy a ticket we saw the entrance price 4200 LKR while the que next to us was for locals 50 LKR. Really? A lot of tourists were upset by this. We decided not to climb it and went to the rock next to it Pidurangala. Save yourself some money and go there. During the climb we only saw 6 other people and the view is stunning. You get to climb and enjoy the view in total peace. It's only 500 LKR. But who knows.. if Pidurangala becomes popular you might have to pay 843975379 LKR in the near future.

I found Sigiriya rock as the best tourist attraction in Srilanka. Climbing this rock would take around 45 mins to 1 hour. The view from top of the rock is amazing, The view makes you realize that Srilanka is literally an "Emerald island". The site is well maintained, clean but make sure that you'll ware very light cloths and carry water with you.

Our private chauffeur/ guide paid an official guide to do his job of escorting us up the rock. He hurried us through, telling us of all the nasty accidents that happened and how we could be helped for a price, in between taking phone calls.  After getting to the frescos we had enough and wanted to come down. At this point you can either turn left and come back down or turn right and keep going. The guide took us back down reluctantly, and in such a condescending manner that spoilt the whole experience. I would say to anyone, don't bother with a guide. Read the story and go up at your own pace. Go early.
It was exhausting to climb all the stairs however, the view from the top is breathtaking. It was one of my dreams to go to the Lion Rock, its a must visit in Sri Lanka!!

Four of us on tour stopped off here early morning, although only two did the climb. All good but for two left we managed the museum and gardens which were also good. The lack of climb for two was due to some of the reviews which suggested it might be a struggle if any phobias and concerns about heights. Not so much the physical. So great photos all round within the group.

A 'must see' -  - climb up and back in the morning, then explore the cooler caves at the base in the warmer part of the day.  The museum at the base is also worth the visit - you can leave the grounds and come back later in the afternoon if you're worn out from the climb.
Great views ... Disgusting that the entrance fee has gone from 3200 to 4260 in less than a month for foreigners!
An amazing site and a fascinating insight into a lost culture - but not for acrophobics

This review is written to encourage older folks or those that are not in top physical condition to climb the Lion Rock.  My wife and I are both 67 and I am in very good physical shape while my wife is about average for her age.  Two days prior she pulled a muscle in her calf while climbing the stairs to the Golden Cave Temple at Dambulla, so despite being somewhat hobbled, she had no problem.  We arrived at the park at 8:15 am on 3/2/2016 and spent 45 minutes visiting the museum near the entrance before beginning our ascent at 9:00 am.  The temperature was already over 80 degrees F and the sun was bright.  With wife holding my hand every step of the way, we took it slow, often stopping to take a break or let those behind us pass, we made it to the Lion's Paw Terrace around 10:00 AM.  Going up and down the spiral staircases to see the paintings was slow as people tend to get backed up.  We took time to view the paintings and my wife took lots of pictures.  At the Lion's Paw Terrace, we took a 15 minute or so break and taking pictures, before continuing to the top.  We reached the very top around 10:30 AM.  Spent 30 minutes on top before returning to the bottom.  Reached the parking lot around noon.  There were numerous men along the way eager to lend a hand to those who wanted help at a price.  So if one has no one to lean on, there are many men ready to help.  Remember to take plenty of water, take your time, and treat it as a marathon and not a sprint.  The price was $30 USD.

We took our 4 and 6 year old daughters up to the top. It sure was hot but they loved it! The monkeys are a great incentive to encourage little legs to do the climb! Note: I saw a father carrying his disabled daughter (aged approximately 8) up to the top on his back. Respect to you Sir.

My Husband says I've got Stairs-itus.... It's basically an allergy to things that involve loads of steps up....because my legs are made purely of cakes.  So climbing Sigiriya was always going to be a bit of a challenge for me, because cakes.  In the blistering heat of the midday sun, I got up that b****y rock and it was possibly the most incredible thing I have ever seen.  The views are like nothing I've experienced and the history behind the ruins at the top is breath taking.  The ruins were much more substantial at the top than I thought they were going to be.  Take lots of water and enjoy it.  It's wonderful and totally worth doing.  We were up and down in 3 hours but some will need more time.  Some were like gazelles up there, but you want to enjoy it!

This is an amazing place to visit. Very intense climb but worth it, from bottom to top. We were drenched in our own seat by the time we got to the top so the earlier in the morning you can do it the better but bring lots of water with you.

We arrived around 11 am so it was hot. Took lots of water as it was a tough climb. I'm not a terribly fit person but managed it all the Gym Bunnies came earlier thank god.travelled with three teenagers who also loved this site. The views are amazing. The monkeys on th way up are very entertaing . A great experience

I am obsessed with ancient civilizations - the 8 hour round trip from Colombo was worth it... the aching legs - worth it - the borderline dehydration - also worth it... this Unesco site is a bit of secret - fascinating, complex and romantic in its history and majesty... this site can trace its history back 6000 years with monks being in residence for 2000 years. The sprawling site with cascading gardens with a dark history had me enthralled the whole visit. Climbing to the top was exhausting but exhilarating....at $45 AUS entry it was a little steep but I plan to re-visit and stay on my way through to Kandi next time I visit.
There is a reason that the UNESCO ranks Sigiriya as the 8th wonder of the world. Once you see it you'll completely understand. Lot of walking so make sure you'd prepared.

About 1200 steps to the top.  Part way up is a detour to see gorgeous painted murals.  You are not allowed to photograph the murals.  Watch out after your return to earth:  there is a man with a snake near the cobra' s cave.

We went to Sigiriya Rock early in the morning as soon as the place opened. It was already busy with lines of tourists. You can easily climb to the top but take it easy, enjoy the different things to see at each level,  and don't try to do everything too fast.  The views are stunning and the history is well worth bringing along a guide to explain. Well worth seeing.

Allow a half day to see this rich historical spectacle. Once you have paid entrance, walk through the beautiful Royal Gardens to the Boulder park, then up a series of steep steps to & past the famous Mirror Wall & Frescoes, to the foot of Lion Rock and entrance to the old city. Up a series of narrow, high climbing staircases (not for the faint hearted), leads you to the top where you can take in breathtaking scenery of the surroundings and admire the city as it once would have been. We went to the museum first which provides an excellent introduction and allows you to fully appreciate the real thing once you get up top. Located to the right of the ticket office, included as part of your entrance fee.

Our driver sorted a guide. The history of the palace is fascinating and so easily missed. They are still excavating the area but the engineering used to create the place both on ground and at the top office rock were amazing. It was hot climbing but with the stops for historical updates as well as breathers we coped well and the view of the palace ruins as well as the views were excellent. We though going down might be hard but it was fine. We spent about 2 1/2 hours doing the visit and have great memories and pictures.

It takes a great toll for a person like me with acrophobia - to reach the top of this rock but it's worth ! Trekking on this rock talks about many historic events and it's interesting to know about them. They close trekking by 5 in eve and its advisable to return back in daylight as there are no lights on the way ... Don't forget to carry your water bottles !!!

Recently retired I wasn't sure about the ascent of the rock, and didn't even manage to reach the cave paintings!. Unrelenting sunshine and exhausting heat are not conducive to discovery of the site for an older woman with a bad knee! The many steps between levels are uneven heights and there's nothing to hold on to! Nonetheless, the remains of the water gardens are fascinating and a small-scale excavation was underway. Scenery is beautiful with trees and birds everywhere. The downside is the exorbitant LKR4,260 price - a scandalous 85 times more than for locals! No simple plan or short leaflet is provided, as in European cultural monuments. I got the feeling the archeological sites are subsidized by the foreign tourists (exotic animals for many Sri Lankans).

Beautiful surroundings, fabulous views. Amazing to climb to the top of this place, humbling to think that this had been done so many years ago, bringing up all these building materials. By contrast we were out of breath climbing up once, bringing nothing more than a camera and bottle of water.... Slight let down: there is a point where visitors can opt whether to view paintings or carry on straight up to the top (WITHOUT seeing the paintings). Our guide recommended that we opt to skip the paintings (as replicas can be seen in the museum), which led to us being verbally abused for doing so by another tourist who did want to see the paintings... There should be clearer signage to avoid this kind of unpleasantness.

Is not cheap for non Sri Lankans at 4260 Rp (AUD 43) and you have to supply the energy to get to the top.. The climb is approximately 1200 steps I was told but did not count. Overall could be a hard climb for some. Be careful of helpful people as you may have some one helping you up the steps but it comes at a price. There are some good rest areas so can take you time. You can avoid the spiral staircase climb and descent to make overall climb easier. Also be careful of helpful guides who make you feel like you have to leave via tourist path, not the normal entry gate. You are being taken to many people wanting to tell you souvenirs. Can be a little pushy.

During the morning the climb is on the shady side of the rock.  Very enjoyable although strenuous and hectic because of thousands of Chinese (Chinese New Year) pushing and shoving to get in front.  Hazy views from the top, not for those who don't like heights.  There are over 1200 steps both in rocks, metal staircases and enclosed spiral staircases.  We are 78 and 80 but had no problem as it had to be done slowly in view of the crush.
amazing place. a nice walk in the beautiful gardens then a climb up to the rock to enjoy the view. go there early (when it opens)

Some may be put off by the daunting climb to the top. But if you are averagely fit it won't be a problem. The history, sheer mechanical improbability of its build and the views from the top are tremendous.
A fairly big site with the centrepiece being Lion Rock. It's a demanding climb to the top but well worth it. The entire grounds are beautifully maintained. A must see place.

As the other reviews state, Sigiryia is best visited early in the morning to avoid the heat, and you'll need to take water with you whatever time of day you visit. On public holidays Sigirya will be very crowded - so avoid visiting at these times. While the walk-ways on the outside of the rock are quiet sturdy, the views & sheer drop are dizzying - so not suitable for those with a fear of heights - but also spectacular.  I'm not sure I'd want to visit when raining due to the chance of slipping - perhaps something to consider if visiting during the rainy season. We hired an independent guide for 10 USD and which  made all of the difference to the experience as there is more to Sigiriya than just the climb, explaining to us fascinating architecture and history, ensuring the we didn't miss any points of interest, and even fast-tracking us around some of the queues.

Did the climb, for those of you afraid of climbing it, don't. It is a gradual climb and they have great railings. Very good safety. At the half point they also have first aid, but you won't need it. The view from the top was worth the effort. My advice is do it early morning, you will be mostly out of the sun for the most part.

I was very concerned about climbing Sigiriya.  1200 steps is a lot of steps for a 50+ year old who is mostly sedentary.  Having done it- all of it- I can say that 1200 steps is a LOT OF STEPS but the challenge for me was more than aerobic capacity.  The stairs for the last part of the climb (up the rock face) are bolted to the side of the rock and do shudder in the wind and with shifting weight.  I was actually so scared on the stairs the fact that my legs were tired was hardly an issue.  Coming down is even more scary if you have a fear of heights because you see the ground below you.  As I was coming down, a woman on her way up had a complete meltdown and was screaming/crying.  There is no real way to turn around on most of the stairs and in the end, her daughter basically just shoved/carried her to the top.  On the way down, I just focused on the backpack of the guy in front of me and made it down with only a gasp or two when the stairs rattled in the wind.  Was it worth it?  Absolutely.  The view of the area is certainly nice but seeing a kingdom built by people who carted bricks up stairs even more tenuous than the ones I climbed is amazing.  The ruins are so well preserved that you get a good sense of what the palace was like when it was occupied.  You can see a quick view of the top in many on line photos or in the Duran Duran video shot there.  What about sights on the way up?  The “ladies” are quite beautiful and some of the best preserved frescoes from that era in the world.  The mirror wall is interesting and a good place to see the oldest Sri Lankan writing.  They are worth seeing even though you have to make a slight detour to see them.  For me, the highlight was the palace at the top.  I know a lot of people stop at Lion gate and don’t go to the top but look at the photos and decide for yourself if you want to go all the way to the top.

Climbing the Lion Rock is a must do in Sri Lanka. The views are spectacular. A little tiring but very manageable for all age groups. Make sure you take water as there is non available until the descent.

Make sure to be there when it opens at 07:00. I did and there were only a handful of people in front of me. This means you can walk at your own pace and when you're at the top you can enjoy the view without dozens of other tourists obstructing your view. Because there were so few people this early the climb only took me 15 or 20 minutes. When I went down around 09:00 there were bussloads of people arriving and queueing to get a ticket/climb the rock. So make sure to beat the rush and come at 07:00! Unfortunately it was a bit misty so the view wasn't as spectacular as it could've been. But the ruins at the top alone are worth it.

An amazing trip to see an astounding and truly impressive piece of ancient history. The climb up is a little tiring, especially in the heat, and if possible get there early- not just to avoid the heat of the day, but also the crowds- it is a very popular attraction. That said the frescos are beautiful and the views from the top are truly memorable. One not to miss
One of the best spot in Sigiriya, you can see the marvelous infrastructure developed by human being.

Good place to visit, nice supporting infrastructure I think. But you need to spend at least 2 days to visit this place from Colombo. Be careful with the independent tour guide, sometime they're too pushy.
We were also here 10 years ago and since then the way up has been improved dramatically, making it easier to get to the top.  Best to make an early start to avoid the heat of the sun and the crowds.

When I learned that this was a rock cave where past kings had stayed before, I was expecting that we would be allowed to enter into the caves, so I was disappointed that we only got to climb along the outskirts of the rocks with only one small section that was inside the caves.  The view from the top was really amazing, but there is a section with dangerous stairs that might scare those who are afraid of heights.  Even though I'm not afraid of heights, it frightened me a little when the wind blew and I had only one hand to hold onto the the rails.  I also expected there would be vendors along the way selling water, etc., but there was nothing like that so make sure you bring your snacks and drinking water.  There is a tank that the locals take their water from so we did that when we ran out of water.  There are many "guides" looking to make some money from you.  We found that we were happy to not have them come along.  If you do hire a guide, you can get one for about 2000 rupees so don't get ripped off.  It only took us about 2-3 hours total to get to the top, enjoy the view, and come back down.  It is also a bit pricey, with adults and teens being about $30 usd.
It was a nice to observe the ancient urban planning and check off another UNESCO World Heritage Site on my list.
We both climbed the rock,in the company of our guide/driver.Quite physical at times,but well worth the effort!

Really nice place to visit.  Hard to climb up but when you get up view is really super nice. So many stairs, many people and really warm weather. So trip was really hard but it took us like 2 hours to get up and down.

we left early last Saturday morning form our hotel (which is excellent by the way - Kumbukgaha Villas!!) in order to get to Sigiriya by 7am; we wanted to beat the crowds and the heat of the day! Tickets are sold from 7am…we were on our way by 7:10am. We were at the very top by 8am having stopped a numb roy times along the way to take photos (and to catch my breath!) It's SO worth the 1500 stairs….really really worth it! The views are gorgeous even though there was could and haze about. I suffer from fear of heights and I managed - just about! Don't let the 1500 stairs/steps put you off, nor the price US$30 per person is very steep!! We are very pleased we decided to go; Sigiriya is vey well maintained and there's information everywhere so you know which part of the garden you are looking at etc. A must-see if you are in the area! Try and make sure you go early to avoid the crowds and the heat (unless you don't mind either) especially on a Saturday and Sunday as the locals tend to go on the weekends. I would try and avoid going on a public holiday for the same reason. Defiantly take you own water as there isn't any available to purchase along the route up. Cameras, hats and suntan lotion would also be good! Guides are available at the entrance (car park drop-off site) and there probably is a guide that speaks your language; French, German, Italian etc. we chose not to have a guide. You are met by you driver at another car park…the way to the pick-up car park is clearly sign posted. You also don't walk back down the 1500 stairs which is a bonus!

Sigiriya it's a must do in a trip to Sri Lanka a lot of history in the lion rock. Everybody recommend to climb the rock early in the morning but if you are not afraid of the hot do it after 12 because you gonna be the only one up there I guess. Don't forget the water and good shoes.

What a stunning place to visit! A vertiginous climb leads you to the top of the rock where the King of Sri Lanka built a palace with enough rooms for 500 girls! The view is wonderful. Go as early as possible so crowds are a minimum.

Lakes, ancient ruins, carvings on the wall and great views from the top. One piece of advice: avoid visiting on a poya (fullmoon) celebration day unless you are prepared to be squashed by locals and sneaky monkeys on the way to the top! No need to worry about proper shoes etc..you reach the top by stairs

Everything about this place is magical. First the story about a patricide king who built this complex in and around a huge rock, the effort that had to be put in doing this, and the life of mentioned king. This place is still being excavated, but everything is in almost mint condition. Ascent can be a bit difficult for older people, because of the heat and moisture, and bring comfortable sneakers, avoid sandals. Each level of ascent offers breathtaking views of jungle, lakes and beautiful nature, and on the top of the rock you truly feel like a king! Don't miss this place!
The walk through the garden was excellent. Very well kept. There are a couple of touts beware of them. The climb is difficult but worth it.

World heritage site with lots to be seen - gardens, indoor frescoes, outstanding view from the top. Have to be in good shape to climb the stairs. It takes 1h30 to reach the top. Bring water with you. Beware of the bees and the monkeys. It's quite expensive though compared to other similar sites in the world - 4600 rupees (around $30)

A fantastic place.  We managed to visit in monsoon conditions, heavy rain and low cloud.  The plus was that it was cool at the top of the rock and there were far fewer tourists around.  This place can get very busy and the access paths and stairways to the rock can become very congested.  Not a problem for us.  But it did make the climb up (and down) the metal staircase to the rock treacherous (a couple of people slipped coming down).  But this is a place you must visit.

The remainings of the pallace are truly impresive, as well as the paintings (the gardens not so much). Definitely worth getting to know a history of the place and climb up all the way to the top! It is extremely expensive for Sri Lanka (entry over 30 dolars per person) but honestly - one of the best culture sights they have - worth seing even for such price!

After  seeing the 3400 rupee price  tag ,  a small  group  decided  to explore   a bit, and thanks  to Google  maps found the adjacent  mountain ,  that has an optional  500 eupee fee. the view  is spectacular ,  and you can feel smug watching  the poor fellows  who spent  a disgusting  entrance  fee for the Citadel  mountain. Take care of the wind and sheer  edges.

When you reach the car park the Lion Rock looms above you.  It is busy so you have no choice but to join the throng wending its way upwards.  The initial stages are easy through water gardens, moats and ramparts that formed part of the old town.  You can also visit the museum. The path then gets narrower and steeper with some quite large steps.  It is not over difficult but you need to pace yourself and take several sips of water. The first objective is an area just below a separate staircase to see the murals which I did, although in truth they are no better than the reproductions in the museum near the car park.  As an alternative you can go directly to the plateau where the Lions feet signal the start of the final ascent to the summit. This plateau gives good views anyway and an opportunity to rest and get refreshments.  Most however, including me, elected to complete the last part of the climb up to the summit where the views are spectacular.  At the top there are also ruined buildings and water features. You must take a lot of water on this climb. We saw two tourists on the way down who had collapsed so be careful. Overall, this was hard but worth it.

Go early, pay the us$30 local equivelent, climb all the steps to the top via the cave paintings. Don't worry about the iron steps collapsing they wont in the next few weeks! Have a break at Lions Paw and then take the next set of iron steps to the summit. Get to the top and wonder what Pyscho murders his Father and builds a palace on top of a blooming great rock, lives there for 18 years and then get murdered/commits suicide & you think our modern day leaders are mad! The views are terrific and this is an essential must do, however if you have heights issues be prepared and take along a change of underwear.

Great location. Climb to the top in less time than you think and monkeys keep you entertained on your ascent. Only advice apart from good walking shoes or trainers is to wear a hat. I burnt my scalp not realising how hot my head was getting as it's windy.
A must see! The effort of climbing all the way to the top was definitely worth it. Not too arduous, just take your time.

An easy climb to the top of this rock is definitely worth it for the views that await you. At the top you'll also find the remnants of what was once a palace and it's a sight to behold. A must see if you're in the area!

Sigiriya Rock is a long climb to the top, but once you're up there, the view is just amazing. And if you make sure you're there as soon as the gates open, it's quiet, peaceful and not very hot. Carry bottles of water with you, as you will need it, and Indians get a half price ticket :-)
One of the great heritages in Sri Lanka that you must visit. The Sigiri "Mirror Wall" and the drawings are simply amazing....

This was the busiest place we visited in the whole of Sri Lanka. It is usually so busy that you have to queue to climb the gangways up the rock. The good news is that that makes it slower and therefore easier to climb... but unlike many other places in Sri Lanka, you'll not have the place to yourself!

if you venture this way you must take in the long climb up. Pack water. Wear proper footwear  and clothing. it is a trek. Go early as afternoon is high heat and humid. Careful of people at bottom wo will assist you but at a huge cost. pack your camera. lots to take photos of. amazing!!!
AMAZING!!!! Bring water and careful of getting assistance from people there as it will cost you!

We went to Sigiriya last week. Unfortunately, it was slightly clouded - which helped with the heat when taking the stais upwards but the view from above was not so good. Nevertheless, the frescos were amazing!!!

If you dont know where to go in your next holidays, please consider Sri Lanka! One of the most beautiful countries Ive ever been to. Sigiriya is just one example of the amazing historic places you have to discover. Believe me, Sri Lanka is THE place to be!!!

We travelled from Kandy just to see Sigirya and it was worth it. Beautiful views, plenty of monkeys and lots of history. Overpriced for foreigners but unfortunately this is endemic in Sri Lanka. The rock itself is about a 15 minute walk from the entry point where you purchase tickets. We didn't get a guide but these are readily available at the entrance. There are signs in English dotted about the area and if you have the lonely planet Sri Lanka or equivalent then you have all the info you need.

Having visited the cave temple earlier in the day our legs were a little weary. The first section of the walk up was the hardest, but once you reach the lions claw plateau the final staircase is relatively easy going. For those only wanting to get to the top and not interested in the fresco artwork in the cave, you can bypass the spiral staircase and continue up, just take the right side of the path instead of the left which leads you up the spiral staircase. If you do go up the staircase to see the artwork you come back down another staircase to meet the original path up. Essentially you climb up and down extra steps just to see the artwork. We walked up with our 4yo in an ergo carrier, but for anyone with young children there were 2 groups of very young school children (5-8yo) who walked up by themselves without a problem. The colours and views at sunset are beautiful. It gets dark quickly so remember to take a torch with you.

From afar we thought it would be very challenging to get to the top, but once we started climbing we were taken by the historical details and amazing arts that we did not feel the strand. Some elderly were climbing as well! It is worth every effort. Amazing location. If you are in Sri Lanka go visit Sigiriya, but try to climb the rock as early in the morning as possible, wear appropriate shoes and don't forget your water bottle.

When researching things to do in Sri Lanka this was number one... I think it's a lovely thing to do but it's defiantly not up there with the best! It has beautiful grounds and the trek to the top is very doable. But if you want more spectacular then head to Adams peak for a view!
Leave early in the morning and have breakfast after the climb.  There are lots of steps and a rather scary metal spiral staircase on the outside of the rock so not for the faint hearted!

The entrance fee is quite high for foreigners, however it was worth it. The initial climb was very steep and i suggest comfortable footwear as it started to rain as i was climbing and it gets very slippery. You are not allowed to take pictures of the cave paintings which if found odd? The view once you reach the top is amazing and well worth the climb. Definitely recommend.

A lot of steps very steep in places not for the unfit or faint hearted or hip or knee sufferers! Worth the climb to the cave art but unfortunately we visited on a wet day unable to change as we were on a group tour. Although we remained dry the mist came down to destroy the views and as a consequence we did not climb to the very top of the rock.

Climbed the rock on a hot day, with many other tourists, Worth the effort, just make sure you are ready for a significant climb, and are not overly concerned with heights, and the second phase of the ascent is quite hairy !

The grounds of the Sigiriya World Heritage site is fascinating and beautiful.  There is plenty to learn see and do but the real highlight is climbing Lion's Rock.  With over 2000 steps to the top it is quite a climb but the pay off is worth it!  The view is spectacular.  You can climb to a platform 200 steps short of the top if the height is difficult for you.  Or you can climb up 200 pretty narrow and rickety steps for the final view point and historical site at the top.  It is well worth it!!

Some great views 360 around the rock and interesting history of the site (kingdom). Carefull if temperatures are high it is a bit demanding - although many 60+ people managed to get up there (and back).
Avoid the heat of the day - it's a challenging climb and very popular - we went late pm, I think it is open from day light to dusk Well worth it the views are stunning

Very busy attraction - we did it late pm just before sun down - early morning was the other busy time - avoid in the heat of the day It's a challenging climb for most but well worth it for the views and the history if the place

Sigiriya is pretty expensive compared to something like Angkor Wat, but still worth seeing.  It's one of the oldest examples of urban planning, and in general just a really unique place.  Climb to the top is a little scary at places if heights make you uncomfortable, but I found it easier if I was climbing with a group, therefore not setting the pace, etc.  Great view.  If you have time, there's a nearby mountain that you can climb for an awesome view of Sigiriya itself...we didn't get to do that, but heard it was great.

It is a huge fortress built on a hill... One can walk to the top through the steps... 15-20min walk... Entry fee for Indians is 15USD and for other foreign nations it is 30USD. It covers entry to three attractions... The fort, The mirror wall (there is nothing much interesting), the museum. I saw some people from other foreign countries requesting to allow entry at half price (15USD). I don't know what happened at the end. It will take at least 3-4 hours to spend there... In rainy season steps may be slippery... One may need water to carry as the place is humid and there are no other resources available.

I debated whether to see this as the entrance fee is an eye-watering 4,260 (about 30 USD) for foreigners. Locals pay only 50 rupees. But I'm so glad I did.  Well worth it. It's on par with Angkor Wat for sheer engineering brilliance, but dating back much, much earlier. You must read up on the history of the site before going to make the visit worthwhile.  You will get so much more out of it. Take your time at the site and read all the explanatory signs as you go. So many tourists just rush to the top and miss out on the whole experience. It's truly astounding how they managed to build a palace and city on top of this sheer rock in the 5th century AD. The mirror wall, which clings to the sheer rock face, was built at that time and is covered in graffiti from the 6th to 10th centuries. It's just mind-blowing. Don't climb in the middle of the day. Go early or late. I entered the site at 4 and started the climb itself by 5, making it to the top in time to see the sunset at 6.15pm. There were only about 30 tourists on the summit for the sunset which surprised me so it was lovely and peaceful.  And leaving right after the sun sets means you can make it down before its completely dark but I would bring a torch or a phone with torch. The climb itself is not as hard as it looks from the bottom and the ancient remains at the top (nothing is left of the buildings more than a couple of feet high so you have to use your imagination) and 360 degree views are literally breath-taking. If you are afraid of heights or have vertigo you may want to reconsider as parts of the climb involve fragile-looking (and rusted!) metal stairs and ladders clinging to the cliff face. My only gripe is that for the very hefty entry fee you ought to get an explanatory pamphlet or more comprehensive explanatory signs around the site. Only basic info is supplied on site so you need to read up in advance. And bring lots of water. There is nothing available to buy once you are inside.

Better visit on Rainy season as rain will make the surroundings green and alive .tickets will be issues on 7 AM and early in morning rock climb will easy as cool air  will make you soothing ,climb is not hard but plenty of water and lite snack will be helpful .avoid feeding animals (monkeys,Birds) and making loud noises (possible Hornets attack if noise make them active ) .

With some trepidation we arrived at the site of Lions Rock and were overwhelmed by the thought of climbing, however our guide came with us and iinspite of my husbands vertigo we managed to reach the Lions paw over half way up. The views are amazing and worth the effort. There are young locals who will help you up, be prepared they will want tipping but we were happy to do this as they helped us on some difficult steps and we're happy to share some history with us.

Sigirya is a freestanding rocky outcrop, a little like Uluru in Australia.  At the top are the ruins of an ancient civilisation, as well as stunning view over the countryside. It's best to arrive early to avoid the heat and the crowds.  It seemed busy when I got there at 7.30am but that was nothing to the hordes of people there by the time I'd got down!  There are pretty water gardens which you walk through, approaching the cloud-shrouded rock ahead.  It makes you catch your breath at first sight - and wonder how you'll make it up! The actual climb isn't too bad, although it does require you to be able bodied and have a head for heights.  I am very unfit and found it exhausting and hard work, but I was able to do it.  The early part consists of stone steps, which can be steep and uneven - I actually found this bit the hardest.  Higher up, there are steel walkways and ladders.  These are easier to climb and did feel very secure although if you have vertigo you may find it impossible - the ladders are set into the side of the rock above a sheer drop. There are some things to see on route, including some frescoes (I personally didn't think these were worth the long climb up and then down spiral staircases to see - and there is a way to bypass this part.  If you're struggling physically it may be an idea to give this part a miss to conserve your energy).  Further along are the lion's feet, two vast brick paws on either side of the staircase leading on to the summit.  The views over the misty forests are great and get better the higher you go. Most sections have separate steps for going up and coming down, so you don't have the problem of trying to squeeze past people.  I imagine this is vital later on in the day as the crowds get bigger.  There are men along the route who will attempt to 'help' you along - this comes at a price and really isn't necessary.  Younger solo female climbers may find them particularly keen to offer their assistance - I found saying 'don't touch me' loudly and assertively was enough to get them to back off. I wouldn't recommend doing this in the rain as I think it would become very slippery and also the winds are high at the top. Overall, despite the physical exertion, this was well worth doing for the wonderful views and the fascinating ruins at the top.

Before I left for Sri Lanka, this was at the top of my list! This colossal rock sprouts out of nothing and overlooks the entire area. The views from the top are amazing. Hire a certified guide to take you to the top and tell you all about amazing Sigiriya. An absolute must!
Excellent views, and lovely cool top on (for us) a slightly overcast day. Would advise taking a picnic.

I am 51 and 130kg and I did it. Three hours up and down! Try it, the view will compensate! If you have problem with walking on steps 50 meters above the ground do not do it or at least stop before the final part! Bring enough cash, cards are not accepted by the entrance!!!

Despite its dark history and short life span as a palace this is a wonder to behold. Do not rush through the water gardens which are well worth exploring. Do also go early, especially at week-ends or you will wait over an hour to see the wall frescoes. The climb is steep but the views from the top of the mountain are stupendous.

If you want to see one of the best attraction in Sri Lanka - go to Sigiriya. If you want to see Sigiriya and great views - go to Pidurangala. We managed both in one day and it was the best what we could do.

If you want to see one of the best attraction in Sri Lanka - go to Sigiriya. If you want to see Sigiriya and great views - go to Pidurangala. We managed both in one day and it was the best what we could do.

Climbing up Sigirya was definitely the highlight of our trip to Sri Lanka this past two weeks. We had a guide who was very knowledgeable and paced us very well on the assent. Made the walk up far more manageable and interesting. The actual climb itself isn't to bad, although it is tiring. I'm not the fittest and managed it fine thou and there were children and older adults doing it too. The view on the way up and from the top is awesome which makes the effort all the more worthwhile. Must do whilst in Sri Lanka!!

Walk around the grounds exploring the old site of the summer palace and experience what great engineers these people were 1600 years ago. Then climb the rock. Not too difficult to climb. Steps are straightforward and view is worth it.
The site is fantastic as you walk through the summer palace before climbing to the winter palace. Not a hard climb. I was up and down in 90 mins. Go early.

The whole point of coming to Sigiriya is visiting this 1500 year old rock fortress palace turned buddhist temple. I recommend getting a guide to really understand it's history – there isn't much signage around. Aside from it being a palace built into a mountain and it's hydraulic engineering for the various moats, swimming pools, and watering holes was way ahead of its time. Loin's Gate and the original paintings that are preserved are the highlights of the visit. It's incredible enough to come a day out of your way to see it.

Visiting Sigitiya Rock city is A MUST!!! The ticket is expensive (approx £ 20.00pp) but it is money well spent: the cost includes the entry to the Sigiriya Museum (very interesting!!) and access to the citadel and its gardens!!! Climbing the 1,200 steps is not too hard but it requires some strength, especially in the heat (bring water!!)!! Views from the top are breathtaking...and a perfect reward!!! A suggestion: allow yourself enough time (min. 3 hours!) to relax and enjoy this beautiful archaeological site - which is well maintained - as its grounds are as interesting as the citadel!!!!!!! HIGHLY RECOMMENDED!!!!

Beautiful and interesting place to spend half a day. Mount rise can be really exhausting, because stairs are sometimes steep and crowded with people. But there is enough place for all at the top to make photos and have rest. Be careful of sun, have enough water and you will enjoy this place.

Climbing the Roc is a thing !! Once you have started there is no way or short cut back. But iff you are at the top you will be proud off yourself .You did it and the view is great. We went as early in the morning as possible.The heat is good to handle and there is not a great crowd who is pushing you up.You can go in  your own tempo.

We were told this was not to be missed  a world heritage site..Spend a night in the Sigiriya Hotel ( see review) Work early the next day and walked up the mountain..well worth the effort Spectacular views from all sides. The history and culture is very interesting for the history buffs

We got there and it was crowded of people, all waiting to pay more than 4000rp/ person to go up the lion rock like ants one after the other in a really ready for tourism place with stairs etc. After that we went to Pindurangala Rock and it was amazing, really cheap (500rp) and challenging. We hike it all through nature without a guide needed and once at the top you can see the lion rock and it is such a peaceful place with just three or four more people.

This is a must to visit, probably the best tourist site in Sri Lanka. however for oldies like us it was a struggle, there are twelve hundred steps and they are not easy ones. But the effort was worth it. The views fron the top are splendid and the ruins well worth looking at. However beware the guides, they are everywhere and wait to latch onto you for the least pretext. We were caught by this and could not get rid of the guy and ended up having to pay for something we really did not need. However dont let that put you off its well worth the visit.
Amazing,  breathtakingly moment! 1200 steps to the top! History behind Lions rock most interesting. The rock art a must see!

Wonderful climb to the top, not easy if not in good shape. There are 1202 steps in few phases. Don't forget to take water, good shoes and a hat with you The views from the top are amazing and very rewarding. We used a local guide which was nice - he shared some interesting bits with us The overall visit was about 3 hrs highly recommend it
We were unlucky with the weather, but still an incredible experience, to recommend to anyone, who does not have problems with hights....

Bring lots of water and be ready to walk a lot.  The museum on site is a welcome relief from the heat if you need an escape, but not really noteworthy.  Yes you have to kind of be ushered single file at points of the walk along to the top (narrow areas) but it is all still quite pleasant and beautiful.  Once you are at the top the views are really amazing but of course there is no shade, so bring sunscreen/hat/umbrella.

I felt from the reviews and information I had seen that this world heritage site was underplayed - beautiful surrounding gardens with restored areas of the ancient city to be seen, and an interesting climb to the top of the rock, complete with centuries-old paintings on the rock face. Once at the top not only is there a stunning view but further ancient ruins to explore. Although it is a pricey entrance fee I feel it is worth it. We hired a guide who was recommended to us and he told us the fascinating story behind the ruins and I only think this added to the experience and again was worth the money we paid - and we would usually avoid over spending on these types of things on a trip.

Went with my aunt and mother, and we managed it just fine. Go early because even at 9:30 there were traffic jams in the narrow files to go up. Seriously, we thought we'd be huffing and puffing but had so much time just standing on the steps, it was easy going - except for the crazy heat and lack of water. Coming down the exit path was blocked but my aunt and mother still managed to sneak down it. If you're coming down at a different pace, agree to meet in the "foreign tourist car park" because you could end up taking different routes that thankfully end in the same place.

Worth the effort to make the climb and witness the ruins of the old kingdom. Baffles me as to how they managed to build on such a structure all those years ago! Only down side was we were there during the peak tourist season so there was a bit of queuing involved.

This is a fabulous activity to do. We arrived early, just after 7 am and started the climb straight away to avoid the crowds and heat. The climb is a little tiring, but not overly challenging for the relatively fit. At the top the view is incredible and the ruins are impressive. If there is mist, it does burn off. The museum was not that insightful, but worth popping on to look.

Many other posts will describe the climb. My wife and I are older than 60.   I completed the climb while my wife went part of the way.  There are approximately 1200 steps to the top, with guys offering assistance at various stages ........for a price. The climb includes a spiral staircase, and steel steps. Wear appropriate walking / climbing shoes.  Take water and a hat. I think you have to be reasonably fit; without a fear of heights; and with knees able to  climb lots of steps.

This is something not to be missed if you come to this area of Sri Lanka. It is expensive at 30 dollars each but it needs to be done. The gardens are lovely and there is a museum that we forgot to go into. We read about the history on the internet before climbing which really helped. We werent asked if we wanted a guide and no one bothered us which suprised me. We arrived at 7.30am and there were quite a lot of people there. It didn't bother me as everyone takes breaks at different places. The climb isn't easy, you can break though. I didnt see any easy way down so once you are climbing the only way is up. We wore hiking boots and i was pleased but trainers would do as the steps are very good. To be a bit boring I wouldn't suggest anyone who is very unfit, heart/lung problems or very young children climb. There were lots of Chinese children of about 5 climbing in dresses and sandles but i didnt think it was very fair. The steps are steep but the views are worth it. Stunning!!! Regarding the steps there are some bits that are in a spiral metal staircase and some that are metal steps stuck to the side of the rock. I felt a little scared at times but just keep walking and don't look down until you are at the top. Take plenty of water and enjoy.

Expensive and crowded. Had to do it  as I was there ,wish I had taken my passport as if your country belong to the list of sarc countries you get in for half price Getting up to the top of the rock is not to bad as there a plenty of stop to take  a rest but make sure you take plenty of water The views are lovely when you get to the top

Good climb and interesting history. One of those places that wakes you wonder. We climbed in the middle of the day when there were no tour buses - we met the hoards on the way down, avoid if you can it'd be a day made bad. Expensive but a good couple of hours. Worth visiting the museum, it has a couple of interesting rooms after the first 1 or 2 dull ones.
An impressive place, climbing up the rock and looking at the views and the history. The best time to go is early morning as it is cooler and not as crowded

We arrived and immediately a young man, a guide started to engage with us. We had already been to another tourist spot where a guide insisted on offering us his services and even though we said no initially, we gave in. So this time we wanted to enjoy the citadel and take our time and do our own thing at our own pace without a guide. We realize it's their livelihood and admire their knowledge.  However it became annoying as refusing with politeness fell on deaf ears, we tried to be firm with our "no thank you" and in the end almost had to be rude, which we hated doing. He said it would only cost US$20.  Well it certainly wasn't about the money and I would have rather paid him to leave us alone. We watched another couple go through the same thing and they gave up saying no in the end.  So if you want a guide, all well and good but If you don't, be prepared to be firm!! The effort and adventure getting to the top is well worth it and the view is spectacular. What was appalling was the rubbish at the top.  Hundreds of empty water bottles and loads of rubbish, biscuit packets, empty plastic bags etc. why do people get to the top and expect to dump their rubbish and expect someone else to bring it all down? Why can't people bring down their own rubbish like we did? Such a shame.

Sigiriya Lion rock is a must visit place. We reached on the top within 30 minutes.On that day humidity was about 80% so it was quiet challenging but we made it. The sight from the top is so beautiful.One must go there if you are planning to visit Srilanka. Some people find it difficult to climb up but if you have the habit of exercise you can do it with little effort.

My advice: get there early. We stayed in Sigiriya so we could get there before 8 a.m. The coach parties start arriving quite early, and you'll want to be ahead of them. There are some precarious sections on the way up to the top - particularly the final staircase, which does not seem sturdy or safe - and queuing on them would not be pleasant. The history and engineering of the place is fascinating, but the signs in English weren't great - verbose and jumbled. The hike up itself is not hard if you are reasonably fit. We saw some quite frail and overweight people managing it. The views are lovely. All in all, an enjoyable but underwhelming experience.
Sigiriya world heritage site, truly deserves to be in the world heritage site list , its had so many things to offer, very well preserved  site.

This site is a must for all visitors to Sri Lanka. The walk to the top looks harder then it is.  It is mostly steps and stairways.  When you get to the top you are so glad you spent the energy to do it.  I am 70 years old and had not problem with the Site.

Great experience, although the climb is a little scary, with stairs on the side of the rock. It takes shorter time, than expected, when you are standing at the bottom. A good advice is to start the climb already at 7 am when they open, in order to avoid climbing together with huge travel groups of tourists. When at the top you have a beautiful 360-view of the fantastic surroundings. A must try!

Only got halfway up but I think too old and unfit! Get there at 7 am when it opens and avoid the heat and crowds. Very impressive. I recommend you read about it and watch YouTube videos before you visit.

The sigiriya rock fortress looms out of the countryside and dominates it. At the bottom are the remains of a palace complex. However, it is at the top that the most spectacular ruins are with amazing views over the countryside. A climb of about 600 feet up this granite rock is quite easy given the metal staircase (and the slow pace due to the number of visitors). The historic ruins dating back to the 5th Century AD are fascinating, as are the hundreds of wall paintings of maidens - many half naked, and those that remained out of reach of the Buddhist monks have survived.

Although enrance fee is a bi too high - it is worth it. The view from the top is amazing. Best time  - early in the morning. Don't look down while climbing. And don't let local help you - it will cost you money.

Go early in the morning, before 8 a.m to avoid crowds. And don't look down as you are climbing the metal steps. Although it is a bit pricy - 30 US dolars entrance fee - it is worth it. But don't let local "semi" guides to help you by giving hand -  it will cost you money.

Thus is a must visit place if you are in Sri Lanka. The place and history is very impressive and therefore you must make the effort to take the climb on. I have read somebody saying this is an easy walk....take no notice it is not but worth the effort. An early morning visit is recommended to counteract both the weather and crowds. Wear a decent pair of shoes to help the walk and avoid the hangers on who want to help you up the numerous steps for money.....they back out when it gets difficult. The views are excellent and overall despite the effort well worth it.

This place could be really nice, but SL tourism decided to rip off foreign tourist. You will pay 30 USD to wait in line for a long time in full sunshine. The foreigner price is 75 times the local rate. This is very "reasonable" considering the fact that UNESCO and the Japanese Government paid for the restauration. After you climbed the scary rusty stairs you will find out it was for almost nothing. The place is nice and could have a good aura but the behavior and pricing of the locals make this magic disappear. Angkor Wat is 20 USD per day and plays in a slightly different league. Most of the ruins are in good condition and the settings could be really great. The whole UNESCO Thing went probably wrong and SL took it as a license for extortion. The way down is interesting, you are guided to a tourist carpark and have to do a gauntlet through a lot of vendors all selling the same "handmade" stuff done by their families. If you go, get a guidebook and visit the small museum at the entrance first. Bring lots if water.

We took this journey with a hide which I think is well worth it. It really adds to the climb when you know what you're looking at and what it means. The climb isn't difficult and I didn't feel unsafe at all as I had read in some other reviews. Highly recommend this if you're in Sri Lanka.

Lion rock is one of the highlights of Sri Lanka. We were advised to visit as early as possible to avoid the crowds as well as the heat. Having started our climb at 8am it was not really a too challenging climb and of course it was worth every drop of sweat.

This history of the site and the Rock is impressive in itself, but seeing it first hand is outstanding and breath taking.  I would suggest a visit to the WC and taking water with you before starting up the Rock. Part of the grounds have been restored and shows how the water features and fountains worked via water pressure.  Before starting the climb to the rock we saw monkeys who were quite tame and happy to entertain. The initial walk is on a metal elevation and then on to a spiral stair case which leads to paintings that have been preserved within a chamber of the Rock and show the original vibrant colours.  You walk down an adjacent spiral stair case leading to the mirrored wall.  Walking further to the lions claw before climbing up to the top of the Rock via a very narrow metal stair case. Once on the top of the Rock you could see for miles and it was well worth the trek up.  On top are foundations of the Winter Palace and with a guides help you can clearly see the palace layout. Coming back down was the most scary, if you are frightened of heights, as I am.  Which is a shame because everything is worth looking at.  I found people to be patient and understanding whilst I was walking down, slowly.  The whole climb up the rock is manageable if you take you time.  You do not have to be an Olympic athlete to do this.  There were people of all ages and different fitness levels and there are places to rest and catch your breath. It's one way in and one way out.  At the bottom of the Rock there were people selling trinkets, ice-creams etc and a snake charmer where you have the opportunity to hold the snake and have a photograph taken. All in all it was a wonderful experience and picture perfect.

One of best places I have ever been. It has amazing history and view over the surrounding countryside. Very hot though when we went. Go as early as you can, and wear good shoes as lots of rock cut steps.

Sigiriya was amazing but the thing I remember most 3 weeks after my visit is how it cost us more for two people than our entire day's budget for food, accommodation, etc. the price is outrageous but I guess the visitor does have the choice. The Sigiriya Rock itself is a brilliant visit; there's a lot to see around the rock, not just on it. The walk up is interesting and not as strenuous as some would have you believe. Just take your time... The cave paintings are marvellous and going up the spiral staircase is fun. The views are spectacular when it's clear, but we went up Pidurangala Rock the same day (yes, that's a bit masochistic) and found the views to be better than from Sigiriya. Sigiriya was enjoyable for its history and the climb itself. There are places I would return again and again and Sigiriya would be one of them if I could afford it. As it happens, once will have to be enough.

This is an excellent site with great views. Although expensive for what it is and probably not worth the $30 entrance fee. I do not like that there is a foreigners and locals entrance and separate prices for each. We had a guide take us up for 2000 rupees (£10) he then asked for a tip after the tour as well. He was informative and spoke a relatively good level of English. The climb to the top is 1203 steps. At the bottom there are ruins and very lovely gardens currently being excavated by archaeologists. I do not recommend this climb for the unhealthy, unfit, anyone with bad knees, heart/breathing problems, scared of heights, claustrophobic or children under 7. I'm not fit or healthy at all and I really struggled. The stairs up are either marble, sandstone or man made metal stairs. There are cramped rickety metal spiral staircases to walk up to the al fresco paintings. These are quite frightening and disorientating even for someone who does not have vertigo or claustrophobia. The metal stairs on the final bit of the climb are literally fastened to the side of the sheer rock face. They are slippy with sweat and sun cream and the whole experience of getting to the top was rather horrible. But then you're at the top. The views are stunning. The ruined temple is beautiful and interesting. Please note there is no where selling drinks or toilets at this site. Take water up with you. It took us 1h 30 to ascend and descend and I was proud of myself for completing it. On the way down the final steps end in a hoard of hawkers but there are people selling drinks and ice cream. There are a lot of monkeys and dogs at this site. Do not feed the monkeys. They get overly excited and jump on you for the food. This happened to a woman whilst we were there and it badly scratched her resulting in a trip to the hospital. Overall it is an ok excursion. I wouldn't really recommend it unless it's some you really want to see. There are other rocks to climb in the area with the same views and for free. This place has been highly over priced for what it is.

An amazing site however unfortunately we went over Chinese New Year, and even though we arrived by 8am there were so many tourists that it took two hours to get to the top. It really is spectacular, so hopefully you go at a better time of year! Make sure not to take photos of the frescos - the signage is not very noticeable and because of this the guards have to keep yelling at everyone to put their cameras down (and actually hit one person). Worth seeing if you're nearby in Sri Lanka.

Have a guide, it is extremely helpful especially if you are a history buff.  It is also helpful when walking up the rock.  It was not an easy climb, but it was definitely worthwhile.  The view is incredible and to view the layout of this palace that was once there is very impressive.
Every step you make climbing up the rock is worth it! Stunning views from the top and the sense of conquering the world once you reach the top :)

I was a bit apprehensive about climbing Sigiriya as I have arthritis in knees. Put on knee braces and took trekking poles and the adventure began. It was strenuous but as it was quite busy had lots of stops waiting for people to ascend/descend the steps, which was beneficial to most people. It took less time than I imagined to climb it and once there the views are amazing. The logistics of building such a magnificent palace at the top of this rock are beyond me! Wouldn't have wanted to be a hod carrier! A pleasant breeze and shady places to just enjoy the place and your achievement getting there. If you need help there a people situated at base of steps to drag/ push you if you're not too embarrassed at the thought! The gardens and museum make it an enjoyable experience which I would recommend to all.

Make sure you go early morning to avoid crowds / traffic going up and down. Not good climb for those who don't like heights or suffer vertigo but still worth going to see the surrounding grounds. Be careful of the huge wasps near the top of the fortress as they get angry with a lot of noise and can attack. The view from the top and the sights of the ancients ruins will leave you a little speechless.
Really enjoyed - highly recommend. Though, I'd recommend doing the climb in the afternoon (once the sun has gone down a little) as the walk can be strenuous at some parts.
Great experience, it is a must place To go in Sri Lanka. It is easy to climb for old and young people. When you arrive to the top the views are breathless. It is so interesting place to visit.
A wonderful rock and a great historic site. A fairly vigorous hike up the rock to see the fort built by King Kashyapa. Really enjoyed both the hike and the views.

We visited Sigiriya rock as part of our tour of Sri Lanka and it was one of the highlights. The natural rock formations and the rock carvings make it a truly magical place. The climb is hot and sweaty but the crowds mean that you move at a very manageable place. For anyone worried about whether they can manage the climb, if you can get to the mirrored wall, the rest of it is easier, can be done with as many breaks as you need and well worth it. Go for it!

We were told by a Sri Lankan friend that we had to visit Sigiriya no matter what,  so even though we weren't staying anywhere near it (in Kandy) we made a day trip out to see it. Best decision ever. It was so beautiful to walk around the gardens below the rock and even though there were loads of tourists and we had to line up to climb it, it was such a memorable experience. It reminded me a bit of Machu Picchu in Peru (but less exhausting to climb) because of the magnificent view from the top. It was really nice to see the frescoes on the rock wall as well. The way it is set up you have to go up a steep spiral staircase to see them then immediately go down another staircase. Most tourists only glanced at them before heading down the next staircase but they were actually quite beautiful to look at. I totally missed the mirror wall to be honest. I couldn't see anything. The stairs to the very top are a bit rickety and steep but you could hardly complain when you see how many young children,  elderly and even blind people were managing it. I didn't think the price was too much for how great this was.

Though quite expensive, it is definitely worth the money. Climb the rock as early as possible to avoid the heat and a cue to climb. Great views when climbing and standing on the top is just breathtaking. ! WATCH OUT for the people who hold your hand and want to help you climb the stairs, they will ask you money for it afterwards.

Wonderful culture mix: young woman was using an ancient tool to trim the edges of the paths, and looked much as though she would have done centuries ago.  Then she pulls an iPhone out of her pocket, makes a call then carries on.  You can see these gardens from the top of the rock and they are quite extensive.

The story of how the palace was built 300 metres up this rock which is vertical on all sides is amazing; then when the king dies his brother didn't fancy all those steps so abandoned it and the jungle took it back.  Rediscovered by a Brit in the 1860's and now deservedly a major tourist attraction.  The ascent is hard work but there is plenty of opportunity to rest.  To get to the cave paintings you climb 3 circles of a spiral staircase suspended over a huge drop, all very secure, and it is worth it.  It was crowded but that didn't seem to matter.  It was a staggering achievement to build it all.  The last ascent starts by a massive lion's paw which is all that is left of a 100 foot stone lion that guarded the final ascent.  DON'T MISS THIS unless you have very young children.

We could see the line of climbers circling to the top from afar. with a bit of dumb luck we took the wrong way up all the way at the start, we first saw the caves, the cobra rock and the King's court. You normally do that on the way back. Because most people come there later we had that part to our selves before we merged on the way up with all other tourists. It is worth both the climb as well as the slow moving crowd as is quite impressive. Our advise go at sunrise, in case you are a bit late like we take a right shortly before the climb and do the caves first.

The site is amazing enough and thereby has become a victim of its success. Despite arriving early morning, we were part of a massive crowd trying to make its way up narrow paths and spiral staircases. Of the main attraction, the rock paintings of the so-called Sigiriya damsels, only half a dozen are accessible, supervised by officious guards trying to keep people moving - understandably so. The water gardens at the foot of the rock are interesting and being carefully restored. However, the sum total of this site does not warrant the huge LKR4200 entrance fee.
Surrounded by gardens. An ancient setting for the looming Rock. It's over 1000 steps to the summit, but worth the climb, past old wall paintings up to the summit and its sweeping views.

The view from top is great, but not as a amazing as from pidurangala. Go early, very early, as it's overcrowded after 8am. Tourists trampling on the walls, jamming the stairs. If you're on a budget, instead of doing sigiriya do polonnaruwa (more interesting buildings!) and pidurangala (more amazing view, and the tranquility up there is lovely). It was very hard and sweaty, but absolutely worth it! The view was amazing. Loved the monkeys on the way up and the dogs. I would do it again. Must take water though!
sigiri paintings and the techlogy of the gardening and architecture is really unique

What an impressive site! and that is exactly what is need before you plan on visiting Sigiriya Rock! This a 200 meter high rock and sits in the middle of the cultural triangle. It is said to be the most visited tourist site in Sri Lanka and for good reason too. Almost all of Sri Lankan cultural spots are pretty expensive for foreign tourist, Sigiriya Rock being no exception. A one day entry ticket costs 4200 LKR. And as most other places in SL if you are from a SAARC country (such as India) you get a 50% discount. You need to show your passport for this. Therefore dont forget to carry it with you if you want to save some money. Its always a good idea to start for the rock as early as you can. I think it opens at 7 in the morning, but you double check on what the current schedules are. The reason for starting early are two fold. One since its a steep climb resulting in a good amount of exercise, its wiser to get through it before the sun becomes too hot. The other reason is that the final climb is through a narrow set of stairs which cater to both folks going up and coming back down. Hence you want to avoid as much of the oncoming traffic as possible. The rock compound is surrounded by a moat and lush green gardens. This is a good spot to click a picture with the rock as the background. A memory you will always cherish. Further on are the terraced gardens with stairs cut into them. The stairs are a bit steep, but nothing that you cant scamper up in your regular stride. Keep an eye out for the Grizzled Giant Squirrel that you will find lurking around in the trees nearby. These are not very shy and with some patience you should one of them clamber down the trunk allowing you a good look. For their size you would be surprised to see them jump coyly between trees. Its an amazing sight. Moving on you will arrive at the base of the Rock and this is where the climb gets a bit ferocious. But worry not, a bit short on breath you will arrive at a small landing where you can enjoy the view and click a few pictures. Next you move horizontally on a metal plank, along the side of the rock. Here a person will want to check your ticket (hope you have not thrown it away or left if with a friend who is left behind and refuses to climb any further :)) Once through, you reach the base of a narrow spiral metal staircase which goes up. It surrounded by metal meshing and the climb up is quite steep. There is a metal gate at the base of these stairs and you can see folks coming down on other side through a similar spiral staircase. But no you cannot go through the gate since its locked and you are forced to climb up, as tired as you already are. Up the stairs you go and reach a small cave and arent you glad of this extra climb you did. On the cave walls you can see paintings from the era gone by. Once you arrive back to the base of the stairs you move horizontally along the side of the rock. On your left is a wall which is called the mirrors wall. No its not empanelled with mirrors. Its highly glazed with mud (or something similar) and was supposed to be polished enough for people to see their images. I could hardly make out my profile in it, though. Now you reach a flight of stairs which take you to a compound which is called the Lion gate. You can see a gate like structure through which people can be seen making the final summit to the rock. On both sides of the gate are paw shaped structures. It was supposed to have a lion head very many years ago, which seems to have collapsed some time back. This is good place to take more picture, if you havent been taking any so far. Next you go through the lion gate for the final summit. The steps are steep and not for the faint hearted. Some portion of the climb is over metal stairs that have been bolted onto the rock side. They look rickety with people, who are coming back, too using them. But they hold steady and there is nothing to worry. Its an exhilarating feeling when you reach the top. It took about an hour or less. On the top you can see the foundation of a palace or a small citadel, if you might want to call it so. There are not structures or buildings, only the foundation is what is left. Awesome view on all sides. Enjoy them and click lot of pictures. You can see the  Buddha statue at Kimbissa temple in the distance. Climbing down as always is quicker, though you need to watch out for your steps on the steep metal stairs and give way to people climbing up. For foreign tourists the return parking is different from the place where you were dropped. There are a bunch of shops for buying curios. All in All - you cannot miss this place. You should be able to climb. Fitness is not a major issue. If its overcast, carry a raincoat, you will not find any places for shelter.

First off, the admission for foreigners at LKR3,900 (US$30) I would say is ABSOLUTELY "excessive" compared to US$20 for the Angkor temples in Cambodia (that is not just for Angkor Wat, but for all the Angkor temples in the area) and US$13 for Taj Mahal in India; so as wonderful as viewing & climbing this big rock was, I for one don't think the price was "justified"! In any case, I did thoroughly enjoy the "sights" along the path of the climb (about 45 minutes to an hour in all to the Summit from the bottom which itself takes about 5 to 10 minutes to get to from the ticket entrance) such as the "somewhat erotic" frescoes on the wall of the rock-side cave about halfway up the climb (about 20 minutes from the bottom to the cave), the long yellow 'Mirror Wall' (just below the cave after coming down the spiral stairs) which they probably call it as such because of its "reflecting ability" of sunlight (that I found out while on the pathway back to the ticket entrance after coming down from the Rock at sunset when I saw this "amazing glow" on the face of the Rock on the side where the mirror wall is), the two big "lion paws" just before the summit, and finally the ruins of the palace on the summit (only the basic foundation left, but the brick walls on the sides right below the palace grounds and the short stone stairways leading to & from the palace grounds are still in pretty good shapes, and what more there is like a square-shaped pond "full of water" on one side just shortly below the palace grounds which kind of made me wonder "how" there was water on top of a big rock); I was also delighted by the scene of luscious green forests around the Rock all the way until reaching the distant hills & mountains (and if you look carefully, you'll see a white standing Buddha statue in the forest some distance away from the Rock). The train ride from the Colombo Fort station (the "main station" for both trains & buses in Colombo) to Habarana takes about six and a half hours; upon arrival in Habarana, you could either just take a tuk tuk straight to the Rock for about LKR1,500 (US$12) or figure out some "creative" way (like I did: first a tuk tuk from the train station to the intersection in the city, then the bus from the city to the Sigiriya intersection where you'll see the little "lion paw" landmark, then another tuk tuk from that landmark to the Rock itself), but really you'll actually save only some 500 or 600 rupees (4 or 5 dollars) by not taking a tuk tuk straight from the train station (I also got "cheated" by the last tuk tuk driver who dropped me off at the beginning of the unpaved lane leading to the Rock instead of taking me all the way to the Rock, making me walk that last distance for about ten minutes to the Rock!) so I would suggest just taking a tuk tuk all the way from the Habarana station to the Rock. Also a word about Sri Lankan trains is that you may not get a seat in the class you pay for unless you get on at "end of line" stations; I had that "very unpleasant" experience on both my trips to Galle and here from Colombo (actually the problem was not when departing from Colombo since Colombo Fort is an "end of line" station, but on my return trips to Colombo since both Galle and Habarana are not "end of line" stations; had to ride Class 3 on the return from Galle when I had a Class 2 ticket, and had to STAND on the return from Habarana with no seat at all even in Class 3 when I had a Class 2 ticket!); it may have partly to do with the time being that of the Sri Lankan New Year, but still my experience gave me a "pretty low" opinion of Sri Lankan trains!

Yesterday at this time there were people everywhere and it took double this time, 4 hours. Sigiriya, unique landscape city, created in 5th century AD by King Kashyapa embracing a massive, 200m rock jutting out amongst the lush forest greenery and its surroundings with nature driven architecture composed of buildings, terraces, ponds, paintings and sculptures. There are more than 1000 hand written poems on the mirror wall written by visitors from 7-14 century. The UNESCO declared this a world heritage site in 1982. - The Lion Rock early morning  (very high climb) 1200 steps, 660feet, precarious, slippery in places, very high up on a granite outcrop which is climbed everyday by thousands of people. Near vertical walls and we reach the flat topped area where we had beautiful views of the surrounding country, close by pools and ancient walls of the old buildings that have long since gone. Only a few people when we got there but on our way down there were queues of people. I'm so glad I did this early morning as it would have been very unpleasant when the sun was out (we were in shade most of way up). We bought our ticket for LKR4200.
