This amazing rock can be seen way before you get to the site. Even from our guesthouse! Ans I imagine even from a different town! It's a fairly easy climb, even though it can be very hot. Try to go early morning or as late as possible. I think it closes entries at 5 pm... The climbing itself is fun though theres a ton of other people. The view from top is also worth.

3500 rupees to get near to this. We weren't  going to pay that as we weren't able to climb. Our driver took us to a spot where we could get photos. Very commercial. Silk  shop very expensive and not silk!

My wife and I went with a group to climb the rock. The advise from our tour guide to start early was excellent, as it was a tough climb. we were met by helpers which i tried to gently dis courage but every time i turned my back there was one or two trying to "help" my wife up the rock. I eventually became more insistent and told them where to go, but still had hands pushing different parts of our bodies. At the last staging platform (where the hornets are.. Luckily we didnt see any only the huge nests) the helpers tried to intimidate my wife into paying them. Luckily Im more intimidating and i refused to pay them for the harassment we received. i dont feel the experience is worth the exorbitant fee and its a tough climb. But it is something that has to be done if you go to Sri Lanka
Excellent, view from the top is amazing and the ancient village. not suited to the unfit or pushchairs.  crowd control badly needed some walkways were very over crowded and dangerous..

Great but a rip off for tourists. We almost decided not to bother when we got there and found out the price. Views from the top are amazing but the paintings were very disappointing after visiting other cheaper and better caves elsewhere.

Fantastic views from the top.  Go early 7 am to avoid the midday heat but it only takes about an hour to get to the top from the ticket booth.  My daughter is 7 years old and managed the steps with ease, although if you have a fear of heights you might find it a little daunting; some of the hand rails are rather low for adults.  It's so worth the effort.  The museum takes about 30 minutes to see everything but explains the history very well and is not to be missed.  Overall its a great morning's tour for all the family.  $30 each, children half price and you don't need a guide.
A bit like Uluru in Australia, just how do these extraordinary places appear. It's easy to see because of the natural things that happen on the planet, none the less, still amazing

Loved our visit to Sigiriya Rock. We went at the end of the afternoon when it wasn't so hot anymore and the site wasn't so busy. Great visit. Good to know: entry fees are steep and only cash USD or local currency are accepted. No credit cards.

It's a great place, not known in the occidental history books but remaining of a fantastic piece of history of the country. The frescos are unique and highly emotional if you think how old they are. The view from the top is fabulous. OF course you need to deserve it and take on your fear of crowd, bees attack and vertigo(last climb) to gain this extraordinary scenery. Dont miss it

Go early in the morning (7.30) to avoid heat, but most importantly queues of people. Leaving at this time meant we could enjoy the ascent and take out time. Once at the top, we had superb views of nearby mountainous regions and were able to peacefully walk around with few other people. The ascent itself does have a lot of stairs, but only took us 40 minutes to the top and it wasn't too taxing (I'm over 20 stone). The way down is a separate route, but we were amazed at the queues of people hiking up at around 9am. I think being caughtnim that would have been more frustrating, than fun.
Was a nice experience. There is a great story behind this giant. the most amazing part was the view from the top, gives you a feeling that you have never felt before.

I visited Sigiriya Rock first thing in the morning on the advice on my hotel owner. I arrived at 7am and got my ticket. There were no crowds and the climb up to the top was pretty stress free. There are a few open and spiral staircases and obviously, you are quite high up, so if you aren't good with heights, it is worth visiting earlier so you can take your time on the steps. The view from the top is amazing, well worth the climb. There was a small puppy who was suffering from mange at the bottom of the rock (by the audience hall), everyone seemed to be ignoring him (staff and other tourists). As an animal lover, I found it hard to leave him behind and not help him.

The Sigiriya rock is very popular among tourists andand locals alike, and they are right. It offers an amazing panoramic view of inside the culture triangle from all sides; unobstructed view for kilometres and kilometres. 1 tip is to leave very early. it opens at 0700. therefore you want to be at the top before 0830. as from 0900, it starts getting very crowded, and makes for less amazing photos.

Visited Sigiriya without a guide during the morning (from 9 am to 11 am) and there were already quite a lot of others which ment some queuing in the stairs. The climb itself is not hard and the views from the top are beautiful and the also the bottom water gardens and the lion's paws were captivating. I would recommend visiting the museum which  is close to the ticket booth before starting the trip to the rock itself. It is  very interesting with a good miniature of the Lion Rock and it's surroundings and pictures them as they have originally been. There are a lot people offering to act as guides and also people advertising for different products within the area itself which I found a bit irritating. On the way back you will not be going through the water gardens so be sure to take a lot of pictures from there on your way to the Rock :)

loved climbing up this majestic site. the view was amazing from top. go early to avoid the heat of the sun. bring water to keep yourself hydrated. elderly people not recommended due to the 1200 steps of climb.

A very, very nice place to visit but remember to do it in the morning or late afternoon due to the heat. There is alot of stairs, but unless you are in terrible form, it is absolutely doable - nothing like Lonely Planet depicts. I am a bit scared of heights. If you are also, here is a couple of things: 1) There is a spiral staircase about halfway. You do not need to go up there. It is "only" cave paintings but you will need to go down the same way. 2) It is only the last bit from the Lions gate stairs and up, which is freightening. The rest is broad stone steps with high stone railing set in the stone.

Absolutely loved the hike up those steps and stairs! The site is very interesting - get a guide (there are over 100 of them waiting at the main entrance), I rarely get one, but for this site I think it is worth it. There are so many things to look at and to take in, without a guide you will definitely miss out, specially on your first visit! The views when you get up are absolutely stunning. There was lots of wind on the day I was there. I went in the morning, around 10:30 - didn't think it was that hot, but am sure on a full sunshine day with no wind it gets burning - so don't forget your hat and your bottle of water! I loved the cave paintings and the mirror wall. Kasyapa, the king who selected this site for his residence has some great ideas, the urban planning is fantastic; and yes you have the feeling of being on the top of the world when looking out from the top.

We visited the rock early. We were offered breakfast after in our guesthouse but were glad to have eaten at 7am. The rock is a good climb and even in the early morning, the heat makes it tricky but its well worth it for the beautiful views and sense of achievement. The payment in is too expensive. End of! Would I recommend it? Absoloutly. Saw lots of tourists wearing jeans and long  trousers, not needed!!

We have visited Sigiriya World Heritage Site, surrounding environment was amazing and we enjoyed. People sell's local stuff for little bit cheaper or expensive. when your buying following product please careful.

Arrived early in the morning to avoid the hot sun and was wonderstruck by this great giant rock. Was an enjoyable walk up including some rickety stairs but was definitely worth it! The summit of the rock is quite a large area and we spent some time walking around enjoying the views.

Here I am panning a world heritage site, for shame, lol.  All I can say is don't go on a Sunday morning when there are so many people you are waiting in line to get up the rock. Personally I am not sure it was worth the nearly 4,000 rs to do it, though I'm sure some will disagree. But the view IS spectacular up top. And the climb is death defying in it's steepness (vertigo anyone?) and kind of cool. Also the pictures look cool. Probably I would have enjoyed it more if it wasn't so crowded and also if I had a guide to explain what i was seeing.

The climb to the top was not too tough, complete trip would take about 2-2.5 hours for an average person. Th view is great, reminiscent of western ghats in India but not as spectacular. The structure itself is remarkable and and the history behind the monastery. The fee for entering(about 40$ for foreigners) is too high and not worth the price. SAARC nations can avail a 50% discount at the counter on request.

If you're planning on Lion's Rock for the view, better save 3500 rupees and head for Pidurangala temple and Rock! The view was amazing, but the overall experience was way too touristic and crowded. Whereas the climb up on Pidurangala was an actual climb, and the view is just as amazing. Maybe even better as you can watch Lion's Rock!

We went to Sigiriya in late June 2015. We arrived about 7:30am and met up with a guide that had been arranged by our driver with Blue Lanka Tours. The guide had excellent knowledge of the whole site and its history including the gardens, the palace area and the pools. We took our time making it to the beginning of the climb. It was quite busy and very windy by the time we were half way up but it was really interesting to explore. The site is so open. It’s easy to touch artifacts and walk amongst the ruins. In so many places in the world you are not able to walk all over the site. The views from the top were amazing. We took a tour of the very small information centre/museum at the end which was included in the entrance fee.  We paid 3960SLR each to enter the site and 2000SLR for the guide. We spent about 4hrs there.

It was quite a hot day to climb but totally worth the pain! The view on the top was stunningly beautiful but since we didn't have a guide we did not learn much about the site. I don't know if it's always like that but we felt like most of the time guides just jabbe jabber around and don't really add value to the experience so we tried to go by ourselves and it was fine! We saw old people struggling to get on the top. Because of the heat I would definitly not recommend this place if you're having pain walking.

When you enter Sigiriya area (ticket counter), there is a museum. There is nothing. It is better to skip it and if you come in the morning, to go fast up (you can admire the gardens on the way back), otherwise you will have to wait for slow Chinese people on the stairs.

Wonderful historical site with stunning views when you finally get to the top!  But to do that, you need to be able to climb the 1200 steps, sometimes on rickety stairs, looking down from the edge of the rock!

This was not my first visit to this location. I visited over 20 years ago. The area has improved quiet a lot in regards to toilet facilities and safety. The area has been so nicely preserved and thankfully not commercialized. The view from the top was beautiful and exactly as I remembered viewing as a child. Tip to guests: Bring a few bottles of water for the climb...there are not facilites to purchase. The climb is worth it!

2 adults and an 8 year old boy, we set off at 7am sharp when the Park was just open to avoid crowds. Braving 1800 steep steps amidst strong winds and weak legs, we were the first ones to touch the summit of the legendary Rock that morning and the effort took about 30 minutes. The sense of achievement was complemented with 360degree stunning views. The ruins of the ancient palace are minimal but the scale and magnificence of the place was still palpable . On the way down, the winds felt even more frightening , and the descending journey was made worse by ever increasing ascending crowd. We reached the foot at 9am while the place was rapidly filling up. It was a defining experience for our Lankan trip!

This place should not be missed for its breathtaking view of the great rock. But the entrance fees is a bit too much, 30$, and 15$ for SAARC countries. The fees to be paid in LKR only. The climb is a little tough, but possible if you walk slowly. We had 70 year old people in uor group and they were able to climb. The view from top is awesome, and while climbing there will be gutsy winds. The government has preserved this site and made arrangements and maintained well. Good for photography.

The guides will swarm over you and my husband initially didn't want to be escorted around.  We knocked back several attempts to enlighten us but Sissy with his quiet and friendly demeanor won us over and he explained to us the history and significance of the Rock and what it means to local people now.

In 48 degc heat we climbed this massive monolithe. Beautiful views of the sourounding countryside. No wonder this was never conquered with its sheer walls. It was a great personnal acheivement to climb this and the highlight of the trip

We stayed at the heritance Kandalama which was not far from Sigiriya (We could see it from our room).  Although the 1222 steps, some uneven, I made it to the top with the help of our guide, with frequent stops on route!  We got there at 9am in the morning and it was not as hot as late in the day so a little easier to climb.  I am a  60+, slightly larger lady so I was pleased to say I made it all the way up and it was worth it to see the layout of the once grand palace, and views.

I knew it is must see but I was surprised with the history of the place during the visit. The ticket is around 30$ but it is worth it. Make sure you visit the museum first and get ready for your climbing experience. If you are fit, you need an hour time to reach the top without breaks.

I have hired the Sandy Land safari jeep during my vacation in Sri Lanka and I am really impressed about the carefulness and the adventure which we discovered in Minneriya National park in Sri Lanka. The jeep is ideally arranged for any adventure safari and also they know where are places with nice site seen and also where the animals gathering. Thank you Sandy Land Safari

15years since my last visit, Sigiriya was even better than I remembered. We hired an official guide to begin with, from the car park but he had on official guide badge, he was with every penny. He went and got us freezing cold water, and didn't try to overcharge us made sure the kids went to the loos, take your own loo roll. Once we set off he really paced the climb stopping regularly to give us lots of history, he helped the children and myself and protected us from a couple of "helpers" my little girl had a bad ear so he took us to the first aid post. It took us nearly 2hours to climb but he gave us so much information we hardly noticed the climb. At the top there were quite a few people who were very tired and hot who had obviously rushed up. Please please if you go make sure you climb right to the top because the views alone are stunning but the palace is spectacular, it is so easy to image king Karsapa lounging on his throne watching his concubines bathing and dancing. My favourite of the visit are still the cave paintings a must visit for any art lover.

There are a lot of rickety steps up a sheer rock face, so don't attempt this if you are afraid of heights! I was a little nervous but it was worth the effort, as the views from the top are spectacular!

Sigiriya is a must see for Sri Lanka, but feels more like a tourist trap than a National Treasure.  The climb and view are worth it, but this place is definitely a work in progress.  Was expecting more information during our walk/climb.  If we had a rupee for every time we got accosted by a local here, we'd have paid for our vacation.  Didn't see one official looking Sri Lankan except for the lady who collected our $30/person fee.  This is a theme across the island--bands of locals filling a national vacuum because the government isn't equipped nor concerned about its heritage.
Sigiriya is a must see if you visit Sri Lanka! Amazing views from up top. Quite interesting alternative theories about the significance of the place too if you keep your ears open...

It is a very nice place...especially if you reach the top. It's like you have seen what a beauty Sri Lanka have. With the breathtaking view. A must see in Sigiriya. Just make sure you will wear your comfortable cloth. No dresses and skirt please..

You'll enjoy it more if you are fit as it involves a lot of walking and also climbing up stairs. Two things that struck me were the warning against hornets (loud voices may provoke them) and very strong winds that could sway your steps. Once you huff and puff to the top, the view is absolutely beautiful and scenic, and you could imagine the vast palace ground in its heyday. There's hardly any shade at all, so apply a lot of sunblock. This is truly one of the top attractions in Sri Lanka!

We went late in the afternoon and thoroughly enjoyed the experience. Hired a guide, which was money very well spent.  His English was very good and without him we would have been walking around merely seeing things rather than hearing all the stories and history surrounding it all,  which was fascinating. Guide was min 2000rp and well worth it.

I visited in July and loved the site. The climb is quite intimidating but it's definitely worthwhile. Monsoon season actually has more to do with wind than with rain in this area of Sri Lanka and know that on some staircases towards the top of Lion's rock you will be pushed about by the wind in July. I was told it's even worse in August. On the flip side, you won't have to worry pretty much at all about mosquitos or hornets (which can be quite nasty in LK.) Overall the site is an incredible ruin and testament to an ancient exotic culture and world. Would highly recommend it.

It takes a little effort to get out to Sigiriya (it's about a 4.5-5 hour drive from Colombo right now due to road work) but it's definitely worth it. I was primarily interested in the rock fortress, but the gardens around the rock fortress are actually quite interesting as well. The views from the top are out of this world. Just know that this is a serious amount of stairs and climbing. Especially when you are on the original stairs - they are quite steep and you need to be reasonably fit to enjoy the attraction. I will say though that if you are afraid of heights, the staircases have all been nicely and securely enclosed and the groundskeepers have done a nice job of protecting the site and the tourists. The frescoes were by far my favorite - 2000 years old and still vivid and gorgeous. Would definitely recommend.

We had a wonderful guide/ranger called Neil to talk us through the entire visit. If you can arrange it, book this chap. We went at ~1pm which we were wary of but the temperature was completely bearable and most of the tour buses go for lunch at this time so the crowds were thin on the ground. It's really important to take a bottle of water(or 2) with you and a hat as you'll be exposed for 90% of the walk.

Sigiriya is best seen at the crack of dawn. We got up early and enjoyed and a driver took us in a tuk-tuk to the Ancient Palace. The park opens at 7am, so be the first in the short line to grab your tickets. The admission is a bit “self serve”. If I have any advice, it is to make sure you start your ascent within an hour; firstly to beat the heat and secondly to make sure you don’t have to share the views at the top with anyone else! The panoramic view spreads for kilometres and the breeze creates a deafening silence that you can’t help but enjoy. It all becomes quite clear why this was a sought after location to build a palace. This is prime real estate. Cole points out the best time to see Sigiriya Take your time at the top, wander around the ruins and take lots of photos - before you know it, the place fills up and the staircase back down to the bottom has a waiting time.

First thing to try when visiting Sri Lanka. Usually it opens at 7:30am but when we came there, they decided to open at 7am and you can already see a long line of tourists at the ticket booth. Can cover for 2 to 3 hrs back & forth. Go during the morning time as it can get too hot on the afternoon.

Rising out of the jungle this ancient wonder is on par with anything that ancient Egypt and other ancient archeological sites around the world have to offer.  From the mirrored wall rock face, to the UNESCO listed frecoes, to the gardens, pools and aquaducts, it still amazes me how they managed to do some of these things such a long time ago.  The view from the top is amazing - better still if you can afford it is to fly Cinnamon Air to Sigirya and catch a glimpse of its magnificence from the air.

Without doubt the most impressive site in Sri Lanka. Breathtaking views (and at 1200 steps a pretty breath-taking climb) that reward those brave enough to climb some pretty 'interesting' steps up the side of this monolith.  Make sure you take hat, water and your camera as you'll need all of them!

This is a UNESCO Heritage Site. I appreciated how they are able to preserve this. You need to climb flights of stairs that are steep so be careful. Better to be there earlier as it won't be too hot and not too many tourists yet. Or else it will be crowded and you'll be stuck in the stairs waiting for the long queue.

We went to sigiriya and had a good time. The site was amazing and the weather that day was beautiful. The unesco site is definitely worth visiting. But plan to have more time there. Perhaps a short picnic at the top would have been lovely There a big crowd and there was some queue cutting. Perhaps the authorities may want to look into this. We had a German family cut in from of us after we had waited for 40 mins. It definitely left us unhappy.

Sigirya is a must do in Sri Lanka, it is an amazing geological formation, has amazing rock art and significant culture significance, plus great views from the top, however it is very overpriced, hope the money is going to preservation of this and other less visited attractions in the region.
A definite must for your trip to Sri Lanka. Outstanding views and an amazing story behind all the ruins as well.

Impressive site which is well run (unfortunately not always the case in Sri Lankan tourist destinations). Even if you are scared of heights it is worth doing. The steps are safe and there is always a hand rail. There are also self appointed people, who for a small fee, will encourage you to go further.  A guide is really a complete waste of time and money in our opinion as they just want you to go up to the top asap so they can get back to make more money. Also we heard that if you stay longer then they demand more money from you. The paintings are beautiful. They are well conserved and quite bright. As the area with the paintings is quite away from the main path and up a spiral staircase you feel like you get quite a bit of space with the paintings which is good. The top is impressive with great photo opportunities of the surrounding countryside. One tip is to do the museum at the end rather than at the beginning since it is best to get up to the top before it gets mad busy.

Sigiriya rock nowadays really depends on the ancient 'legends', it is a place where only tourists go, you will not see Sri Lankan citizens (expect for the ones that sell you souvenirs). In my opinion the place is really overpriced (25 USD!!). The rock is nice to climb, the views are good and the environment is clean, but it is really not worth 25 USD (compared to The Grand Canyon which is 15 USD, or Amsterdams Anne Frank House 10,30 USD). If you go, go early in the morning (7am)! It is not too hot to climb then and you won't melt at the top. Later in the morning busses with tourists arrive and there will be a traffic jam going up the stairs. You might consider going to Pidurangala Rock in stead. It is just next Sigiriya, has the same view (plus a nice view of Sigiriya rock), and is not expensive (yet).

Definately go early and wear comfy sandals or shoes. The view at the top is fantastic. Lots of steps and very steep iron staircase for the final part- not for the faint hearted or those with heart or lung problems

It is quite far to reach to the top but it really worth it, the view is amazing. The history is really interesting. So many good spot to take picture. This is the best place i've ever visited here in Srilanka. You should go there early in the morning to avoid the crowd. And be careful with the big chipmunks, he bites for sure :)
This was one of the highlight of our trip last year to lanka....weather was nice and views from top great....take a bottle of water...

It was a very sweaty 1202 steps to the top, but it was worth it. I nearly bottled it as I'm not good with exposed heights. I started the final assent at the mouth of the lion and after a few steps I turned back. Someone on the way down told me that after the first section it's not as steep and the up and down lines run on separate steps. This was enough to convince me. Oddly, I found coming down much easier and not as scary. The history of the area, as well as the view from the top, makes it worth a visit. There are porters available to help you make it to the top. My father-in-law (78) used one to help him make it, which he did. He tipped the porter Rs1000 at the end.

An iconic Sri Lankan monument that is a must see when in Sri Lanka.  Climbing the Rock is mandatory...the rock is covered in art on the way up and the history is an astonishing chapter in Sri Lankan history so make sure your guide tells you the story. The view from the top is spectacular and worth the climb.  Get there super early as it can be a very warm climb.

Our family were a little daunted by the 1200 steps but like everyone else this was not as difficult as it first appeared. We thoroughly enjoyed our visit, did not use a guide but simply visited the museum and then made our own way, viewing the fresco's, gardens and finally the amazing view and landmark at the top. A must visit

This is well worth the long walk and hike up to the very top. The views are amazing and the experience is a lot of fun. Make sure to visit the museum (included in the ticket price) just to better appreciate what it is you are about to see (in terms of the historical background). A must see on a trip through the "Cultural Triangle" in central Sri Lanka. ^_^

This is a hard excercise in work out . The climb and the fee to go there are steep . But , worth it . The view and the experience after reach it makes it worth .People with the knee problem are advised not to try . Perhaps , stay aound at the ground .

The whole area has been upgraded since last time I visited and would recommend people to visit The rock climb is a must and the ladders/steps are much safer now than 10 years ago when I last climbed it!! The rock paintings are still as clear as they were then. Watch out for the locals offering you a helping hand all the way to the top and back down again. The initial request can be quite high!!! Great views from the top and the history of the place makes good reading.
Despite queuing to climb the rock in both direction, it was still very special site to visit. Recommend visiting the site in the morning to avoid the queues and hot weather.

We were a little taken back on getting to the ticket office and forking over $30 for entry, this is disproportionate to the cost of travelling in Sri Lanka but it was worth it. We were amongst the first few to be heading up the rock in the morning as we arrived very early to avoid the heat as much as possible. The steps were hard work for some but it can be taken easily in short bursts and rests, we saw many elderly people making the stairs look easy, though not recommended for anyone who is very afraid of heights or vertigo, at points there is metal stairs that some would be uncomfortable using. The main reason to visit is the views, once up you don't want to come down! it is a full 360 of the horizon with such greenery. Make sure you go early and drink plenty of water

We went off season so it was not that busy and there were no queues. It took us about 45mins to get to the very top and it's worth it. The views are unbelievable! It is a long hard walk up the steps but you definitely have to do it. Beware of the wind at the top so hold onto your hats! Also wear trainers or comfortable walking shoes it's much easier! So glad I read earlier reviews advising the same!! It's really hot at the top so take enough water too!
A must do. Even though it may be pricy, consider it a must. The view is stunning. Make sure you do it late in the day.

Worth going to see, quite amazing, dont miss it!!! Taking one star off because of the entry cost, why are they gouging tourists in sri lanka, they should have student pricing. Locals only pay 50 rupees? And foreigners pay 3990?? What a rip off, even india doesnt rip you off to see something far more spectacular at only13us dollars fpr taj mahal for god sakes. Even temples in cambodia are 60  us dollars for a three day pass!!!

We climbed lion rock in the afternoon and took around an hour and a half to do. The views were amazing and was defiantly worth the climb up! The steps are steep when going and can be a little slippy so be careful!

We went here on the same day as Dambulla cavetempels because its not far. We started at sigiriya, so it wasnt to busy at the stairs. Its relativly expensive, ignore the people that want to be your guide, lonely planet told us all we wanted to know. We climbed halfway to the frescoes of the naked ladies. They were so nice. Our legs hurted because of climbing adams peak so we didnt go to the top. There were little monkeys around the rock. Its a nice attraction, there are annoying people that want to sell you things, but overall we liked it.

I've been so very fortunate to have climbed Sigiriya twice now and each time it has been a thrilling experience.  Make sure you go early though as it does get quite hot once the afternoon rolls around.  The climb is not very difficult however, comfortable walking shoes, sunhat and plenty of water is a must.  The best way to tackle this climb is to have a private guide (which you can organise through your tour guide or at the gates) and that way you will get a comprehensive history of this magnificent site.  Be prepared to see some amazing views whilst climbing and once you get to the  frescoes take a moment to soak in the rich history and beauty that has been lovingly preserved here.  There are numerous photo opportunities along the way and make sure you stand on that last step at the top once you get there.  Truly an experience not to be missed!

We climbed the rock early in the morning before it was too busy to enjoy, or too hot! That had been good advice. It was not as difficult as we had expected. I was really amazed at how much remained of the site. There is no shelter up there and the foundations and the brickwork was in a reasonable state of preservation. The views were magnificent. We could see great distances in all directions. It was wonderful to view the site below us and marvel at the clarity of those ancient ruins. As we were descending the rock there were loads of people coming up. We had been lucky to had enjoyed this impressive  structure with only a few other visitors. Loved it.

Sigiriya is basically the remains of a complex of two highly fortified palaces in the jungle. One at ground level, and one on top of a 200 meter high natural rock. It is a Unesco world heritage site, and it is clear to see why: a world class ancient ruin complex, and a majestic natural setting. After the ticket stalls, there is a museum, which provides good context and introduction to the site, and will make it easier to imagine what the ruins would have looked like in their original state. Although you can visit the complex by yourself, we really enjoyed having a (pre-arranged) guide, who could point out the details and generally bring the ruins to life. The guide also helped us avoid the many salesmen and 'guides' who sell their souvenirs and services at inflated prices and distracting from the experience. After the lush lower gardens, the steps begin, and about halfway there is a spiral staircase to an alcove with vivid frescoes - definitely go see these. Then you pass a wall called the mirror wall which has ancient graffiti (probably more interesting for scientists than tourists) and climb up to a flat area where you can rest. The remainder of the climb is up a steep metal staircase attached to the rock, which is definitely not recommended if you have a fear of heights. Heavy winds make this climb a thrill worthy of any amusement park. The view at the top is magnificent. We went late afternoon, and it was not busy. The afternoon light was wonderful. Looking around the ruins it was not difficult to imagine why a 5th century king would have chosen this site - especially if you have staff available to bring everything up the rock. Practical tips: - we recommend to prearrange a guide - this will avoid lengthy negotiations and the potentially disappointing experience of having paid too much for a bad guide. - take plenty of water. The climb is strenuous and even without this effort you would need to drink a lot in the summer heat - take at least 4 hours - go early morning or late afternoon - the heat is less and the light is much better for enjoying the view and for taking pictures

I would recommend this for afternoon, because of stunning photo you want have from approach to this site and you want sun to shine on this rock place. Be prepared to walt a lot and climbing a lots of stairs in very hot weather. This trip has lke 3-5 levels (bottom with terrace gardens and gates, lower middle with cave paitings, middle with torso of lion statue, and upper palace with amazing view around with almost fairytale mountaing in far far away and nice green plains around. Take a sun protect creme with you, more bottles of water, good shoes (but it is doable in slippers). Entrance fee is 3500 LKR (30USD). Beware of fake helpers during your visit - they will try to help you with hands to stairs, try to guide you etc .... they will ask for money after it! Also beverages are very expensive here (200LKR for coke etc.). There will be many sellers with every kind of crap (tourist stuff) you do not need: masks, coconuts staues, beads etc.

Our visit to Sri Lanka was centred around visiting the Lions Rock - it's an awe inspiring place. The sheer size of this place takes your breath away. It's important to cover up as you'll be climbing stairs to the top - fully exposed to the sun. If you're not a climber - then try to get to half way point - views are still amazing.  But if like me, the only thing that mattered was getting to the top! Then once their - you can find a shady spot and really take time to enjoy the magnificent views. Absolutely worth every step!
it was hard to walk up to the top but the views at the top are magnificent! Strong and warm wind at the top...feel so good!

Sigiriya Rock is an amazing place in the Sri Lankan history. This place was chosen by King Kasyapa, more the 1600 years ago, to be he’s capital. He build the palace on the top and also made the gardens in front of the rock. The most amazing thing it that during his reign (and years after) the rock was painted white. And his artists painted amazing frescoes of his beautiful wives all around the rock. Some of the frescoes are still visible, they are amazing well preserved and beautiful to see. These are the world famous “cloud girls”. Another interesting aspect is that Siriya Rock has been a hot spot for hundreds of years. Archaeologist found small statues of “cloud-girls”, hundreds of years old and they believe that this are souvenirs for visiting tourists. On top you have a great view of the surrounding area. The surrounding of the rock is very beautiful anyway, take your time to walk around and enjoy the nature. The museum is not that great but it offers a lot of information about the rock. So just visit it to learn more of the history, you already paid for it. In some seasons there is a small risk of bee attacks. They have hiding places and doctors on site. But if you allergic to bees, please get some information about the risks per season. In the high season it can be crowded, best to go in the early morning (also better temperature). Must see in Sri Lanka!

initially we were in 2 minds to  visit this place as the entrance fee is 2000 lkr for indian nationals per person.  the rock is around 6000 stepz but it doesnt feel a huge climb. more important the way to reach the cave and then the rock was amazing. must must visit for all visiting sigriya
Indeed the 8th Wonder of the world is in Sri Lanka which an every tourist must visit and climb  the historic and heritage site. Beauty and Breathtaking
The walk up to the Lion Rock is quite strenuous involving many hundred steps. However we managed it and the view at the top was outstanding.

The gardens and the climb up to the rock is basically it. If you have come this far, it would be mad not to climb up the stairs, see the wall paintings halfway and continue to the top. It is less daunting than it appears to be at first. It's amusing to see monkeys retrieving plastic bottles from the bins, biting a hole in the bottom and sucking out the dregs. Soft drinks are their favorite, they don't care for water much. Just like humans, they shouldn't, but it is amusing all the same. They ought to station a sweeper up there to keep the place tidy, though. There's quite a bit of garbage. Monkey-proof litter bins would kill two birds with one stone.

The rockalready looks amazing in the flat surroundings. However, once you have begun to climb up is when you really get struck. After conquerring the 'please do not break down while i'm on it'-staircase you arrive at the amazing wall paintings. Then you walk up even further, to eventually end up climbing yet another flight of scary stairs. But, all that aside (i'm confident it is all safe and sound), the view on top is awesome ans sigiriya is a must see. Go early to avoid large crowds and the simmering heat of day

This was probably my favorite thing to see in Sri Lanka. The rock fortress is magnificent and has great views of the surrounding areas. However, even with hundreds of school kids slowing us down, it took us less than 3 hours to "see" everything, including the museum (which was a bit disappointing). It's doable as an independent travel day trip from Kandy by public transport. Would not recommend staying there overnight, unless one is also visiting surrounding temples and Badulla. Also, the weather was extremely hot except for when it rained for 15 minutes. And the rain came down super hard, so bring an umbrella.
Put on your foot a tennis shoes because you will walk for more than 1000 stairs up to the top of the hill. its worth it

this is a marvelous site. it is just an incredible achievement to be able to make that huge rock into a living "castle". On the other hand, it must also tell you that paranoia is not a modern disease! the walk up the steps make this a high activity site. But it is manageable, there were SL ladies in their 60's walking up barefoot!! Definitely worth the climb. the views at the top are stunning!! be aware that there will be touts in the site that will "insist" on guiding you. you can refuse firmly. there are also men who hang around and try to "help" u up the lower steps. ladies beware.

We went towards the end of June in the afternoon to catch the sunset.  It was a great time to climb, not too crowded at all and the late afternoon light made our photos look amazing.  The view from the top is stunning.  We stayed up the top for a long time, just resting and gazing at the view.  There was a stiff breeze blowing which made the climb more pleasant temperature-wise.  The climb up to the frescos up a spiral staircase was fairly hairy but well worth it.  The frescos came out well in photos too.  We loved the green vegetation at the foot of the rock and took time to wander round the ruined foundations down there too.  A bizarre site was the snake charmer at the foot of the rock who was playing to his cobra while sitting on a box containing a massive python.  We weren't bothered by anyone hassling us really, we just had an amazing time.  Visit this place, I would suggest in the afternoon for a more relaxed experience.  We got there at 3.45pm and there was plenty of time to climb up and down again before dark.   Amazing place and a must see if you are in Sri Lanka.

What a wonderful World Heritage Site!! The climb is a little tough but the historic relevance, the remaining frescoes, the landscape and the Citadel are worth climbing. Make sure to hire a local guide to hear all the details and historic facts. Porters are helpful but make sure you agree on a specific fee before starting to climb.
Just the fact that this is a World Heritage Site is a reason to make the climb. Beautiful views and magnificent history

When you travel Sri Lanka don't forget to visit this awesome amazing world heritage. Superb creative structure who made by king Kashyapa (477-495 AD) it is most valuable historical monuments of Sri Lanka.
Brilliant in its size and landscape. The climb is hard and not for those afraid of heights. Take plenty of water and avoid the 'helpers'

A huge citadel built on top of an immense rock.... loved it!  The walk up is challenging, but achievable... at least if you want to get to the Lions Paw Terrace, which in itself affords amazing views.  Above the Terrace, the walk to the Citadel is not for the faint hearted, or those scared of heights, but if you're up to it .... I recommend you go for it!

Sigirya’s Lion Rock is one of the Sri Lanka’s premier attractions and an ascent leaves lasting memories to rival any other. It can easily be reached from Polonnaruwa or Dambulla if you are staying in either but to avoid the crowds, the heat and to enjoy an early morning view of the rock as it rises above the surrounding landscape it’s a good idea to stay in Sigirya itself if only for a night. The closest town is Habarana on the main bus route to and from Kandy making it easy to reach with a tuk tuk from there to Sigirya being a good option. If travelling by train some guidebooks name Habarana as the closest station - this is wrong, Habarana itself doesn’t have a railway station. The closest to Sigirya and the one you should ask for is Pelugaswewa though if you pay for or reserve a seat at a main station like Colombo Fort and ask for Habarana they will almost certainly give you a ticket to Pelugaswewa. Incidentally, if you are travelling direct from Colombo Fort there are only two trains each day at the time of writing, the better choice being the 6:05 train to Batticaloa (it usually leaves from platform 4) rather than the night mail train leaving after 9pm for the six and half hour journey. If you miss this you can head to the nearby Mawatha bus station where the number 48 will take you fairly close as it heads to Polonnaruwa. If you do take the train to Pelugaswewa you should bear in mind that the station is quite isolated. If you have booked accommodation in Sigirya ask them whether you can be picked up and failing that your best option is to walk to the main road, turning left out of the station, to catch a passing tuk tuk. Closer to the station you might be asked for 2,000 rupees for the journey while on the main road 1,500 is more typical. You may be able to bargain but your options are limited with just a couple of small roadside stores in sight. The site itself extends around the very obvious Lion Rock with the only entrance being on the East side. It opens at 8:30am and is open until 5:30 pm with a fairly high admission charge to foreign tourists of $30 for adults (children being half price). It’s not a religious site so skirts and shorts are acceptable and you will benefit from both sensible footwear and a hat - there is no cover on the summit. With over 1,200 steps to the top of the 200m, high rock it’s also a good idea to take water with you. The Rock lies fairly centrally in a roughly rectangular moated complex roughly 900 by 800m in extent so you should allow at least half a day for a full visit. For those fit enough that leaves more than enough time to walk or ride across to the neighbouring Pidurangala rock, climbing to the top for its amazing viewpoint. On arrival you will find a number of potential guides keen to offer their services for a fee. The advantage of a good guide is the better understanding of the site the guide will give you and the knowledge that you are unlikely to leave having missed something noteworthy. The disadvantage is the loss of control, in that your guide is likely to choose the route you take around the site and the slower pace as your guide stops to explain various points of interest. The latter may not initially seem to be a problem, but perhaps the best idea if visiting early in the morning is to ignore the remains in the grounds and head straight for the rock. You can always return to these afterwards and finish at the Museum while making the ascent your first priority helps to avoid the crowds that pick up quickly during the morning as well as the midday heat. We did this and we were glad we did, but as we headed for the Lion Rock we passed several small groups, couples and a couple of families who were stopped by some feature or other with their guide. The climb up has a number of places where you can stop for few minutes to take a breather and starts with a succession of stone or concrete steps. There are two caged spiral steel staircases at one point that go straight up the cliff face (one for ascending visitors the other for those descending) a couple of flat gangways traversing the face of the rock and in the final stages a series of steel staircases bolted to the rock face above the surviving paws of the ‘lion’ that gave the rock it’s title. These zig zag their way up the rock face to the ruins of the palace on the summit. If you feel tired or a little nervous as you make your way up this last part of the route take a moment to notice the myriad of shallow rock cut steps and footings of long vanished stairways in the cliff face that marked the ancient path to the top and think about the effort it took to create them and the head for heights those who used them must have had. If you make your way over to Pidurangala Rock and have a good zoom lens or binoculars the sight of people making their way up and down and the traces of those earlier ‘steps’ is a very memorable sight. One other point to note is the risk from bees I saw noted on several websites and in some reviews before we visited. There are signs requesting visitors to keep noise levels low because of a risk posed by hornets nesting on the site but when we visited there was no sign of them. It may be that there has been a problem in the past but by the time we reached the bottom again and the way up was crowded with people many of whom were very audible there was still no problem. It would be a pity to be deterred by reviews to the contrary and I have little doubt that if the problem does recur staff on site will be warning visitors of it. I won’t go into detail about what you can see because there is a great deal of information and imagery available on the internet but among points of special note are the fifth century semi-naked women that make up the Apsara Paintings. The indications are that these are but a small part of what were originally an expansive gallery of painted figures. You will see these at the head of the spiral staircase in an overhang in the rock that forms a sort of natural landing. Curiously there is no prohibition on photography of the original paintings, but if you make your way over to the museum where the overhang and its paintings are replicated photography is not allowed! A number of other paintings can be seen in rock shelters around the foot of the rock, such as that close to the so-called ‘Cobra Head’ Rock, but none are as well preserved or extensive. Another famous but less visually impressive feature is the ‘Mirror Wall’ that you will pass on the way up to the paintings. This almost looks like a modern plastered construction but is another historic part of the site and bears ‘graffiti’ for which it is well known dating from around the sixth century onwards. This has a simple rope barrier to help protect the ancient verses and sundry comments that are now barely visible for the most part across its surface. Sadly that hasn’t prevented more recent visitors from adding their own and here and there these are more obvious evidence of the passage of visitors with no respect for the site or the cultural heritage of the Sri Lankan people. The best stop for a breather and a drink of water is the large open area where once a giant brick built lion stood guard over the final ascent to the palace, the steps climbing up through his mouth – it must have looked stunning. Today all that remains are his giant stone paws, a favourite spot for photographs and posing tourists. If you want to have any real chance of taking a picture of your loved one standing beside the lion’s paws without others intruding you will have to get here within the first hour or so after the site opens. Taking in the expanding views across the tree covered plains below as you climb on from this point the way is at first a steep series of steps followed by a series of gentler zig zagging steel staircases that look more precarious than they clearly are. These eventually emerge to face old brickwork and a few last steps, this is the start of the palace complex formed of a series of brick walled terraces and walls with incredible views across the surrounding landscape though there are no surviving structure you can walk into. There are also no shops or vendors here and shelter from the sun is limited so you may be grateful for that hat you carried up and the water you still have with you. The return trip initially involves descending against the flow if people coming up, but once below the level of the lion’s paws your route takes a different path down. If you make a mental note on the way up of where the path across to the Cobra Head Rock is you will find it easier to locate on the way down as the route naturally leads you towards the car park. At this stage though, having been to the summit before it filled with visitors you can take your time to explore these features, the remains of the various water gardens and the boulder garden. Here and there you will see more apparent steps cut into boulders and rock faces. Not all of these were steps, many were the footings for structures that were built on them – a practice that can be seen elsewhere as on the rock outcrops near Gal Vihara at Polonnaruwa. Passing over the inner moat on your way to the site entrance you can bear left to the museum. In all honesty, having paid $30 to enter the site it felt like little more than a money making exercise to then ask for an additional $5 to enter the museum! Nevertheless, if you do you will find a modern structure with remains from here and elsewhere along with some reconstructions. There is a clear route to be followed through the museum and in this sense it was well designed, but there probably isn’t enough to merit the charge unless you have a particular interest, especially after the wonders you’ve just seen and photography is banned. We found no souvenirs on sale in the museum itself though to the left on leaving there is a small shop not associated with the museum that had a couple of simple guidebooks and tourist items. Another, closer to the museum entrance, was the official shop with more expensive souvenirs and slender guidebooks in different languages. If you plan to visit The Lion Rock during your visit to the island though you would be well advised to keep your eyes open for guide books earlier in your trip. We found some that were more details, better illustrated and cheaper – why they are not on sale at the site itself is slightly puzzling. In fact we found a better one at the airport heading home than we managed to buy at the site itself. One last point worth noting is that the crossroads by the inner moat is also the best place to find a tuk tuk that will take you North to Pidurangala Rock if you want to attempt it, or you can walk it taking a fairly clear route along dirt roads that initially follow the line of the moat. It’s a little under 2km in total and admission once there is 500 rupees. The climb is rougher over mainly rough stone steps and with a scramble in the final stage to reach the summit. It has a reclining Buddha in a rock overhang below the top that was apparently once the largest such figure in the world.  If you feel fit enough to manage it after the Lion Rock I would recommend it – the two complement each other and the views of the Lion Rock are magnificent. To sum up, if you want to get the best from a visit to The Lion Rock and have the time to enjoy it I would recommend staying in Sigirya itself if only for a night. Aim to get to the entrance as early as possible taking water, a hat and at least $35 per adult to cover admission charges. Wear sensible footwear if you want the climb to feel a little less precarious and don’t worry about reviews suggesting bees or hornets are a real threat. Head for the rock first while you still feel fresh and before both crowds and the heat build up, leaving the gardens and other points of interest for the trip down and if you can, fit in an ascent of the neighbouring Pidurangala Rock. We very much enjoyed our visit and we hope you do too and that in some small way this review is of help. Have fun and make memories.

Citadel of Sigiriya is an UNESCO World Heritage sight and well worth the travel time. We went in the off-season so it was very quiet and nearly empty. Although a very warm day, we took our time walking and climbing to the top of the citadel. We hired a guide for the walk - he was quite knowledgeable about the history of the site; you might be able to do some research ahead of time and feel equally prepared, however, he could answer all kinds of questions, so its worth the extra money. The sight itself is just stunning. Over 1,500 years old, the site begins below with the outer moat and then an inner moat. From an ancient catapult to a dancing hall, ancient graffiti, and natural thrones, Sigiriya is intriguing, magical, place. The view from the top is reason enough to make the climb. The climb itself can be challenging in parts. The original steps (white marble!) can be narrow and varying in depth, and the "newer" steps are iron attached to the rock. I'm sure it's safe but it was a little scary going up and down..especially if you're intimidated by heights. Nonetheless, make the climb!! You will never find another place like Lion's Rock.

Having read the past accounts of visitors to the place I must say we were expecting the climb up a lot tougher, we were even thinking we'd be lucky to get to Lion rock and back, and probably it would be better to conserve energy for the climb to the summit and pass the steep vertical staircase section going upto the frescoes. However, we took our time going up - pausing every now and then (not looking at the watch at all), and pretty soon we were at the top! We even saw the marvellous frescoes too. Being mid-day there weren't many people going up and very few people at the top. We managed the climb up in a just under an hour, stayed up for some 20 mins before going down again which took around 40 mins.Overall the total time spent from the time of purchase of tickets to the walk back to the car park was just around 2 hours. Entry fees : Rs. 3,900 per person ($30), or if you are from a SAARC country (India/etc), you pay Rs.1,950 ($15). Recommendations: Must carry water, comfortable loose clothing that offers protection from the sun, cap or hat, good walking shoes, camera, cap or hat. Maintain silence, hornets are known to attack now and then. While you may not get stung if lucky - it will take a considerable more time for the coast to clear and you are able to climb again. Stop as many times as you want, take pics while you are getting your breathe back and enjoy the superb views all around and pretty soon you will find yourself climbing the last few steps to the stop. The view from the top is awesome and the feeling that comes from the realization that you made it will overcome any tiredness you feel! Going down is quicker, the foreign tourist car park is closer to the base of the rock than the other (main park). Here's an approximate idea of the time required: Climb to the Mirror Wall (20-25 minutes) Climb to the Sigiriya Frescoes (3-5 minutes) Climb to Summit and Sky Palace (20-25 minutes) Decent from Sigiriya Rock (20-30 minutes) Overall, strenous but not tough. If rain is forecast unless you like getting wet, carry protection, there is no shelter on the route at all, except for one or two places. Last entry is at 5 pm.

Definitely worth doing if you are in Sri Lanka, although you wouldn't plan a trip just to see it as per Borobudur or Angkor Wat. Everyone's advice is to start early, but unless you are staying close (and we weren't) then you will end up being there during the heat of the day. It's certainly hot, but not unbearable (we live in Malaysia so we found it quite comfortable, but if you are not used to humidity then it will feel somewhat sticky). We had a guide (we paid him Rp 2000, which seemed to be the going rate when we asked around before going) and arranged that before we went. But you could certainly do the visit on your own: it's obvious where to go - the only two things to note route-wise is that you go up and then back down the spiral staircase to see the frescos and when you come back down from the top you follow the signs to the tourist car park (which is off to the left when you reach the bottom and was pretty well signed) if you are travelling in a car, because that is where your driver will park. The good news is that the tourist car park is much closer to the rock than the main car park, which is where you enter the site. I suspect that starting in the middle of the day means fewer people: despite it being a national holiday we didn't feel that it was overcrowded. Is a guide worth it? If you are not on a budget then I'd say yes: they can show you some interesting things that you'd otherwise probably miss (the old water fountain features, aspects of the frescos such as the fact that all the faces are different and there are some errors etc.), you do have peace of mind that you are headed the right way and we certainly didn't get hassled by anyone else. Things to bring: hat, sunscreen, comfortable footwear (someone's flip flop came off on the staircase and tumbled a hundred feet below), plenty of water. I also stuck a change of shirt in my bag and felt much more comfortable swapping into that before getting back in the car. The climb looks more daunting than it is - unless you are afraid of heights or very much out of shape then it's nothing to be daunted by (there are plenty of old folk, young children etc. who make it up without a problem). The pace of the climb is a leisurely one and if there are people on the staircases then you are going at the pace of the slowest, which might seem a little frustrating but in fact means that you should not be out of breath. Nice views at the top - don't forget to go up that last step on the top! Not quite sure what to say about the hornets: you can see the nests 20-30m off to the side of the last staircase but despite plenty of noise from the people on the rock there was no problem and the guide seemed relaxed about them. I think that you'd be most unlucky if they were a problem. We combined the climb with a visit to Dambulla in the morning and then three hours elephant watching at Hurulu Eco Park in the late afternoon...a full day out of Kandy but a rewarding one.

We went to this site early in the morning, around 9 and hired a guide, Nilan - he was knowledgable, stopped at various points to allow us to take photos, and was mindful that the heat was not necessarily something we were used to. We reached the lion terrace then went on to the top. It is really worth the effort  with the terraces and bases of the buildings still intact. The view is spectacular.  If you like birds, watch out for the Peregrines that roost in the rock face!

He was very informative and was also of help in knowing where best to rest up in the long climb to the top of the Sigiriya Rock Fortress. I cannot deny that the climb to the top, given the heat and humidity, was hard going at times but the views at the top of the ruins of the summer palace and the surrounding countryside will live long in the memory. Spectacular place. It is really suitable to name as the 8th wonder of the world. It should be so, It is really wonderful and amazing.

We were a little shocked about the cost of the entrance tickets! However, the trek to the top of the Lion Rock was amazing. Wear comfortable shoes, carry an umbrella or wear a raincoat, carry insect repellent spray (I'll tell you why, in a while), carry water and some snacks, and carry a hiking stick, if necessary. Keep your backpack light. If you have altitude issues, remember that you will have to climb almost vertical stairs; be prepared. After a walk through the gardens, we started our climb slow and steady; rain had made the walk-path and stairs slippery. As we climbed, rain water flowed down on us. The greenery was fantastic. At one point, the stairs became narrow; was used for both ascending and descending. Half-way up the path were the Lion Paw/Gate and the mirror wall with its frescoes. The paintings are beautiful. Be careful while climbing the last bit of the rock; the wind can be harsh, as you ascend. The top of the rock has ruins of the King's palace. The view from the top is breath-taking. Walk around the entire site to get good views; exercise caution when at edge. This place has several birds, and is definitely great for bird-watching on a sunny day. We spotted a Serpent Crested Eagle, sitting undisturbed on a tree. While being absorbed in the beauty of Sigiriya Lion Rock, please be aware and cautious about wasps/hornets that can get disturbed and attack severely. This is when the insect repellent spray can come handy! If you are near the shelters that are built, please enter the shelters; allow others also to stay safe. Tip: Good to carry an umbrella or raincoat. "Noise may provoke hornet attacks"; keep an insect repellent spray. No water or food available at the top of the rock; carry water/food. On a rainy day, watch your step on the slippery stairs. Give way to others.

What a sensational experience !  Walk through the gardens appreciating the complex layout with the majestic Rock shining in the sun above. The height may seem daunting standing at the bottom but a steady pace is all that is needed if you are reasonably fit. Good idea to sit at the Lion Paws and have a good drink of water before the majority of the climb. The frescoes where outstanding in clarity and unlike any other I have seen in Sri Lanka. Reaching the top, the 360 degree views are breathtaking of the surrounding countryside, gardens below and the white Buddas in the distance. But the most amazing is the remnants of the citadel and how it is constructed on top of this rock so long ago. An engineering and human feat. I spent at least half an hour at the top to explore and  absorb the views.  As others have commented, I would also recommend take lots of water and a snack, wear lace up shoes for support and stability to climb up the many steps, have both hands free to use railings for safety , use sunscreen and wear a hat as it is exposed for almost the entire climb. Also note there is no toilets. It is not possible to stop in many places on the climb as the width of the stairway is narrow and many people are moving in both directions. I found the climb exhilarating and a truly memorable experience and a highlight of the many  archeological wonders in Sri Lanka.
don't forget a bottle of cool water.  Even on a very hot day this is still worth visiting.  Sadly enough, as for most cultural sites in Sri Lanka for Western tourists : it is overpriced.

The excursion starts with a walk in the gardens, it very peaceful and beautiful. After a 10 min walk, you start to climb the stairs for around 1h. Most of the path is in the shadow, but plan to wear a hat as the summit is on the sun. No need to tell you that you will need a lot of water on your way to the top.. The view is just amazing, a great experience! You will take a different path to the bottom that will last around 30 min. There is a museum that you can do, but once again, we went straight back to our hotel to have a refreshing swim before to check out at noon and heading to other activities

We would recommend spending your time walking around the rock and surrounding areas. This is a must if you are in the are, we couldn't recommend this more during a visit to Sri Lanka!

Our tour guide Karnal De Silva picked us up from Colombo airport, and after a 7 hour flight from Beijing, we were told we will have to do a hike. But the surprise was yet to come. When we arrived after a couple hour drive, we looked up the rock and he pointed to it and said "yeah... you're going up there". Wow. It looked high - very high. ~ 2,222 steps. As he walked us to the foot of the rock, he gave us an overview of the magnificent history of the rock, and the palace that once existed atop. The hike might sound bad to some who are out of shape, but it can't be missed. There are a ton of excellent viewpoints all over, and particularly interesting are the lion's feet near the top. What really boggles your mind as you walk up, is how they carved the steps from the rock. The entire journey lasted ~ 3 hours, and on the way down, we were treated to a python and cobra show. Very interesting. Remember to bring lots of water and snacks! I couldn't see any bathrooms but you will likely sweat out all the liquids from your body anyway. Sigiriya Rock was a great recommendation from our wonderful guide, and a start of an unforgettable 10-day journey.

Tips from a Sigiriya conqueror: 1. Bring a walking stick, drinking water, a towel or wet ones and if you must, a camera in a knapsack to leave your hands free for support and balance; 2. Wear light clothing and comfy sports shoes (or you'll be stripping down to your undies like a French girl did this morning... Talk about French lace!); 3. Go early in the morning, say by 8 a.m., because there isn't much shade up top; 4. Clear bladder and bowels before ascending as there are no toilets up top; 5. Walk with an equally fit (or unfit) partner, angling your feet sideways as you navigate the stairs (no Charlie Chaplin-ing, please) - the company will be good as you urge each other up and up and up; 6. Smile your tiredness away, tell yourself "Love the Rock" and know you'll never be younger than you are right now; 7. Tell everyone you meet who looks defeated, "You can do it", give lots of thumbs ups; 8. Don't concentrate on just climbing - look at the Rock and feel its magnificence, it'll be here even after we are worm-food; 9. Look out for the 3 white Buddha statues dotting the landscape below; 10. Know that the walk down is an easier route and don't be surprised when you start thinking of ways to make the next climb less painful.

Nice and interesting place. Next time I would not bother with the guide - he may knew a lot but we could not understand him. Later we found out that some other friends had the same experience. Or before taking the guide test him if you understand him

Sigiriya Rock is totally worth the climb. Not only for the breathtaking views and the history of the palace involved, but also for your personal achievement. It's not easy to climb all the stairs in the humid heat, but you feel so proud once when you have reached the top. I climbed with my 2 children (12 and 16) and they also liked the challenge!

If you are anywhere near this Lion Rock or even not near this Lion Rock, this is a must visit. The whole cultural experience is surreal and the hike up to the summit of the rock is not difficult for the average person. In just one hour or less, you'll see one of the most amazing breathtaking views in the entire world. Sigiriya is a UNESCO listed World Heritage Site for a reason and the only reason you need to go out of your way to make this a must see/must visit.
Tough climb, and a little nerve racking being so high but well worth it when you reach the top and take in the breath taking views

We visited early morning to beat the crowds. I'm not great with heights but the climb was fine for me. Leave time to take pictures and take a seat and enjoy the magnificent view for a while. We didn't have a guide but found the guide books & Google covered what we needed.

Yeah I climbed all 1200 steps and more.... So worth it! The view was lovely from the top and I've got some great potential FB profile pics! Lot's of tourists but definitely worth a visit here. Was slightly surprised but how expensive it was to get in but it is a world heritage site. The museum was very empty at the beginning but got more interesting the further in you get. Definitely visit here if you are in the area as it really is quite something at the top and even on the way up to the top!
the place is worth to see but does not worth the entry ticket. you can alternately visit his twin rock located 10min away by walk and which is free

an excellent climb, with a stunning view at the top. at this time of the year there was no obvious wasp movements despite the scary signs! it was very interesting and beautiful place. well worth the climb!
A nice peaceful walk around the garden areas before one climbs Lion's Rock. In excellent condition, frescos. Breathtaking views from the top.

Sigiriya is one of the most impressive ancient complexes I've ever seen. The wonderfully thought-through system of the aqueducts, pools, passages, decorations, and stone carving left me in awe of the abilities of local people more than 15 hundred years ago. And the speed with which the place is said to have been built is absolutely astonishing. Leave enough time to walk at the lower level, climb up the rock (may become quite a hard climb, given the blazing sun), marvel the pictures on the rock, and take lots of pictures. I don't recommend combining Sigiriya and Polonnaruwa on the same day, as most of the tourist routes and guides suggest - you'll have to rush either one or another, while both deserve a good long time to explore. Also, be sure to either use the service of the guides, or do your homework and read the place's history and legends beforehand, so that you know what to look for. And do bring plenty of water, since the climb is quite tiresome and its very hot during daytime. The entrance fee is USD30, plus the guides ask the same sum or more, but the place's worth it.

A Must See - make sure you get a competent guide to explain the features of this amazing place that was so far ahead of its time.  If you can climb the rock but take your time and be careful of the small steps which can become slippery when wet.  There are at least two staging areas on the way up where you can transfer to the. "down" stairs but try to make it to the Lions feet if you can

Even in the pouring rain, climbing up Sigiriya was worth it. If it's raining when you go, don't turn back. Keep going. It was still very much worth it. The amazing achievements of the people who carved the rock, built the citadel and lived there 1500 years ago are astonishing! It's worth visiting the museum first to understand better. Don't bother with a guide if you're unsure. I got all my information in the guide book. My 5 year old daughter made it to the top on her own. Just take it easy.

If you are visiting Sri Lanka, seeing Sigiriya is a must. Visiting the place and imagining what this would have been 1500 years ago would definitely leave you amazed. To avoid the heat, it is better to climb up early in the morning. Ticket counters open at 7am. Tickets costs USD30( LKR3900). SAARC country visitors get a 50% off. Do carry your passport to get the benefit. It is better to climb the rock straightaway and go to the top and see other attractions like the gardens, after coming down. That will help you be at the top, before the crowd and the temperature increases. During your climb you will first see the frescos ( whatever is left). Once you come down the spiral staircase after seeing the frescos, you will see the mirror wall. The size of the wall, the shining surface and the fact that this was built 1500 years back impresses you. However what is written on the wall may looks like graffiti to a layman. Before you take the final climb to the top, you can see the Lion paws and the shoulder. Though the final climb may seem difficult, it is not that difficult and you are bound to lose some spectacular views and the remains of the palace, if you choose not to climb. If you have a fear of height, just focus on the steps and keep going up. At the top, in addition to the remains of the building, you can see the pond and the throne. When you come down the rock, take time to enjoy the boulder garden, cobra hood cave, Octagonal pond, Water gardens and how the rock was fortified with the multiple walls and moat. Do visit the Museum since that does give a glimpse of Sri Lankan history and of Sigiriya. One of the short videos give you a feel of how Sigiriya would have looked like at its prime. Museum ticket is included in the main ticket. Please note is that, in case you are proceeding to foreign tourists car park while coming down, you will not be able to see the gardens or the museum. You can keep your footwear on, at Sigiriya. Do carry enough water. Do plan around 3 hours or more for the visit.

Sigiriya Rock Fortress is a architectural marvel indeed. Its hard to believe that a big palace existed on top. The water pumping system built during ancient time is nothing but a wonder.  The view from the top are breath taking Well you need to climb up to see this. So be ready for a 3 hour climb. Do take a guide else we might not be able to understand the importance of this place. Rates are negotiable. Visitors from SAARC get 50% discount on tickets. Although its highly priced, its worth it.

If you love hiking, Sigiriya is a must in your itinerary. Its a steep climb to the top from the Lion Rock Try to reach as early as possible to beat the heat. Hire a guide who can explain you in detail about Sigiriya. Its amazing and truelly deserves to be on the World Heritage Site list of UNESCO. Carry plenty of water and be careful with the monkeys.
Wonderful cave paintings and an amazing view if you make it to the top. 1202 steps!

It is vey hard to contemplate how a whole community lived up on the top of this steep rock citadel 1500 years ago. There was the king, his harem, swimming pool, throne room, all hundreds of feet straight up. There were remains of painting on the walls, also from that time.

This being the start of our trip we were excited to climb up the 2000 steps not knowing how steep they were at times. With temperatures soaring to 35deg it started getting more difficult and finally when we reached the top it was only to see the ruins of the palace which were hardly any left. They should put up cable cars for all types of visitors old and young can go there

It is one of the highlight of the journey.  Climbing the lion rock is a challenge.  It was very hot when we visited there .  There is no place to buy bottled water.  So everybody was drinking a tap water from a dark black water tank.   If you have issue with that, be sure to carry 2 big bottles of water!  One run out too quickly.

The wall frescos are amazing. Try & reach in the early evening hours as the sun is very strong till about 4pm. However tickets & entry close by 5PM so reach before that. SAARC country residents get a 50% discounted ticket. It is good long walk 7 climb so wear sensible shoes & carry water. Monkeys are there so be careful with food.
You have to be sporty to do this! The paintings in the cave are beautiful. The landscape at the top is amazing
Stunning site to visit. The climb is steep but can be done in phases. Get on site as early as possible before it gets too hot and too crowded

A magnificent rock that although is challenging to climb is certainly worth it. The sheer history and geography makes if special and the views at the top are amazing. We climbed it as an older couple, avoided all the 'helpful' guides wishing to help us along the way, hoping for sizeable tips and made it readily. We took breaks along the way to catch our breath. There are strong guide rails to help support the climber as the steeper parts are accessed. Some of the steps are quite steep and one of our party is afraid of heights, but still made it. It is recommended that the heat of the day is avoided. We started our climb at 3pm and it was quite hot and humid then. Early morning or late afternoon are the best times. Bottles of water should be carried and a camera ensures the magnificent sights can be catpured.

This rock is an amazing testament to the ancient history of the area. 2 hours minimum is needed to both climb the rock and take in much of the archeological remains etc. Although it is a reasonably expensive place to visit, it means the site can be preserved for centuries to come. We did not use a guide but were then approached at a number of intervals to use one whilst at the rock, but still declined. Be aware that 'guides' also try to help you physically up many of the steps and hope to get sizeable tips for helping you. Avoid them as although there are many steps it is 'doable'. The views from the top are amazing.

As long as you can handle stairs, this climb is not difficult but there are a lot of stairs. Bring your own water and some time to rest along the way and enjoy each level. If heights are a problem you can easily get to the Lion's feet without any crazy drop-offs and the view is stunning from there as well. Well worth the climb, even more so if you like to explore ruins.

Well worth a visit - very impressive. I was a bit worried by reports of thousands of steep stairs and heights - as I'm not great with heights. I think if it rained it would make the steps slippy but it was a beautiful day when we went. Neither of us is in the best of fitness but we had no problem at all with the steps and I even made it the whole way to the top across the slightly scary iron staircase stuck onto the rock!
