This is a 200 meters high rock fortress constrcuted in 5th century AD. Located 300 meters above the sea level and  175 kilometers away from Colombo. If you visiting Sri Lanka then this is a must see place and should be in your must do list.It will cost 30 US dollar per person for entrance ticket. You can see amazing Sri Lankan engineering skills in 5th century AD when go on main entrance which is western gate. You can see water garden, boulder garden, terrace garden, paintings, mirror wall with graffiti and then finally to top. Best time to go is 7.30Am or 8am.you can kill the heat and avoid caught up with wasps or bees(Some times).

I managed to get to the Lions Paw but couldn't face the final steps to the very top. My husband went all the way with our guide.  I'm over 70 and suffer with arthritis and asthma so I found the climb hard but take your time and it's fine. The reason I didn't make the final stage was due to the "open" staircase. I have a fear of heights and regrettably I just couldn't do it.  It is a must see place but definitely go early morning as we did, much quieter.

OK, so this is a world heritage site - and rightly so. Sigiriya is breathtaking - its sheer size, the scale of the associated construction works, the landscaping and the ecological ingenuity (really smart water conservation 1000+ years ago), together with ornamental gardens, swimming pools, fountains and the fortifications make this absolutely awe-inspiring.  The views from the top make the climb (around 1200 steps) worthwhile.  Don't miss out on the slight detour to see the frescoes.  There are plenty of resting points available en route to the top, so don't be put off by the prospect of the climb.
Fantastic place, but beware huge crowds (particularly Chinese) and queues after 8.30am and very nasty hornet attacks which have hospitalised people regularly.

Really is well worth the effort to climb to the top. Fabulous views and our guide was excellent (Worth paying the extra for a local who knows the history and also can assist you when you are struggling on some of the more strenuous parts of the path up) Be sure to watch out for the hornets nests half way up as many tourists have been badly bitten

Such an amazing place - it was a beautiful place to walk through and I really enjoyed it. You could see the ancient ruins still and it made me feel a little bit like Indiana Jones, wandering through the ruins. The gardens are beautiful and very peaceful to walk through, providing some much needed shade. The garden pools are still working and continues to be fed by underwater conduits. You have to climb up a lot of stairs all the way to the top but it is well worth the climb. It is quite a long climb so be sure to wear some walking shoes - do not do it in flip flops like I did! My calves were aching the next day!! Once you are at the top you have such great views of the surrounding area - makes you wonder how they managed to build all of this thousands of years ago. We arrived late afternoon, around 3pm so the crowds were pretty thin there - we didn't really have any issues with queueing.or massive crowds.
Do not go to Sri Lanka without having been on the top of The Lion Rock. Unfortunately many seems to have this opinion and the queue was a bit long, but is is worth it.

See my other reviews as the come on line Like the cave temples I would definately recommend a guide and there are lots waiting in the carpark area, these are all official guides. This was one of my highlights of historic sites in Sri lanka. Like many sites this is not a place to visit if you have access issues, there are a lot of steps. The architecture design of this place is just absolutely incredible such engineering so long ago. One tip though get your ticket back from the guide, we forgot and they would have made a nice keepsake
We used one of the local guides which must be recommended. The place was a bit crowded. Don't buy anything!

We were on a guided tour and our guide helped us negotiate the crowds on the platform/steps.  Lovely place but maybe some control could be exercised over visitor numbers at pinch points. Historically fascinating, beautiful views, and an exhilarating climb.  The top of the rock was totally different to what we expected, like a mini Machu Picchu, Beware hornet hazard near the top.  Lots of warnings about this and signs asked visitors to be quiet, unfortunately, some visitors get very exited and loud.

Climb is pretty easy due to stairs. Local guy told us to go there first thing in the morning - really good advice. We were almost alone at the top and we loved the place. Saw a ton of people queueing up during our descent around 9 am. So grateful we got up early. Admission was almost 4.000 rupees. Pretty steep for Sri Lanka but totally worth it.

I really don't know how one can compare Sigiriya and Pidurangala. Yes, the price of Sigiriya is higher, but except the rock as itself, a wonderful archeological site is included. It is well maintained and still being restored (I felt I gave money for good thing). Sights were amazing. We recommend to go as soon as possible - Sigiriya opens at 7 am - definitely the best time to visit, to avoid queues and high temperatures. One of the TOPs in Sri Lanka!

Well worth a visit to the top, if you can make it. Frankly, some tourists we saw were kidding themselves, one very large lady with child on back looked like she was about to pass out half way up, much to the concern of my husband! But anybody with a reasonable level of fitness can easily do this - and there are always locals to help you for a fee! We had to queue for a while to see the murals, which are beautiful and a must see. After that, plain sailing to the top, great views, interesting, and not a hornet in sight (at least not when we were there, unlike the day before..........the trick is to avoid noisy crowds of tourists apparently. Stick with the quiet ones!). Very large queues had formed on the stairs by the time we were leaving...and was getting very hot.. Ps I was here 33 years ago. More developed on top and at least there are now railings, not just footholds in the rocks!

Breathtaking views from the top. A long slow climb up to the top but worth every step. Got there mid day - so hottest part of day - but this meant we managed to avoid most of the morning crowds - we saw them coming down as we started to ascend. There is a risk of hornet attacks - which will mean they close the steps - and do not get a refund - again avoid the crowds and less chance of being impacted. Do not forget to check out the museum at start (near car park) to get an idea of what the fortress is all about. Loads of monkeys around the Lions paw.
absolutely a must to visit! note that entrance fee is an unbelievable 30.00 usd (my stay in dambulla for 3 nights was less)

It's massive, impressive - and usually very crowded. If you're fit and determined then by all means make the long and arduous climb. I salute you. But if you're a senior citizen like me, not too steady on your pins (like my friend) or have small children (like some other visitors) you can just stroll through the gardens, admire the view and see the cave paintings in reproduction in the small museum which also gives you an insight into the history of the site. You're on holiday - so do what you want to do.

We visited Sigiriya with its Rock Fortress, Lion Rock. The grounds are beautiful with helpful explanation plates to each area. Its an energetic climb up to the top of the rock with a stop on the way to see the Heavenly Maiden frescos. Well worth the effort.

Undoubtedly the best time to climb is the moment to doors open. It is far less crowded at 7.15 when I started to climb. The steps are steep and on occasion uneven so wear suitable climbing shoes. The only downside to an early morning climb is that the views from the top can be a bit misty/cloudy so one does not get full advantage of  the panorama of the surrounding countryside. Upon descending, I realised just how valuable the early start had been. There were hoardes of tourists lining up to attempt the climb and many were going to be obstacles.

Alas, humanity sometimes degrades or destroys the very objects it deems desirable. Imagine 1000 sweaty tourists crammed together cheek by jowl -- this is no exaggeration -- waiting in a queue for over one hour in the hot sun, trying to simultaneously climb the very narrow stairways up to the summit. Most give up halfway at the "Lions Paw" terrace. What should be a wonderful experience with great views is more or less ruined when other peoples' sweat rubs off on your shoulder and arms; when the staff rush the herd along and allow only two minutes   to view the ancient frescoes. And all this after paying entrance fees that exceed the already high price to view Italian and French museums and monuments. The whole experience is very sad. It is sadder than the crowds on a sunny summer's day at St, Mark's square in Venice. One may grumble at the extortionate ticket price to see the Last Supper in Milan -- but at least they then give one 10 brief minutes of relative peace to view the art.
Yes, there are a few stairs but we went there with kids age 2, 4, 5 and 7 and they all did it Story of the place is interesting and the view is really nice

We heading out early for this landmark and we were glad we did; even arriving at 9am meant we only just missed the queues to get up! Saying this however, the main queue was to the wall paintings (up the spiral staircases), which you can miss out if you are more interested in just getting to the top! We were a little nervous about getting up as it looked fairly rickety, however were felt very safe. It takes about 30 minutes to get up with no queues and we loved spending time looking at the views and striking our yoga poses for a good picture! There are guides at the top who will take your photo and tell you about the history of the palace. Beware, this does come at a price - they go in high but seemed fairly happy with our hugely reduced offering! It costs a fair whack to go up (£15), at least in relation to the cost of living, but it was definitely worth it.

Sigiriya is worth visiting for the views and the landmark itself. Getting to the top is really enjoyable and the ruins are great. The big problem with this place is the crowds. Luckily we got there early enough to avoid the worst of the tourists, but it was still bad. I won't specifically call them out, but one countries tourists in particular were very poorly behaved. They were jumping ahead in line and creating a lot of noise and disruption. If you go, you will know who I'm referring to. Again, get there as early as possible, scale the rock quickly and enjoy the sights, then get out.
it took us 4 hours to see the whole place including the museum. Plus the line was very long. Kind of scary at certain points. It is at half price for SAARC country citizens.

Arrived at about 9.30am but the place was already packed. A slow ascent but well worth it as a truly stunning site and breathtaking views. Climbed with a 7 & 10 year old and they had no issues at all. A uniquely memorable experience.

Read a lot of the reviews and was a bit concerned about hornets but we did not see one. Thought the entrance fee was a bit steep but after we had been there we were impressed at how well kept the site was so feel it was value for money.

660 feet high rock is a majestic sight. Famous for best Water/Boulder/Terrace gardens, Mirror wall & Frescos. Site plan is a unique one. King Kasyapa build Sigiriya city during 477 - 495 CE. Best time to climb Sigiriya is morning. Must see Sigiriya museum before explore the rock. Museum alone is LKR.600 and if you buy Entrance ticket for LKR.3950 then you can visit Museum also FOC. Pidurangala is another nearby place you must see. Small amount charge as Entrance fee and also can find local guide to show you the way to the summit.

The museum was very good and the grounds beautiful but we came to climb the Rock. We joined a massive queue on a set of steps and inched along in very humid weather. After 40 minutes we had made some progress but were not even on the rock yet. Would have taken an hour just to get to the bottom of the spiral staircase. We went back down different steps and it seemed guides were bringing people up those steps to join the queue ahead of everybody else. Might explain why we queued so long but we paid 30 dollars each for the privilege of lining up. Even at that point the views were beautiful, and we met an iguana on our way back down!

We expected quite a lot, but considering places in India and china, this was not so impressive, and the high entrance fees raise false expectations. there are views from the top - but all Sri-Lanka is beautiful views. best seen from the bottom! and it is not that necessary to enter.

We arrived about mid-afternoon, only to find that the site had been closed beyond a certain point because of hornet attacks.  Some young travellers were upset because they were told they could not get a refund - and the cost is relatively high. As we were staying in the area for the night we decided to come back in the morning, which we did quite early.  The ancient grounds and gardens leading to the rock itself are quite magnificent and very well maintained.  They have a similar feel to some of the sites around Anchor Wat in Cambodia.   You then begin the climb to the rock.  If you do not have a head for heights this can be challenging, but it is worth the effort.  The ancient frescoes in the long gallery are particularly beautiful.  You then make your way to the "Lion's Paws", and begin the climb to the summit - past the hornet nests.  On top the ruins are well preserved and the view is truly wonderful.  I can safely say that I haven't come across anything quite like the rock-top fortress in all my travels.  Definitely well worth a visit.
breathtaking views from the Rock! very nice hike with the kids. it's just beautiful. we found monkeys everywhere. great experience

Why this is not up there with one of the world great wonder's I never know. 1st,when we arrived you are met by local's offering to assist you up rock ok if you need I little help .they doing it for tip (can't blame then) 2nd(the climb) you do not have to be an Olympic athlete .because the guide stop's on a few time's to give you the history on some of the painting's on the rock .our guide took his time because our group consisted of all age's .3rd ( Man and women made structure's) will have you thinking how on earth did they do them on a place like this .4th(the view) better than any man made structure on earth .eg millennium eye . Just breathtaking 360 degree angle . Nearly forgot you walk up one way and down another .so there is no standing for other's to pass

We had trepidations as we had read the various TA reviews about cost of entrance fee etc.  We had already climbed Pidurangala Rock, so we had something to compare it with.  We arrived early but it was still busy, but not overly so.  We weren't hassled by any guides because we had a Sri Lankan guy with us.  The entrance fee is 30$ but covers museum entrance, fardens and the frescoes.  The rock is awesome from below and the entrance.  The gardens are well manicured and very pretty. The walk up the rock is hard and strenuous, some steps are small, some are deep, some stone and others metal.  Some do not have handrails and you are passing people going up and coming down etc.  Your pace can be set by who is in front of you, and how fit they are, which can be a godsend or frustrating depending you your own fitness levels.  We got to the top by about 8:30am, on a partly cloudy morning and i was 'glowing' by the time we reached it, so do take water and think about a hat. The frescoes of buxom ladies were very good, still very colourful and easy to see, not behind glass.  Signs clearly say no flash photography but lots of morons chose to ignore this, or can't read!!  Access is by sprial staircase which was entertaining at times. The mirror wall was disappointing. The Lions Paws on first viewing were a little underwhelming.  I think because you see them in so many photos, expectations are high.  Also, everyone stands in front of them to get a photo (us included), which detracts a little from them. The climb up is well worth it.  The views are excellent and the ruins on the top are very interesting esp the Kings Chair and the swimming pool.  The climb down was a little scary in places.  Again, Cobras Cave at the bottom, a little underwhelming.  We went to the museum at the end of the day, and it was okay. Overall, our memories are:  awesome, unique, good VFM for European tourists, Huge, spend 4 hours + there easily.  It could be a challenge if you are not too mobile or are afraid of heights. We did both rocks and both were completely different experiences.  Would definitely recommend and would have regretted it if we hadn't climbed it.  You also get a free DVD with entrance fee.

I can only say that Sigiriya has it's own magic and impressed us with it hugeness, exceptional nature viewes and a big quantity of monkeys. We have made a photo with buddist monks on the top of Sigiriya Rock, very close to the sky which has increased our impression.

The climb up even in the early morning was quite heavy going, but not so bad that I needed the local man to push me up using his hands on my backside! I told him rather quickly that he wasn't required for me! The stairs are steep but once at the top it is stunning.

This was a great morning!  We had a very good local guide who made the place come alive in terms of the history, the walk, the structures, and the plants and animals on the site. The climb is well worth it as the view is incredible.  Kids liked it all especially the various animals they saw (monkeys, snakes, crocs, lizards, etc.).  After we went on an elephant ride near by. My advice is don't do this. It's unique and interesting but leaves you very uncomfortable on the condition of the animal.
We arrived at 8.30am and already there were big crowds, but it was a weekend. It was absolutely worth going, not only to see the beautiful frescoes but to look down on the area from such a height.

Now 3950 RS (Feb 2015) this is very expensive. Perhaps a passport ticket to this, the Dambulla caves and the two ancient cities would be a consideration for the tourist authorities. The rock is a s steep climb and not for the faint-hearted. Worth it for the view from the top, but not for the rather uninteresting ruins. The frescos are interesting. The mirror wall would benefit from having a bit restored so you get an idea of what it must have once looked like.

I start this review with the caveat that the attraction of Sigiriya depends almost entirely on how much you like archaeological sites. Personally, I don't love them, so my review is a bit coloured on that basis. The museum and the gardens constitute the best part of the site. The museum is well laid-out and just the right size for a crash course in Sigiriya's history and significance. The gardens are also pleasant, giving a real insight into what the site once was. When you go to climb the rock, however, you join a lengthy queue slowly snaking its way up slightly rickety spiral staircases. The queue is a bit chaotic and queue-jumping is rife, which can be frustrating after an hour in the sun. At the top of the rock, there's little left bar the foundations of the monastery. The views are good but not great, and there is little shade. Unlike sites with more complete ruins (such as Polonnaruwa), it's quite hard to see the majesty of the site in its glory days. I don't have any complaints about the price, which I think is fair for a world heritage site. I simply felt underwhelmed by the whole experience.

The views from the very top of the rock are stunning! Completely out of this world. Take water and make sure you wear sensible shoes. I read some review saying you didn't need to go to the top... I totally disagree. Only go if you plan to climb to the very top!

Loved this one!! Got there early (opens at 7) and beat the crowds and worst of the heat. A great workout getting to the top, but the views are well worth the effort. Dodge the 'guides' you don't need them.
This is a spectacular place and not to be missed. A superb World Heritage site. Take your time climbing up, keep quiet to avoid wasp attacks, enjoy the view and marvel at the construction.
Don't forget your water and beware of all those steps if at all unfit!  Guide explained everything well, a truly amazing place, a real feat of human endurance, all for one king.

very interesting museum though absence of air conditioning during our visit made it a somewhat sweaty experience The translations of the ancient graffiti are a must and quite amusing.I did not climb the rock on this visit having done so previously.The lions rock and cliff paintings are stunning and worth the effort. the ruins on the top are frankly disappointing and unless lucky the view may be shrouded in mist. MAJOR WARNING there is a sign at the entrance to the site warning that if attacked by bees to stay still and silent.The information we were given was that these bees are in fact hornets/ wasps and the day before our visit a group of chinese tourists had been attacked and so severely stung (their guide even more so) that they had to be taken to hospital. it is therefore important to listen what your guide tells you about how to minimise the risk

if you are afraid of heights as I am, head there early in the morning when the park opens at 7am. We were one of the first one to go up so no stressful crowds or waiting in the stairs (which would have made me panick). You also avoid the heat, crowds and hornets! Amazing time to take pictures as well. We are in very good shape but the heat makes it harder.... We didn't find it difficult and it also gave you time to take your time and enjoy the scenery.

The small museum is interesting. The rock fortress, with the water gardens and fountains is marvellous. Somehow, one does not feel difficult to climb 1202 steps up to the top of the rock! Guides typically agree for SLR1,000/- for SAARC visitors.

It was a hard climb and not for the faint-hearted. I made it, albeit with some help from a local guide. Not being in the first flush of youth I arrived at the top rather red faced and hot, but my gaining the summit  evoked a cheer from my companions - a Saga group. This was a marvellous, though somewhat exhausting tour of Sri Lanka over 12 days. A very worth-while adventure from Colombo to Habarana in the North then all the way down, via Kandy, to Beruwala in the South and back to Colombo. I really recommend it.

that tourists balk at paying $30 for an astounding attraction such as this. Maybe they are backpackers doing "Sri Lanka on $5 a Day?" Sri Lanka is not a dirt cheap destination, like Laos or Cambodia. Get over it. Sigiriya is worth the price of admission, in spades. The rock fortress is imposing and ususual, and once you get the top, the views are gorgeous. Not to be missed.

I have never seen such a strong green in my entire life. The park around is amazingly green and the wild animals are all around. There is a special quality about the light on the site. And more after climbing all the steps you are rewarded with a splendid view, peace and all you can see all around in the far view too, is nature. I really loved it. Might have been that The Lion King was inspired by this amazing site. Must visit!

One advise: go early. Once tourist buses start coming in, it's much harder to enjoy the peaceful beauty of this site. Avoiding the crowds also lowers the risk of experiencing a wasp attack, triggered by loud noises. Note that the upper part of the rock (from the start of the staircase between the lion's pawns) is closed off in case of a wasp attack, until it is considered safe to go up/come down again. In other words: you might be stuck for hours up the rock, or in case of a busy schedule don't have the time to wait and get up there. The view on top is amazing nonetheless and invites to mesmerize about the work and hardship that was put into the construction of the site on top of this rock. Pretty expensive though, and no refunds are provided in case of a wasp attack.

Citadel of Sigiriya - Lion Rock is very good spot to experience a chunk of the history of Sri Lanka. This is a place to visit for active people. Photographers can have a field day visiting this place.

This was my second visit to Sigiriya, my last was ten years ago. The experience this time was disappointing. I have no issue with paying for access to a important and very significant cultural artifact. However, charging Rs 3900 is significant, especially for a site that has nearly 10,000 tourists visit a day. That is nearly $300,000US per day. The site is overrun with disrespectful tourists who have graffitied the mirror wall and the rock throughout, strewn rubbish across the site. Tourism companies have donated rubbish bins that are unused - despite the huge amount of money collected. Beggars and hawkers are rife throughout the site (including overpriced guides, who gain access for very little money, fleecing the tourist), that cause the loss of the ability to take in the awesome sights. Lastly, tourists are not well informed or advised by their tour leader or by the Ministry of Archaeology - you MUST be fit to climb this wonderful site, if you have pre-existing medical conditions, poor mobility or other challenges, then admire it from the bottom of the rock. If you fall into the category of unfit or medically at risk, then you simply put other attendees at risk.
Fantastic climb, views are superb. Had a few issues with the wasps the day we went but the mad panic eventuated to nothing. Thoroughly enjoyed it.

For anyone interested in archaeology, geology or Sri Lankan history this is a must. The climb is not particularly strenuous but make sure you take a bottle of water. My recommendation is that you do the climb as early in the day as possible. It opens at 8:00am. In doing this you avoid any tour buses and school kids. It is pricey at $30 per head. There is a combination ticket which takes into account 2 other sights for $40 total. This is much better value.

Emblematic of Sri Lanka. Get there early before the temperature gets too high and too many visitors arrive. It a significant climb up steps. Take your time. There are young men who will offer, for a price, to assist you to climb the 1000 or so steps. There are a few points at which you can take a rest. The cave paintings are accessed via a spiral staircase on the side of the rock. If you don't like heights miss this bit. However, you will then miss a fantastic collection of paintings of women of the royal court. These are often used to represent Sri Lanka. When it's busy you may have to be assertive to get the photos you want. Great view of a modern statue of Buddha from the staircase. The mirror wall is interesting. Useful to have read up about this beforehand so you understand what you are looking at. There is a good resting point at the base of the final climb on the metal staircase. Once again you need to be OK with heights.  The staircase is a bit nerve racking. The last climb is well worth it.  Fantastic views to be had as well as very interesting remains. Suggest you take a bottle of water with you as no refreshments availed until you complete the rock.

This is one of the top tourist destinations in Sri Lanka but they have not yet done anything about the swarms of hornets that regularly attack tourists. Proceed with caution and listen to your guide. They have wire cages to hide in when the swarms come (attracted by heat and noise) but those unfortunate people that do not get into the cage will get stung. Three people were taken off to hospital when we were there. Really rather frightening. It is a beautiful and impressive place but something needs to be done to make it safer.

The gardens are lovely and the site of the citadel sticking up from nowhere is amazing. Don't think you have to climb the rock to appreciate it. And the day we were there they had closed the climb since the swarm of bees that exist part way up had stung some tourists that day...so use some caution

We are in Sri Lanka for 4 days. Once arrived, we went straight to Sigiriya area. And on the way pass by Dumbulla which have a temple you can visit too. If you would like to go Sigiriya lion rock, go early at 7.30am as the weather and time just right with not much crowd yet. Entrance fee bit expensive USD30 per person. Once you bought ticket, go first to the musuem which just next and behind the ticket counter. After knew the information then proceed to climb the rock. Interesting place with the effort of climbing. Once you reach the top, lots of photos can be taken however provided the weather is good. You will spend around 2 hours in the rock. Be careful of the steps and wear proper shoes.

Honestly I felt part of a joke: the place and the rock are amzing but really they don't worth Rs. 3500 ($30) when locals pay not even Rs500!!! We renouced to go in, we refused to pay this ridicolous amount for climing a rock! Sri Lanka government has to improve services and price otherwise in few years they won't have anymore turists!

Like the rest if Sri Lanka, you need to separate the site from the management of the site. Sigiriya is just amazing, up there with Macchu Picchu, Tikal etc as amazingly situated ruins, which - even with the crowds - are evocative and mysterious. The views from the top are the icing on the cake and the climb up, while strenuous, is really not too bad - my daughter who has only just turned 3 managed up to the Lion Paw which is 80% of the way. The management of the site is poor and the best thing you can say about it is that it is clean. 30USD is in excess of European prices and it's hard to see where the money is going. Not on the museum, which contained some interesting exhibits (and is architecturally strong), definitely not on maintenance or signage and surely, with the millions collected each year, it can't be beyond the wit of man to clear down those hornets (we were unaffected). Still, once on to the steps and boulder gardens, the price is soon forgotten!

There appear to be multiple postings for this attraction on TripAdvisor (at least 3 on my quick count), but it is a 'must visit' place for any tourist in Sri Lanka. Yes it is quite a climb (I actually counted 'only' around 1,000 steps), but there are several good stopping places on the way up and it is well worth the effort for the great views on the way - and then from the top!  Just go early in the morning to avoid the heat of the day.
Essential to be  here when its opening at 7 am. Lots of steps iin a very hot climate. Great murals..A must see in Sri Lanka

Its quite expensive, around 30 US Dollars,but its worthy! It takes you about 2,5 hours visiting the whole area and there are a lot of steps to do but when you arrive the top you will feel lucky! :) Bring hiking shoes!

I had read about the history of this fortress on various sites and hence was more intrigued to go and have a first hand experience of the place. We started our climb around 12 noon, so it wasn't that hot and with a little cool breeze it felt pleasant. I loved getting clicked there. This experience was something new to me as we climbed open stairs, then through a spiral stairway leading to the frescoes cave. Then through the open side ways and iron stairs. The view and the climb up didn't feel exhausting but exhilarating. The view on top was awesome which shows in the pics uploaded by me. Please carry enough water on the way up and wear shoes. One rather unfortunate incident happened to few of us. I had read that the wasps there are dangerous and sting if there's  noise around. Few of us were stunged by wasps on our way up. I would blame the authorities for not making the life saving jackets mandatory and not educating the visitors to keep themselves fully covered as the wasps their frequently attack. On inquiring , they said they dont have sufficient jackets to provide all the visitors. So guys, as soon as you reach the place where you see the paws of the lion, you will see open place where few jackets are kept. Please take them with you in case of possible wasps attacks. Although they were quick to rescue us and provide with the antiseptic and medicines, but the damage was done, and I had a swollen hand for next 4 days , and the visit to the doc wasted my time and gave me unnecessary stress. The fees for Saarc countries is 15 usd and for other foreigners its 30usd, but the authorities find it difficult to keep enough life saving gears.

When you are in sri lanka this is a must see.  It is often called the 8th wonder of the world.  We found the hike to not be very strenuous and the view spectacular.  Lots of people.  The paintings were amazing

This is a must when you're in central Sri Lanka. We took a bus from Dambulla, 50 rupi p.p, straight to Sigiriya. At the west entrance you buy your 30$ ticket if you're not from south east Asia (SE asians 15$). We got there around 10am and it was packed with people so we had to stand in a long line for almost 1 hour to get to the "mirror wall". Eventhough we paid a lot and stood in a looong line this is a sight you don't want to miss!
This was a very steep and strenuous climb and not for the faint hearted. We did it in late afternoon which was best for temperature and view.

This is an expensive attraction at US$30 per person. I’d advise people to get there early and to avoid weekends or public holidays. We got there around 9am on a Saturday, just after about half a dozen tour buses had dropped off their customers. This made the climb up very slow and laborious. It isn’t a difficult climb but I would wear sturdy shoes and a hat as it can get very hot on the top. We headed straight to the top, only looking at the Frescoes and Mirror Wall on the way. The Frescoes are amazing but because of the volume of people, the attendants were hurrying people through so it was difficult to take a good look at them. There’s not much to see at the top, the 1.6 hectares is terraced with the foundations of ruined buildings and a large pool, but the views are good if you get a clear day. On the way down we looked at the Audience Hall and various gardens. Watch out for the monkeys if you take food. As soon as we took ours out they were over in a flash and we had to put it away again fast! Refreshments and toilet facilities are in very short supply at Sigiriya Rock. The only refreshments I saw on offer was water and cool drink bottles being sold by touts where people come down from the rock. The only toilets I saw were one lot outside the complex and some in the museum. We called at the museum on the way out and the toilets in the museum were dirty and there was no toilet paper, soap or paper towels. The museum would be a good venue for a coffee shop as there is a lot of free space. The exhibits are surprisingly sparse, although the few that there are were quite well labelled and relatively interesting. There is no doubt that the attraction is spectacular, and the landscaping is very creative. Was it worth the entrance price? Probably not – but if you managed to go on a quiet day the experience would be better.

About 20min by bus and 10min on foot from Dambulla you arrive to the entrance of the Sigiriya complex. A quite steep entrance fee, which is already mentioned in the rest of the reviews. Overall is the complex interesting, having a guide would definitely be better, but one can also go on its own due to the infos along the way. There are a lot of steps and it is quite hot (bring water) (beginning of January) but the view from the top makes it up. At the top there are only some small areas in the shadow (few trees), so bring suncream. At the base of the rock there are various things also to see. Worth visiting.
1200 steps worth the effort to climb this rock.It's a Must.On the top you can enjoy a fabulous view at 360°

It is essential to go to this site in the early morning before it gets hot and busy as there are 1200 steps to climb and coach parties come during the day. We were there by 8am and had very good access to the rock. Our guide and helper were helpful but you need to be firm if you do not want a helper to accompany you. The views are outstanding and there are some interesting wall  paintings and lots of history associated with this site.

A tricky climb and beware of hornets!  A good few people have been attacked here we have heard and it is put down to people being noisy!  The nests were apparently built onto the rock itself but we didn't see them and had no problem.  We heard horror stories of people being stung en masse and needing hospital treatment.  The gardens and rock temple/palace itself are absolutely incredible.  I was struck by the sheer size and location.  Not quite like anything I have visited before.

We reached Sigiriya at 8 am, even though we hoped for 7 am as we read in earlier posts that it could get very hot.  Fortunately, it was a cloudy day. We crossed the moat, then the Water and Fountain gardens.  Our guide informed us that parts of the1, 600 years-old hydraulic systems underneath the fountains were still functioning.  We then proceeded to the Boulder Arch where I saw a notice to not make loud noises as it could disturb the hornets. Fortunately, hornets weren’t a threat that day, although there have been posts by TA reviewers who have gotten stung. Several steps up and we reached the Rock garden. From there, the climb became more challenging as we went up many steps that took us past a series of terraced gardens. From the terraced gardens, we went up a metal spiral staircase that took us to the “Sigiriya damsels” frescoes (480A.D.), a handful that remained of what was once a tapestry of 500 damsels covering a large swathe of the rock surface, high above the plains. These frescoes painted onto wet plaster have surprisingly maintained their vivid colours, possibly because of the use of mineral rather than plant dyes.  You can see several mistakes made by the artists painting them such as the damsels with an extra thumb or hand. But as these damsels were minor figures in the tapestry, to be viewed from below, they were possibly not rendered as perfectly as required. Look out for the damsel with the “Mona Lisa” smile at the end of the row. There is a separate spiral staircase for going down to the Lion Plateau. On the Lion Plateau, are two enormous paws, what remained of a gigantic lion carved out of rock. As we walked into what would have been the lion’s mouth, we ascend a long series of steps up to the pleasure gardens of King Kasyapas, and finally to the summit where his palace was.  What is left now is just the foundations of his palace, which are surprisingly not that big; but what a view he would have had. To get the most out of this visit, go very early to escape the crowds and heat, and take your time to savor the genius that went into planning and building this site.
fanastic views- and history, not for the vertigo sufferer. Take water and set off early- had a guide so alitle history and chat on the way up - lots lots of steps..

One of my best experiences in Sri Lanka. Bit of advice: 1. Go as early as possible in the morning - the hornets respond to noise and may attack if busloads of noisy people are climbing the rock. 2. Hire a local guide, not only will he give you interesting facts but he also has access to the refuge where they keep the protective clothes. Be sensible, in the past,  people have died under the attacks of the hornets.
Good place to visit. Should consider arriving at the rock early as possible if not you tend to get burnt and energy drained with the sunrise. Gets rather hot and humid towards afternoon.

I would like to make note that I could barely breathe when I got to Sigiriya and was pretty sure that I had a fever coming on, but all the same I was very excited to see this place and climb to the top.  It was raining off and on so the climb was slippery and messy, but I pushed ahead.  My guide Karew was amazing though.  He kept an eye on me and distracted me from my cold.  The walk up to the rock is through three levels of gardens (water, rock and terraced) and then you ascend a spiral staircase to the 18 remain frescos (of 500), before going back down and over to the Lion Gate (just the paws remain).  Then you walk and walk and walk, until you have climbed all 1200 steps (this is from the first garden).  Plus there are 2 more little steps on the main platform on the top (Karew had a giggle when he made me climb them to take my picture). It was a great climb.  You descend rough the same way, but in the Rock garden you diverge and exit through the Cobra gate (there is an Elephant gate in the rock garden).  It was quite a climb and even with my cold was able to really enjoy myself (and not die).... Note: I am a little disturbed that there are 4 entries for the same location, but I went with the first one....

I enjoyed the frescoes part-way up - fantastically well-preserved.  Even the views from the lion's cave, about half-way, were good, but I thought the final climb, mostly on metal stairways attached to the side of the rock, was quite fun.  Not for those with vertigo, but I felt quite safe.  It wasn't as strenuous as I'd expected, but best to go early morning or late afternoon to avoid the heat of the day.  For those not keen on any part of the climb, the little museum at the entrance is very good, and has an excellent fibreglass representation of the frescoes.  All the explanations on the museum displays were in Tamil, Sinhalese and English.

Quite a strenuous visit...and not for those who fear heights...so why did I do it?! If you visit this area of Sri Lanke, you have to visit Sigirya Citadel. I've never been so scared in my entire life as I was the day I climbed up some rather dodgy looking metal stairs hanging off the sheer face of this huge rock...in fact, I almost back out. But after much starting and stopping and cajoling from my partner, I reached the top and was rewarded with the most amazing set of palace ruins and a breathtaking view that I'll never forget! There were a few people there with small children - I don't think I'd take my 3 year old granddaughter there, not exactly secure with sheer drops and no warning signs, plus the risk of hornet swarm attacks and not so friendly monkeys! I think it's a place that can only be truly appreciated as an adult...without that fear of losing a child over the edge of a rock cliff! This is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. As such, the volume of visitors can be extremely high so be prepared for jostling in places on the stairs that you may not feel entirely comfortable about - especially when you take a look down! You will be bothered by locals offering to help you whilst visiting. They insist they're 'employed' to help visitors and they will help...but they will expect you to tip them fairly generously after they've hekped and they may be very persistent and difficult to shake off, so be prepared. A MUST DO!

The Sigiriya Rock is definitely a place to visit when one visits Sri Lanka. It offers a great panoramic view once you've reached the top of the fortress. One does not need any local guides to know about the place if you have a travel book handy. It is a bit of a hard climb for people not used to it but the breeze helps you cool down on your way up. Do take some drinking water or food along if required.

My favourite thing in Sri Lanka was Sigiriya, the hike was awesome, the views are amazing and the remains of the palace and citadel make your imagination fly. We wanted to see the sunset but beware, right after the sun goes down it gets dark very very quickly and as you start descending you get nervous as there are very few people around, and (in our case) absolutely no official guards or anybody that can help if something happens. Bring a torch with you but consider not staying too late if it's only two of you and definitely don't do it if you are alone. Also, as everywhere in Sri Lanka, beware of all the people trying to charge 'tips' for absolutely everything you do or don't do. Beware of the wasp attacks, no one will help if it should happen!! Also, lots of stray dogs around, mostly of the friendly kind but stay away from them, no one know about any diseases.

Little Tough To Climb up But Its worthy To Spend Energy.Over More then 1000 Years of Paintings Really Very Nice & The Fortress Basement Telling So Many Story's of Past Years Civil Engineering Technology Polish & security are so Friendly With Tourist. Very Important is Store Your Bottles & Snacks Bag You Never Find This From Your First Step In entrance.Enjoy Your Every Seconds. Ask Documentary CD in Ticket Counter Which is Free.( Ticket Rate is Hi For Non SARC Country's).

This is an amazing site to see and climb. Its almost unimaginable that anyone could build anything on top of the rock let alone a citadel. The path/steps up the rock are sound, but can be very slippery when wet, and many of the rock steps are un-even and worn. This is probably not a climb for the unfit or un-sure on their feet, although having said that there were lots of older people and small children on the climb when we were there. Its a one way path for most of the climb so it would be difficult to turn around if you changed your mind. When we were there a number of wasp nests had moved in to the location of the final part of the climb. I was really impressed that the park authority took their presence so seriously providing warnings, attack instructions and even a wasp refuge in case of an attack. Incredible views from the top that really gave perspective to the area, and made the dodgy staircase and wasps worth it!
BBeware it is quite a climb to the top and some with a fear of heights might not enjoy it.  However seeing the ruins at the top and the views made it worthwhile for me.

One of the first striking things was the disparity in price between local ilvisitors (50 rupees, less than a dollar) and foreign visitors (3900 rupees- 30 usd).  Inside the gardens were very beautiful, a lot of monkeys who try to steel from you ( one of them even grabbed a backpack that was on a tourist's back, trying to steal it), so be careful and try not to leave anything unattended. The rock is brautiful from afar, since about halfway up the climb (which is not difficult at all), we were stopped because as we found out 30 minutes later, there was a wasp attack. We waited, hoping that the wasp thing would be taken care of, but even after bringing some soldiers(!!) and equipment, we were told that maybe in the evening we could come back and maybe we would be able to climb to the top. Well, for us that was impossible, since we had planned a 9 day tour of the country ans were leaving for anurhadapura that very day. We went to the ticket bix, asking for refund, explaining the situation but of course they really didn't care, said no refund. But the main reaaon we got fruatrated was, during the whole wasp attack, and even though they told us that until evening we wouldn't br able to climb, at the ticket office they were still selling tickets and NOT telling tourists that they would not be able to climb the rock! On our way back we saw several groups of tourists pass us and 15 minutes later came right back! So, basically if you are lucky, you will get to climb the rock and pay enormously unfair amount of money or still pay enourmously unfair amount of money and see monkeys.
Easy climb for anyone with a basic level of fitness, well worth it when you reach the top, especially the view across Sigiriya

If you visit just one attraction in Sri Lanka it should be this one. Hiking all them way up and seeing those ruins on top is just breathtaking. And the paintings, sculptures and history along the way. Such a great experience. We arrived an half an hour befor the park even opened and it was totally worth it - first in and had everything to ourselfs. Really has another vibe to it if no other tourists are around. The hike up is not very easy but if your in good health it shouldnt be a problem. Yeah the entreance fee is rather expensive but its totally worth it. If your too cheap - skip all the other places and just come here. :-)

I've never reviewed a natural or historical site on TripAdvisor because it seems rather silly. But before visiting Sigiriya (in early Feb 2015), I wish I'd known about their massive hornet problem. The translations were inconsistent -- sometimes "bees," sometimes "wasps," sometimes "hornets," so I have no idea which are actually lurking there -- but there were signs all over the site saying "Beware of Hornet Attacks," "Be Quiet So As Not To Provoke Hornets," "No Refunds Given for Hornets" -- so clearly it's been a problem for awhile. Sure enough, when we'd climbed about 2/3 of the way up the rock, we were stopped by someone in uniform, saying that we couldn't go the rest of the way because of "hornet attacks". About 20 minutes later they let people up again... but how sure can you actually be that the hornets are gone...? Our driver said they sometimes give people protective clothing, but it seems a bit distracting, viewing historical sites under fear of wasp/hornet/bee attack. This would be less of an issue if the climb weren't so dramatic (or if there were some sort of access road) but it's a sheer rock face, so the prospect of getting stung by a swarm of hornets and not being able to get medical attention, particularly if you have an allergy or other sensitivity -- or a swarm showing up and being trapped -- without a 45-minute climb down is pretty terrifying. There's no easy way out. Beautiful site, historically fascinating, one-of-a-kind, but we didn't get to see much of it. To drive 3 hours, get charged $30 and then stopped halfway up because of hornets -- massive letdown. Get a trusted source (guide, hotel, etc.) to call and ask about the situation before you commit.

My wife and I did a tour of Sri Lanka in October 2014. One of the sights we had set our minds on was Sigiriya. It was certainly worth the visit but the entrance ticket cost for foreigners was a bummer. Nevertheless, I think it is worth paying the money because the Rock Palace is spectacular in itself and in the views that it affords as you ascend the steps. If you carry your passport and you are from a SAARC country the ticket cost is subsidised so avail of the subsidy - without a passport there is no way you will get the subsidised tickets. It sure does make sense to start early for the climb because you will be climbing in the shade and not in the sun - if you have to do it in the sun it can become quite uncomfortable as the rock reflects the heat of the sun as you climb. Beware the rather narrow and uneven steps carved out of the rock face - it means you will need to climb mostly on your toes and if you are not used to walking on your toes it takes its toll on your calf muscles - good non-slip footwear is important. Starting early also means you get to avoid the crowds. The climb is best done in a relaxed manner - don't rush it. The frescoes half way up are beautiful and resemble the Buddhist art that one encounters in the Ajanta & Ellora caves of Maharashtra, India. If you have cardiac issues this climb is not for you - although there is a medical post at the base and at the top of the rock. The other issue you need to be aware of is the presence of wasps that build their nests in the rock and in the surrounding trees - there are notices warning people not to make too much noise so that the wasps don't get disturbed but when there are crowds there will be noise and there are several instances of people getting stung and having to be taken to hospital. The Lion's paws are the symbol of Sigiriya and they are made rather well. The gardens at the base of the rock are also quite nice and make for a nice photo backdrop.

I've wanted to visit since a saw Ian Wright climb Sigiriya years ago on Globetrekker. Many write that it's expensive. Well, it is, compared to what local people are paying but it would be utter stupidity to deny yourself a visit to this piece of history. However; it's not compared to what you payed to fly into Sri Lanka. The paintings of the courtesans are beutiful and the Lion Paws are imposing! And the view from the top is great! The climb isn't even that hard (however take a big bottle of water because it's hot!) Don't miss out!

In the way to the rock, there are beautiful gardens, called the Royal Gardens, where brides and grooms use to take pictures. We had the chance to meet a couple with the beautiful dress and took a picture with them. You have to go to the top of the rock. The view is very beautiful and it's worth the hard climbing (many stairs).

It's a little bit tiring to clim all the rocks, but doable. The views from the top are worth it. So take your breath and go all the way up. The story behind the rock is surprising. We enjoyed it all along, from the beautiful royal gardens to the painted gallery, and the top of the rock.

Although a bit touristy and definitely overpriced, this attraction is definitely worth a visit, as it will most probably be the most iconic landmark you will visit in Sri Lanka. We did it with two small kids (4 and 2 years old) at a pace that the bigger could manage (the smalest was carried in a special backpack), so anyone can do it. Would recommend a morning ascent, as almost the entire path is in shadow. Definitely worth a visit.

Be very careful of wasps. We all got stung today. Dozens of people attacked and nothing you can do. Stuck on a dodgy staircase with no facial protection, you are a sitting duck. And the fact you have to pay $30 for the pleasure of being stung, better to stay in Kandy. Four admitted to hospital today.
A beautiful slice of history preseved but do ensure that you take a bottle of water with you as it gets very humid the higher you climb.

If you go to Sri Lanka a trip up to Sigiriya is well worth it. It's a fair bit of a hike. I went with my 12 year old daughter and she found it a breeze! I on the other hand did struggle (just out of practice!) It took us about 45 mins to make it to the top and 30 coming down. The steps are very steep but there are places to rest. The view is spectacular! On a side note the resident wasps were not there which was great. However, if you are allergic to wasp stings make sure you carry your epi pen as they do not have them at the first aid station. Also make sure you make it up in the early morning before the mid day sun hits the rock. Also take water with you as it can get humid but at the top the view is spectacular and the breeze is wonderful. You will be invigorated afterwards!

One of the must see places while visiting Sri Lanka, Lots of stairs,  good exercise not really exhausting, but no need to hurry, just take your time, take your camera, every few steps something amazing, footprints of culture, great views!!!!

This is an amazing ancient site - you should not miss it! The grounds are worth seeing and the history is fascinating, but you really do need to make the effort to climb all the way to the top to get the full experience. Go early in the day before it gets too hot because it is a long, strenuous climb - take it slowly and enjoy the view and the frescoes half way up. There are a lot of young men offering "help" which I rejected. The view from the top is worth the climb!

This place although pricey was a fantastic trip. Just the gardens before the palace is enough to go there. It has a fantastic view and a great history. We went there without guide but there is a lot of written information there.

Truly a must see whilst visiting Sri Lanka. Sigiriya Rock deserves it's place on the world heritage list....although probably not the 8th wonder of the world as they claim. Carved into a huge monolith, the site combines both cultural and natural beauty. The climb to the top is not for the unfit or those scared of heights but the reward for the hike are absolutely stunning panoramic views and ruins of the former palace. The entrance price was steep ($30 per person)....as it frankly was for all the tourist sights we visits. In general, I was a little annoyed at the inflated entrance price that awaited us at each cultural site we visited in Sri Lanka. Sigiriya Rock was however, more value than most.

A must-see from the historical approach to Sri Lanka. Amazing to see what human ingenuity can achieve when driven by a faith and how much that faith can demand from its faithful followers. Students of military studies can also appreciate why a civilisation would spend the effort to turn this into its capital and fortress. Sure the walk and climb is long and fairly tough at certain points, but the view from the top is a reward for that hard work. However, as pointed out by other reviewers, there are 2 levels of prices and while I don't disagree on principle of citizens versus visitors, the price differential is just too  great to not have a feeling that of being ripped off as easy meat. That's a reality that the whole of Sri Lanka's tourism industry and its tourism ministry must address. It should not be  case of killing the golden goose that lays the golden egg. No one likes to feel fleeced and the entrance fees here certainly comes close to that sensation. The experience would have been immensely more positive if that price differential was addressed. Be careful of touts along the way offering to show you this and that. They just want money for showing you the obvious. Just politely turn them away and walk on. Lastly, the exit is different from the entrance and one would turn left at the foot of the rock to head towards the exit. Not clearly marked, so be extra aware.

Get there early- when they open.  There are many locals who hang out who try to help you and then they demand a tip.  My only complaint was constantly telling people no thanks and then at the end a very nice man told us which way to exit, which was already quite clear, and then began following us and we kept saying thanks but we don't need your help- we are very fit and in our 40s- but he kept following us, then asked for money and when we said no he became very angry.  He literally followed us for maybe 3 minutes. You can get to the top, take photos and get back down in an hour if you are in shape.  It's an amazing site to visit.

It's no wonder that Sigiriya is a World Heritage Site. It is one of a kind (though it does have certain similarities to Machu Picchu but that was built 1000 years later!) and well worth the thousand odd stairs you climb to reach the ruins of the ancient palace. As you enter the complex you have the opportunity to visit the museum which gives you a good impression of what they believe the palace would have looked like. Passing through the water gardens you can see how clever the engineering capability was in ~500 AD in this area. The climb is steady and it is advisable to take some drinking water with you as it can be very humid. We thought the warning sign at the ticket kiosk 'beware of the bees and waps (stet)' was a joke but no, we were halted from making the last stage of the walk to the top because some noisy tourists had stirred up a hornets nest high on the hill side. 10 minutes later it was fine to continue upward. Be on the look out for monkeys too! They can smell if you have bananas in your rucksack and will try to get them! The view from the top (weather permitting) is great. Look down below and see the ornate gardens. Look into the distance and see the surrounding hills, forests and a towering Buddha statue. You can but admire the technical skills and organisation that must have been required to build a palace in such a challenging position.
From the garden to the top of the rock, it's a really beautiful and well preserved archeological. The view from the top is stunning and by itself it's worth the climb.

Its so nice, well maintained, the view is something that must see as words can’t describe, we felt so great when we reach the top. The number of people we met and talked with is unbelievable. The best time to clamp is early in the morning (before 10 am) and make sure you take a drinking water along
Entrance is 4000rp. Servise is horrifYing. Although there is much more beautiful rock like 1 km from there
Leave early in the morning to get there for around 7.30-8 to get there before the heat and the crowds.

I could not get over how many people - both old and very young, that climbed up this rock...barefoot, in heels, large flip flops....but so very worth it. The paintings are stunning and in such wonderful condition. Apparently the King who built it, had to leave here daily to administer to his kingdom. But he did not climb up this very tiny, perilous steps but had a lift installed on some sort of pulley system. Elaborate gardens, irrigation, theatre for plays and dancing girls.....! All this in the  5th century!!!! Staggering and very wonderful and humbling. Visit if you can.

Ok. Getting straight to it with the Pros: 1. World Heritage site and attached History to it. If you want to avoid the guides, read up about the rock and then go to familiarise yourself on what it is about. 2. View from the top is very nice. 3. Highlight of Sigiriya. Cons: 1. The Climb. It is quite a climb to the very top, so better be prepared with sun screen, a Hat, and bottle of water. 2. Not enough signs on what is what. they make you reliant on local guides who will charge you a lot of Money. 3. Entrance fee: Bloody expensive. Do visit the museum after the climb. it may help you close all the links.
Getting up early (7am) is recommended if visiting Sigiriya - you can avoid crowds and heat.  The climb to the top is worth the effort at the end. Magnificent.

Excellent feature. We only got as far as the entrance to the upper ruins, through the lions paws. Even that was spectacular. We are both getting on in years, but fairly fit. Any further up, on metal staircases would have pushed our luck i a bit too far we felt

It is truly magnificent place. Not only the rock with the ruins of monastery or as the legend says the king palace on top. The soundings are equally beautiful. The remaining of the water, boulder and terrace gardens are worth to stroll in. It is far best to visit the site early in the morning before the crowds appear. Because the bottle neck can be the system of metal stairs for going upward and downward the crowds doesn't mean only lower comfort of the visit - it can actually mean waiting in the queue. It is also much nicer to climb in lower temperature. It definitely opens at 7.30. For us the best was the climb itself, the views from the top and the gardens at the foot of the rock. Of course you visit famous paintings with erotic motives and the "ancient graffiti" if you can spot it amidst the contemporary ones.

This was the highlight of our stay in Sigiriya. We went early morning just ahead of the main crowds and before the heat of the day. The gardens at the bottom are well laid out and looked after. The murals part way up are amazing and worth the few extra steps up and down the spiral staircases. The climb is not too challenging - so long as you have a reasonable level if fitness - and there are enough stopping off points on the way anyway, including at the lion's paws. The final climb from their is the toughest part, but well worth the view from the top.

This is a great experience and one of the 'musts' of Sri Lanka.  It is a climb and it is hot, so take it easy, a bit at a time and make sure you have water.  Take some time to have a look at the lovely cave paintings.  The view from the top is one of the best.

As others have said, you go to the "foreigners" entry ( yes it says that!) and pay a fortune. I got to the point  where there was a queue to go up (and down) a narrow external spiral steel starcase that takes you to the most wonderful frescos, or so it said. My driver/guide's version was that they were "restored" by an Italian after being irreparably damaged. Hmm Add in the hawkers and the con artists trying to get to lead you up for a fee, only disclosed at the top, of $US 15. Overrated, poorly labeled tourist box ticking exercise, I did not join the queue but left.

A trip to Sigirya requires some background knowledge of the historical site in order to appreciate the UNESCO listed World Heritage Site. As you make your way up, you will be amazed at the history and how well the paintings are preserved. Although the climb to the top can be a bit steep for most people, you will be rewarded with a cool breeze and of course, a beautiful scenic view of royal garden. Make sure you carry a backpack so you can carry some water. Locals will offer to guide you, would especially help if you think you need assistance to the top as they can help you climb. Be ready to pay a hefty price of 39,000 rupees at the door.

The most stunning UN Heritage site we have ever seen - however, the climb to the top is EXHAUSTING and is not for everyone. Wasps inhabit the crevices near the top, so please be VERY quiet when going up the final stretch of stairs (from the lion paws upwards). Do NOT use flash photography, as it irritates the wasps. Overall, worth seeing once on your trip - carry lots of water to drink for the climb.

The park is very well laid out, the path to the top is easy to find and the incredible amount of work that went into restoring this site boggles the imagination. Bring a bottle of water, both telephoto and wide-angle lenses for your camera and watch out for bees.

A must see ancient kingdom. Ticket prices for foreigners were a little steep but well worth it. I would recommend climbing it on a clear day since the views are absolutely breathtaking. Also early morning or late afternoon would be better to avoid the heat. Keep in mind it closes at 6.00.

Has a decent museum which had a video - educating us about the place. The climb took about 1.5 hour with frequent stops to admire views. The place looks more amazing - in an aerial view (there are flights but we didn't opt for it). Stayed for sometime on the top - though the ruins on the top do not give us much idea of how the palace might have looked. But the water systems in place are worth pondering about. Historical, stunning views. Need to understand the historical facts beforehand to appreciate the place better.

We have just returned from Sigiriya Rock, my wife and I payed £40.00 this is equal to a weeks wages for locals, at best it is Ok, not for the unfit as there is lots of climbing,we were not allowed to the highest point as 25 people had been stung by angry hornets and we're rushed to hospital, which we are told happens! All in all OK.

go for it..its is a long stair climb..but do it, take it easy if you feel tired, enjoy the view take pictures drink water..the paintings on the wall are well preserved, thanks to the way they cut the rocks so no water can enter the cave, the artist has to be very quick when painting as the plaster will dry up in few minutes, that's why there are few drawing mistakes like a painting with three breast nipple and two left arms..the mirror wall is still has its shine and you can see the reflection of the painting on the opposite wall.. the roof of the rock was the winter palace of the kingdom.. do take a guide they are very knowledgeable, and make your climb worthy. our guide was include in our tour still I  tipped him RSL 1000 was very pleased. wear good light joggers, (the local were climbing bare foot!!). and climb light just carry a bottle of water and your camera try to climb in the afternoon so less heat and the sunset from the top is amazing ..happy climbing.

We enjoyed this immensely . Unlike other visitors, it worked that we visited this in the afternoon. That meant it was was 28 degrees (luckily a  slightly cooler day). Take plenty of water and a hat but it was no problem climbing the 200 metres. Well worth the views and the whole place very interesting.

This was perhaps the greatest landmark of our visit to Sri Lanka. To climb the 1200 steps and reach the top was fantastic. On the way you can watch topless rock paintings of high standard and observe the various features of the passage up. It wasn't too bad actually, there are a number of parts that are level going mixed with shorter or longer stairs. And it's in the shade (they thought of that!). The difficult part is that many steps are not wide enough for our feet so you have to walk partly sideways.

We liked our trip to the rock. It is a good climb (not too bad if you in an OK shape) and there is a wonderful view. Intrance was 3900 rupees pr person. A lot of people but not too crowded. We had a guide (our driver told us to pay between 1000-1500 and we gave him 1300 rupees). Would strongly recommend to agree on a price (as with anything) before the tour.

This was the most amazing of the heritage sites in Sri Lanka for us - it is not for the infirm or unfit as it involves a serious climb although the descent is easier. For us, the climb made it more special. We went late in the afternoon and it was not crowded and there was a nice breeze at the top. We thought that there were adequate railings and fences - much better that in other Asian countries. The site is large - a lovely series of garden areas at the base before the climb starts. The frescos are a detour  after some of the climb and are most impressive especially as they have not been restored. The lion's paws at the base of the final ascent are amazing - one can only wonder what the site looked like a thousand years ago. There are wonderful views from the top where there are lots of ruins - just foundations of buildings. It is expensive for tourists to visit but I thought it was worth it and I am sure that the money which is collected by the government goes into maintenance of the area which is extensive.

Sri Lanka is not the easiest place to get around, with a large population, SE Asian road practices and unfortunately, for us, the presidential election in progress, meant that average road times were around 35km/hr. With drivers consistently sticking to their story and saying we'll be there soon, not giving a time of arrival, stopping for directions every major intersection and limited english lead to a great deal of frustration for the most part of our trip. Arriving at Sigiriya, without tickets as the driver went to the wrong gate, we managed to get a discount ticket direct from the entry, so if time permits, i would try this to save 900Rp each? Now the above may sound like a big whinge, but it is more to emphasise the appreciation for the destination. This place is amazing, and all was soon forgotten when standing in front of this exquisitely modified monolith. Some will no doubt miss the marvel of engineering in the small details. What was made here, and still stands, after millenia, is nothing short of breath taking. It is easy to see why the location was chosen, but the imagination to turn what most of the rest of the world (at the time) would have seen as a big rock, into a living, breathing and sustainable settlement is astounding. In the small detail you will see carved tracks in the solid rock to channel water to catchment areas, even along the walkways other horizontal channels to break surface tension are visible which would have reduced the deluge of water running onto the head of anyone walking the paths. The highly polished plaster wall (mirror wall) is a testament to the artisans of the day. Plastering that has been outside and exposed to the elements for all this time and still holding its polish is not something i have seen anywhere in the world and highly doubt we could even reproduce these results with today's technology. Getting here for 3pm is a great time, to give yourself time to climb to the top and enjoy the walk and see the sun set from the top. remember your hat, water, sunscreen and most importantly fully charged camera with a large memory card!
This should be amalgamated with Sigiriya which is the top attraction and worth a detour

It's a very long walk up, and quite a few people couldn't manage it. HELPFUL TIP. If you don't feel up to it, you don't need to go, as there is a museum at the entrance which has recreated the cave paintings in actual size, so it's almost as good as being there. There's also a mock up of what you see at the top, with a short 3D film of what it would have looked like. I spoke to some people afterwards who didn't go to the top, but didn't know about the museum (included in ticket price) either. That being said, I did get to the top, and it was worth it as the views are amazing and the size and perspective of the site are extraordinary. Do not miss.

Not much more to say, really. Sigiriya is spectacular; there's no denying its beauty and achievement. And everyone knows it's one of Sri Lanka's premier tourists sights, so complaining about hordes of tourists is disingenuous. The 3900 Rs that it costs, though, is gouging, pure and simple. I'd love to know where the bulk of those entrance fees disappears to.

Liked absolutely everything about this place. It is absolutely fantastic and fascinating. It almost rates up there with Angkor Wat. My tip, get a reputable, accredited local guide. It will be worth what ever you pay. You get so much more out of it. Besides, you paid that much to get here, what's another $20?

Definitely recommend you to do the effort. Starting the climb at about 7 in the morning was perfect for us as there were very few tourists and the temperature was very nice for climbing. Very nice views as you go up. As well make sure you see the drawings of Sigiriya ladies as you climb. Once on top take your time to enjoy the views and walk through the walls of the old city. It takes about one hour to climb with small breaks as well. If you are afraid of heights be sure not to look down on your way back. As we were going down we were glad that we came earlier as big groups of people could be seen climbing up.
Went in Jan 14 Beautiful place. Stunning views. Make sure you take a camera with u and wear decent shoes. Once visited is plenty. Worth one visit.

Yes, it's beautiful, I agree, but the price of 3900 Rps (€ 25,- ) per person is just too high and the value for money is just not good. National Parks in the USA are more beautiful and less expensive! Impossible to give 4 or 5 *. Together with Yala NP this is the only place where I had the feeling of being a stupid tourist... The only thing you can do to avoid the tourist busses with russian, asian and european tourist is give it an early start and start with the climb. Afterwards you have time to visit the gardens. The view from the top is great and we spent an hour  under a tree enjoying the view. There is not much information on the Rock or in the gardens, so your travel guide is the main source of information. I would strongly advice you no to take a local guide with you, because they are all in a hurry and you will be back in 1,5 hour or so.
I liked the climb up to the top of the rock and the amazing views from the top. I disliked the fact that some areas of the path are narrow on the climb.

The Lion Rock is definitely a real world heritage site to see. But the passage to climb the rock does not provide any support for elderly and infants like erecting railings etc to catch hold of, though they collect an hefty entrance fees. The last stretch of vertical ladder climbing seems to be a difficult thing for aged and weak built tourists, leave alone their climbing the same way erected spiral steps before to reach the (Ajanta like)cave paintings but night not be on par.

This is not for you! The first climb is ok as its sort of in the rock itself, so you can't really judge how high you are. However, the last bit, with the steps bolted to the side is pretty horrific for anyone who has an issue with heights. I thought I had conquered mine, but oh no! Going up the steps were terrible, coming down was ok. Overall it was an interesting trip with some nice views and our guide was good and help prevent the 'sellers' from hassling us on the way down. All I would say is if yu don't like heights, don't bother with the last bit as the views are pretty good anyway without putting the fear of god in you!!!

It is really amazing landmark. Built in only two decades it is an amazing achievement of the ancient people. The view from the top of the rock (around 200 meters high) is breathtaking! It takes some time to get there (quite a lot of steps) and I would not recommend it if you are afraid of heights. Bring water, at least half a litter per person! :)

This site is amazing. The fortress is beautiful, and the climb is fun. However be forewarned that some of the steps are narrow and can be slippery in the rain, so this could be difficult for elderly or disabled visitors.

Sigiriya is a must do in Sri Lanka. Along the climb there are interesting gardens and cave paintings. There are extensive and interesting ruins at the top (and a great view). If you are fit you will not find the climb too difficult. Thankfully touts and tacky souvenirs are restricted to the exit. Unfortunately entry prices are steep.

I will not say too much due to fact there is already plenty of reviews but this place is must see. Of course u have to take guide who will explain all history connected for this place otherwise u will just climb reach the top and see beautifull view but u will not know all the rest. Entrance fees are not cheap and guide will ask for cca 15-20$ additional but it worth ,be very carefull with hornet which have a nest on the last stage of climbing toward the top,they can attack sometimes. When we were climbing it was rainy afternoon so they didnt attack we even didnt see them but on other hand visibility from the top in days like that is not sharp so suny day would be perfect and everything will be clear . Never the less we were happy to see that miricle ! As well carefull with steps ,they are very narrow.

Definitely worth a visit! Quite a climb but the view from the top is spectacular! We went there in late afternoon so it was not so hot. Be aware of pickpockets - monkeys there are stealing food. We saw how one took candy from woman's pocket. :) It seams they are the real kings there now. We were wondering how the King climbed up and down in old days.;)

Yes it's 1200 steps, but well worth it for the view you get at the top!  Our driver found us a reputable guide who was very knowledgeable and we paid him 2000 rupees for his efforts. We started climbing at 3:30pm which was still pretty hot, but well timed to see everything and have good lighting for photos from the top. This should not be missed!

Heading there I was dreading the idea of having to climb up 1200 steps. That's 60 stories up. On our arrival we met our guide that told us two tips. 1- Buy nothing from the merchants scattered along the track, just smile and saying thank you politely without even acknowledging their goods. 2- Unless you are elderly, don't accept anyone's offer to be helped along the track. It's 25$, and you don't need it. He was right The climb took 2 hours from beginning to end. The guide was slow, patient, and explained in major details all information related to the place. He made us wait and rest few times along the way. The climb is exhausting and physically demanding, yet reaching the top, it was very much worth it. The views were stunning and simply breathtaking.
