Must do if you are a history buff. Take a good guide with you to explain how they had such clever and insightful planning hundreds of years ago. The view at the top is stunning. The climb is not easy, but not difficult- even for a non fit person like me. Tip: try and climb as early as you can. Preferably soon after sunrise. The weather can get really hot. Dont forget to take lots of water, and also to wear sunscreen.

I had been to this place 2 weeks back. Although, technically it was not there peak season but I enjoyed the place a lot. The key points that attracted me are the architecture of the entire site, the view from top and the nice trek that u get to do will climbing on this huge 4000 feet structure. Moreover, we had a great person with us named Thiwanka Nipura Bandara who was guiding us through the wilderness. The awesome scenery got topped by his wealth of information, pleasant behaviour and his sense of humor. We also visited other places in sri lanka like Anuradhapura, Mihinthale, Pollonuwara andNuwara Elliya.. They all had lovely view filled with serenity. But u can always expect some uniqueness in their expression of beauty. Essentially if u are fond of nature's innocence and its interplay with wilderness... I will suggest Sri Lanka as one of ur recommended destinations....

It is an amazing sight. A gigantic rock in the middle of an amazing green landscape with hundreds of artificial lakes that you can admire from the top. It was not as 'touristic' as I feared from reading some of the reports here. We did not take guide and the walk up there. We came in the morning from Kandy and started after a light refreshment in a near by hotel where we learned that the bees were quiet on our day. The 360 panoramic view is very nice. The snake charmer on the way down was not happy with his 5€ tip and on hindsight I will not support his business of keeping 2 snakes in small boxes next time.

Great thing to do if you are in the area but I wouldn't travel hours to the area especially to see it. Fantastic views and fascinating history. Not one for people who are afraid of heights as the stairs are narrow in parts but they do seem perfectly safe. No need to get a guide as you can do it yourself and morning or evening would be best as midday heat is pretty bad. I went early afternoon and it was fine but needed water.

If visiting Sri Lanka and you were only able to visit one site - this is the one. We visited as part of a pre-arranged around-Sri Lanka tour with a driver (who doubles as a tour guide), however when we arrived at Sigiriya, our own me and my wife had our own dedicated tour guide from the site to show us around - much better than being part of a group as we could go at our own pace. I won't lie - it can be physically exerting at times, especially the higher you get, but the rewards are worth it - the views alone are breath-taking, let alone the 'sights' of how a previous civilisation lived. The history behind the 'Rock' was fascinating - monastery to ancient fortress and well worth the circa 3 and half hour tour to the top and down again. Make sure you take a bottle of water and a camera!

Sigiriya is one of the many places you must visit if anyone comes to Sri Lanka. You can explore the remains of the castle in the top of the rock . Also the view from the top of the rock is breathtaking. And rememeber to visit the cave painting once you visit this place. When you visit beware of the wind and hornets. Also pack enough water before climbing. The best time to climb is in the morning.
You need to save some energy to climb the rock. The view is stunning! Don't go when the sunshine is too much. Sunset time will be a smart choice.

This ancient rock fortress is a must for any visitor to Srilanka. The ancient drawings on the rock is so beautiful. The climb up to the fortress through the lions paw and also the view from the top of the rock is amazing. However, be aware that stinger bees are close by and you should not make a big noise.

We were advised by some locals to go early in the morning to make the climb. They couldn't be more right! We were there by 7am, but it's was still a hot and sweaty climb. The bonus was reaching the top and being one of only a few people there. When it's not crowded you can really appreciate the magnificence of the palace which once stood here. Despite the breathtaking views, the real winner are the ruins. Imagining the logistics of living here and understanding the incredible feat of construction can only be appreciated at the top!! (And part way up - check out the little caves that apparently the soldiers once defended from - scary!) But, honestly get up really early and be ready to climb at 7am, avoid the heat and crowds. Take lots of water too :-)
Dates back to first century! How did they build the palace on top of such a huge rock? Cool to see what they were capable of so long ago.

It was an awesome sight.Our tour guide took us around the area and explained to us the history behind same which was very interesting.Myself and my wife did not climb the rock because we felt that 197 metres were too much to climb and the entrance fees of 35USD per person to be ridiculously high.
A stunning rock mass known as the fortress in the sky. It is a world Heritage site. The high lights are famous frescoe paintings,the mirror wall.and an elephant ride.
Most amazing climb to the most spectacular views....a real pilgrimage for the soul.  Rich in history and many beautiful cave painting and archaeological ruins.

My colleague was right when she said I had to go to Sigiriya!  The 200 metre climb with ancient paintings along the way was just spectacular.  The view from the top was magnificent.  The history behind the rock is very intriguing so be sure to read up before you go.  Try and set out on your climb by about 9am as it gets very hot. I've travelled extensively through Asia and Europe and this is like nothing else my husband and I have ever done.  Well worth  it.  See Dambulla Caves just down the road while you are in the area.

We visited the rock site but unfortunately did not climb due to various reasons: we were not dressed appropriately for such a high climb, it would take a lot of effort, we were slightly scared of the height. Instead we went into the museum which gave us full picture of the rock, its history and what is up there. So overall we enjoyed it.
like the place. but too crowdy...tickets- local Rs 50/-, foreign Rs >3000/-. very bad. locals have to walk ~1km to the rock. unfair in both ways.

Sigiriya was the largest and most sophisticated single construction project ever undertaken in ancient Sri Lanka, and as you walk the grounds and climb the rock itself it's hard to contemplate how it was ever completed. Getting the top does take it out of you, so bring water. Having said that, our guide was 60 and he bounded up the stairs like a mountain goat. In parts the stairs are iron, bolted to the rock face with a sheer drop to the bottom. I'm not afraid of heights, but even I found that a little bit scary. However the climb is well worth it when you reach the top, the view is spectacular.

We were a group of family members in the age range from 53 to 65, who visited a few UNESCO heritage destinations in Sri Lanka recently. We started the climb of Sigiriya Lion's rock citadel, early in the morning, when the site opens at 7 AM when, it is not very hot and not too many visitors. Initially, the climb is gradual, when one walks through the garden areas. Then the narrow and steep marble steps require careful climbing. The climb to the cave paintings of Sigiriya damsels, is through a circular metal staircase. Then, you walk along the edge of the rock enclosed by the mirror wall and by the time you reach the lion's paws, about 2/3rds climb is over. Slow and steady climb, stopping to enjoy the views around, makes the climb less tiring. From here, a metal staircase along the edge of the rock is helpful for support and firm footing. There are many wasp (hornets) nests around this area, and too much noise irritates them. The trick is to silently and swiftly pass this area to reach the top to see the ruins of the King's palace and swimming pool, and great views of Pidurangala rock and refreshing greenery. The climb of 1200 steps gives a sense of achievement and fitness. It is too hot and sultry from 10 am to 3 PM. Early morning or evening climb is advisable. We climbed up in less than one hour, and the total time spent by us, for this climb up and down, was two hours. Taking a guide would be helpful.
Go early when its cooler. Climbed 700 odd steps to the 'feet' of the lion. Lots more after that! Views are magnificent. The murals are astounding. Snake charmer on the way out was 'interesting'.

Jaw dropping, remarkable site.  It's hard to describe the feelings of standing amongst such a sacred and ancient setting. Bring water, wear a comfortable pair of walking shoes and, of course bring your camera (don't have too heavy a load though!)...you'll want to reach the top in as good as condition as possible to appreciate the sights before you.  Do it as early as possible in the day to avoid the crowds and the heat that will set in early. A guide is a great idea.  I felt a little disappointed with our guide as he tended to rush things but he had excellent knowledge of the site.  One day I will go back and take my time...it would be easy to spend a day here savoring the sights. If you are prone to motion sickness, wear travel bands or your preferred method of dealing with it.  I felt dizzy and nauseous going up and down until I put the travel bands on. Yes it's pricey compared to other places in Sri Lanka but definitely one of our highlights during the trip to Sri Lanka.  You can actually see that the money is put to good use, unlike other places we visited that despite having amazing history and tourist value, were unkempt and covered in litter.

we arrived mid morning as it wasn't so hot and not many tourists. We knew there were 1200 steps to the top but lost count after about 20 lol .Once you get to the top and look at the view, you forget that you just spent half an hour scaling a huge rock. But to think the prince lived here and people would do this every day. Amazing
Incredible place. Worth visiting it. Bring water on dry season! It's expensive even for western visitors.

Sigiriya is old. Very old. And it's a ruined fortress - so of course there won't be much to see. But with imagination and thought it is quite remarkable. The scale of the fortress at the summit is mind-blowing, and seeing the gardens laid out below like a dusty Versailles was quite something as well. It's a lot of climbing, it's hot, bring water. The frescoes are worth a quick look. We had no issues with hornets. It was very windy when we visited, some were buzzing about but they didn't seem to be flying in any control. We had no guide and took no 'preventative waterproofs'. We were hassled once by a 'guide' but with a firm and polite 'No' he disappeared. I also shrugged off the snake charmer's friend at the bottom who tried to grab my wrist to take me to see it. The price, as everyone says, is obscene for what it is and where it is. For the price I would expect many more signs explaining what you're seeing. That said, the Japanese-funded, and seemingly little-used, museum near the cafe/ticket stand is worth a visit to understand more about the history. Sigiriya is often said to be the one sight you must see in Sri Lanka, I wouldn't say it's the best but it feels like a key part of my visit to the island.

As I later found out to my cost, However as we arrived earlier by car and with our own driver we began by visiting this massive UNESCO site beginning at the well laid out museum and working our way towards the formidable looking fortress rock. As you begin to enter the area you will have to fork out around 3,900 rupees each for this privilege around £20 or $30 which is what us "Foreigners" have to pay as the non PC signs inform us. My wife then took the sensible option and stayed behind with our driver Ash along with some cool drinks, while I marched on myself regardless, I was also well aware of the hornet notice signs warning of the dangers. I then found myself walking along and marvelling at the vast amount of ruins which were everywhere while the Imposing rock just seemed to get bigger, along the way you'll see plenty of wildlife including monkeys etc. There are also around 1200 steps going up here into two levels which can be pretty demanding, and really aren't for the unfit to be honest but, there is a hospital tent nearby which was quite busy which was hardly surprising. After a while I reached the Frescos of the naked ladies which were fascinating to look at and well worth this part of the climb, moving on I then reached the lions feet took a breather and noticed the eager crowds had thinned down a bit made their excuses and retreated back, as this was the really steep bit of the climb which I estimated to be around 300 feet up. I also noticed that only around 20 or 30 people were climbing to the summit, so happily armed with my own anti-hornet issue outfit consisting of T-shirt, Shorts, and a pair of Trainers I began to climb up the steep steps and I as reached the last flight of stairs I felt a buzz on the back of my neck, thinking it was fly I killed it..Bad Mistake.... It was a hornet..! This hornet had now marked me out with it's Pheromone for attack, it was then I heard this almighty buzzing like a model aeroplane, before I knew it I was engulfed in a swarm of hornets and what I thought was just a nuisance turned into a fight for life as these insect were going for my soft spots eyes, mouth, ears and even my nose. Before anyone thinks this is an exaggeration, don't underestimate the power, aggression or the coordination of these insects, they can scatter herds of elephants no worries. Being on my own I was in a desperate situation trapped on the stairs, and now one of them had got under my eye lid and bit me on the eye as well as stinging me too so I was blinded, even worse they were in my mouth and I was killing them with my teeth as well as grabbing handfuls of them too. These hornets were trying to kill me and the venom was now starting to take affect as my legs were buckling and I was now hallucinating badly, I made one last desperate attempt to get out on my hands and knees when I heard a voice, it was a local guide up here dressed in a hornet suit who kept trying to pull me out and telling me to run. I did my best but kept falling down amongst the ruins up here, this guy was called Ravi and he guided me to the other side of the Plateau where the wind is very strong and told me to hang on to a rail and the wind blew the hornets off me. It was then I collapsed and came to with Ravi pulling the barbs out of my face, I lay there for about 30 minutes lapsing in and out with the shock, he was very concerned and wanted to get the Sri Lankan military in to get me to a hospital nearby. I politely refused and he offered to help me get back down but, before that he had to go and fetch me a hornet suit as the hornets had marked me with Pheromone for further attack and were waiting for me. During this time I did manage to see the fantastic views but, with one eye shut and my face looking like John Merrick the elephant man. I couldn't even visit the ruins which is what I climbed up to see in the first place, going back down the stairs we both looked like astronauts and the heat was overwhelming in them. Ravi kindly escorted me back down the rock just in case I took a bad turn and I don't really remember too much either, except my wife getting on to me. I also rewarded Ravi for his efforts in helping me as it could have turned out a lot worse, he even commented that it was the worse attack he's ever seen up there, I would like to point out the time of the attack which was 13.00 on the 2/9/14 I say this as there were some fellow tourists who were watching from a safe distance and did nothing to help....THANKS GUYS HERE'S HOPING IT NEVER HAPPENS TO YOU.? I'm telling this story as if you're caught like me then try and run to the other side of the Plateau where the wind will blow them off you..! Even better bring a pair of swimming goggles with you, at least you can protect your eyes, as for me I ended up on a course of anti venom tablets with blurred vision, temporarily losing the use of my left hand, and my entire Immunity system collapsed causing me to catch a severe virus which resulted in getting antibiotic's, even now I'm still finding the odd barb in my head. Not quite the souvenir I had in mind, and yes I did enjoy my day out regardless, I also do believe the sound of my camera lens cover clacking away triggered the attack . And once again many thanks Ravi for your help as it could have been a lot worse up here..!  As for me I bear no grudges with the hornets as they were only doing what nature intended ...Protecting the colony..
Great view from the top, but nothing much else up there,  interesting walk through the ruins at the base.  Lots of monkeys.

An amazing place. A fortress build on top of the rock! 1021 steps to climb, this may seem a lot but there are plenty of resting / viewing galleries. It is awe inspiring how this place was built. The views from the top are magnificent. We did encounter hornets so if you have an allergy be careful at the top section. Would recommend a visit in the morning to avoid the heat of the day
The place is worth visiting the view from the top of this rock is amazing. The climb is long take some water and sunscreen.
Great view from the top, sense of achievement, amazing structure. Quite busy in off season. Don't want to think what season would be like!

If you like altitude, ruins and places with a story behind them, Sigiriya is the place for you. Put simply, this massive rock was used as a fortress-cum-palace for a king to defend against an attack. There are two parts to the climb; the first is from the foot of the rock to the (suggestive) Sigiriya Murals and the Mirror Wall, the second from the Lions Gate up to the top of the rock. The view from the top is like something straight out of a movie. The climb up is very worthwhile but there are some things you can do to make the most out of the visit (which costs 30 USD for tourists) For starters, there are wasp nests in trees around the Lion's Gate. In the event of a swarm, you will not be allowed up to the top of the rock and the ticket is not refundable. Thus it is best to go there early in the morning as there are lesser tourists at this time. Lesser tourists equals less noise and a lesser chance of a wasp attack. Also, time your descent so that you reach the bottom before 6.00 PM as there are wild elephants that inhabit the surrounding forests. Secondly, bring a cap and some water to protect against the sun and heat. There are no shops anywhere except the base of the rock. And be prepared for very strong winds once you reach the top. Also, I don't think you'll need to hire guides for this attraction, pretty much speaks for itself.

Built by an obsessed monarch in the 5th century, Sigiriya or Lion Rock is an astonishing feat of engineering and construction. The most striking portion of Sigiriya, a terracotta and grey core of rock set in the cultural heart of Sri Lanka, rises a sheer 200 metres above a forested plain, its flattened summit sloping gently. A series of moats, ramparts and water gardens remnants of an ancient city spread out on two sides of the rock, with the remains of a pair of giant stone paws still guarding the staircase that leads to the summit, once occupied by a royal palace. Designated a World Heritage Site by UNESCO in 1982, Sigiriya is best preserved city of the first millennium, showing complex urban planning around the base of the rock, combined with sophisticated engineering and irrigation skills in the palace perched on the summit. It is considered it to be one of the oldest tourist attractions in the world with visitors recording their impressions in some of the earliest-known graffiti. For just two decades in the 5th century AD, Sigiriya rose to prominence following a power struggle between two brothers, and an act of patricide that saw the then king walled-up alive by his son, Kasyapa. Fearful that his defeated brother would return from exile to extract vengeance, Kasyapa shifted the capital to Sigiriya and in 477 AD, he ordered the construction of the magnificent city around the base of the rock, and decreed that his palace should stand on top, a fortress that would keep him safe from retribution.

Probably every Sinhalese school kid makes this arduous trek, and it's worth it, to see the fortress built in the 400s by Kasyapa the usurper-king, who ruled for many years, but always knew that the rightful heir, exiled to India, would someday raise a force and come back (as indeed eventually happened). Go first thing in the morning, before it gets too hot to climb to the top. Make sure to see the beautiful rock paintings in the overhangs, and try to imagine what it must have been like to move all of that stone to the top of the plateau with the primitive technology of the time.

Probably the most amazing place in Sri Lanka, Sigiriya is such an intriguing place to visit. Almost 200 meters high, rising out of the plains, it is amazingly developed both for the visual senses and in terms of defenses. From the moment one steps through to the Water Gardens, then through the various strategically placed stairways, and the Terraced Gardens and on to see the beautiful Frescoes, the amazement does not fade one bit. The Mirror wall with so many comments from visitors who came to see the beautiful ladies (Frescoes) and onward to the giant Lion Paws, through which we passed upwards to the summit where one can see the ruins of a great Palace, and many ponds and cisterns for water collection. The Gardens below are said to be one of the oldest and most extensive in the world, for that period. After admiring the view of 360 degrees we descend slowly, through the Boulder Gardens, where a snake charmer awaits with his Cobra and Python. Our driver / guide related to us the story of Sigiriya, and of King Kasyapa before we started up, and that in itself is an amazing story, of Patricide, Suicide, Battles on Elephants and intrigues in the royal court ! Altogether, a truly wonderful experience and a place not to be missed !

Sigiriya is an experience in every sense.  An ancient citadel sat atop a spectacular outcrop of rock, reached only by a steep (and, once, much more precarious) path.  Tickets aren't cheap (about $30 pp, half for 12s and under) but it's worth it.  The walk begins on the flat, through the old water gardens, and then climbing up some steep stairs to the first major attraction.  The portraits of the damsels are located on a wall high above the valley on the rockside, accessible only by a spiral stairway which you walk up and then return down again, before proceeding further.  A short climb further and you are at the Lion's feet and the platform from which to climb to the summit.  This is undertaken by walking up a steel walkway of about 200 small steps, before the top is reached and you can explore what remains of the castle. The climb is not a challenge for those scared of heights except I'd say the most severe vertigo sufferers.  The spiral staircase to the damsels is actually slightly more disconcerting than the final climb but even so, it shouldn't pose most people a problem. The wasps were more of a preoccupation in our minds but even they proved less than we feared. High up on the rock are about half a dozen large hornets nests and they have become notorious for periodic attacks on visitors to the rock.  Our advice would be to go first thing in the morning (it opens at 7am).  This is better because the attraction is a little bit quieter (and the wasps don't like noise) and also because there's less of a chance of there having been disturbances before you arrive (sometimes the summit is closed because of attacks).  Unfortunately when we were there, not all the tourists heeded the advice to go quietly so I could imagine in the afternoon it could get busy (and a bit buzzy too!) We didn't choose to take advantage of the (free) wasp protection gear which seemed to amount to little more than waterproof suits with hoods.  I guess in an attack they might provide some reassurance but I doubt they would repel a sting.  Mostly they provided amusement to the crowds - rows of people climbing a steep mountain on a boiling hot day wearing bright yellow waterproofs. Sigiriya is a special place - both for the experience of the climb and also the chance to enjoy the remains of the castle and amazing views from the top.  Worth making the trip.

Sigriya-a city, palace and garden's on a 200 metre high rock-is known locally as the 8th wonder of the world.The word Sigriya means the Lion Rock. Sigriya is Sri Lanka's most famous landmark and has been declared as a World Heritage Site. Built in the 5 century AD, this magnificent complex of geometrically laid gardens, pools, fountains as well as oldest surviving murals of maidens was the palace of the King Kasyapa. The Complex consists of the central rock, rising 200 meters above the surrounding plain, and the two rectangular precincts surrounded by two moats and three ramparts. The 650 ft monolith was once a rock fortress and a royal citadel from 477 to 495 AD. The most significant feature of the Rock would have been the Lion staircase leading to the palace garden on the summit. All that remains now are the two colossal paws and a mass of brick masonry that surround the ancient limestone steps and the cuts and groves on the rock face give an idea of the size and shape of the lion figure. There are also remains of paintings in some of the caves at the foot of the rock. Of special significance is the painting on the roof of the Cobra Hood Cave. The cave with its unique shape dates back to the pre-Christian era. The pleasure gardens on the western side of the rock are studded with ponds, fountains and promenades showing a glorious past. The miniature water garden just inside the inner wall of the western precinct consists of water pavilions, pools, cisterns, courtyards. The largest water garden has a central island surrounded by water and linked to the main precinct by cardinally oriented causeways. The fountain garden is a narrow precinct on two levels. Western half has two long and deep pools, with shallow serpentine streams draining into the pools. Climbing up the rock (not for the elderly) from the paws of the lion you will see monkeys and the Mirror Wall, a highly polished rock surface that still shines and reflects today. A long climb to the top is rewarded by a panoramic view of the surrounding jungle.
