In case you are planning to visit this amazing place I recommend you to stay at Sigiriya (preferably at Camellia Resort), so that you can cover Dambulla, Anuradhapura and Polonnaruwa. The entry fees is a little high for foreigners, $30 per person and half the price $15 for people visiting from SAARC countries. However, the money spent is worth as you reach the top of the mountain. The requirement of a guide is unnecessary at this site and I'm sure figuring out on your own is much fun than with a guide. The climb to this mighty rock is about 1500 steps, a mix of rock and iron stairs. While you climb up, there are a series of moats, ramparts and water gardens on either side of the rock. However, the most striking portion remains the Lion staircase. The staircase represents a huge Lion figure with its giant paws on either sides and a narrow staircase in between. Climbing the staircase is the toughest part in case its raining or its too windy. The half of the staircase is made of iron steps and I caution to climb carefully as they are very narrow and sometimes slippery. The view from the end of the staircase is excellent giving a multiple ascending plateaus with minimal foundation of the palace that was to be built. I hope you have a great time climbing this mighty rock. Caution tip if its cloudy and drizzling don't forget to carry an umbrella.

We started our Sri Lanka tour with the Sigiriya Lion rock. After landing early morning, we passed through Pinnawela and went straight to our hotel at Sigirya. By 4 pm we were ready to start our climb up the Sigiriya. On reaching there, we found that we need our passports to claim the lower rates applicable for SAARC tourists. This is true for most attractions in Sri Lanka and if you are from SAARC region you should inquire at the ticket counter about the special rates. Lost half an hour in going back to the hotel nearby and retrieving our passports. We were recommended a guide - Pritham by our driver. Going up with a guide who can explain the various facets of the Lion rock is very helpful. We were very impressed by our guide who could speak 5 european languages and had excellent knowledge of the history around the Lion Rock. It is almost a two hour climb to the top. After crossing the moat and entering the Sigiriya kingdom, you start at one of the four entrances. The entrance we went through was the elephant rock - so named because the rock looks like an elephant head. We climbed down a different path and went through the cobra entrance so named because .... you guessed it. :) Mid-way to the lion's paw there is a spiral staircase to reach the caves with all the fresco paintings. This is definitely worth a visit. On the way there are so many places like the throne room, meditation room, public hall, etc which you cannot make out without a guide, because it would just all look like some ruins to the untrained eye. Reaching the lion's paw is not the end of the climb. There is another staircase leading right to the top of the Sigiriya rock. The view from here is simply amazing.

A stunning area and a climb which is not difficult. The routes up and down are well planned and the view from the top quite awesome. The gardens at the base are also impressive. On coming down you should walk to the white buddha, going through more of the site forest areas to a pretty little temple. Worth a vist and closer than it appears from the top of the rock. Note the signs about wild elephants after sunset.

The first stop to the cultural city triangle from Colombo/Negombo, experience a sample of the Buddhist heritage and learn how Buddha was depicted in various poses from Samadhi to chin; learn of his influence in people’s lives through culture, values and his teachings. Sigiriya is another of the ancient capital of Sri Lanka and one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities in the world. It is a world heritage site. This city lies in the banks of the historic  Malvathu Oya, 205 kms north of Negombo. Sigiriya has plenty of rich history to offer to the knowledge hungry tourist. Enjoy.

Climb this rock and the living secrets of the past will reveal before your eyes. Sigiriya Rock Fortress is another World Heritage Site built by King Kashyapa. A citadel of unusual beauty that rises 200 meters above the jungle. This rock served as the innermost stronghold of a fortified town with moat, rampart and extensive gardens all around the fortress to shield his almighty from the enemies. The world renowned frescoes of the “Heavenly Maidens” leads you there through a spiral staircase. When you reach the top, take time to enjoy the panoramic view of the city and take a 360 of the city’s dense jungle and view a prominent white statue of Buddha as it stands visible and in contrast of the foliage all around.
The best attraction in Sri Lanka. Well worth the entrance fees, as the view at the top is beautiful.

This is the one that stuck on my mind the moment I saw it on brochures at a travel show in New York. Boy it did amaze me once I got myself right in front of it early morning this December. There's a quality to its presence that immediately grabs attention, its height like a forbidding fortress hiding secrets waiting to be discovered. So I clambered up those steps, thankfully not in the company of so many others (it's still past 7 am after all) and was feeling happy to immerse myself in this important chapter of Sri Lankan history.

King Kasyapa has build this this palace. An Ancient history were there. Unbelievable ancient technology has been used in there. A fabulous place to visit. Have visited several times. Now the wash room and the other services are well maintained even in a dry zone.
You should climb to the top as the view there is magnificent. Can stay there for a while to see either sunrise or sunset.

Okay, so nobody told that we have to climb 1000 stairs and that too on a steep mountain. It is a difficult climb and the view from top is not that much amazing. Please don't go if you are with elder people or with kids.

I was a little apprehensive to climb Lion Rock as I had read reviews about how hard the climb was and that there were lots of hornets! I have to say, the climb was pretty easy (although if you hate heights this might not be the thing for you!), the stairways were all well maintained and pretty solid and the views were AWESOME. We didn't see any hornets either (apparently it was not the season for them) and it was also pretty quiet- we went at around 8.15am and were up and down within two hours. It can get busier (and hotter) later in the day though. Definitely one not to miss.

The walk through the gardens was a great lead-up to climbing the rock. At the base it seemed like there were quite a few routes up, ultimately they all lead to the same staircase, but it was fun exploring in the shade. Don't feed the monkeys unless you want a whole troop after you. The climb itself is easy and the view from the top is incredible. We didn't use any guides and I don't think it diminished the experience. I'd recommend having a Coke or something at the little kiosk before entering the gardens because you'll get pretty hot going up. There are lots of drink vendors before the car park once you get down though. The price of the ticket is quite steep but there's not much you can do about that because this is a must-see attraction.

there is not too much to see, but I was so disappointed after paying  $ 30 entry (or 3900 rupees), I expected to see something more than a few foundations and less than ten frescoes. The problem maybe is : I love to travel and I have visited several sites but the difficulty to visit and the huge price make this site absolutely not interesting for me
Most of the sign boards were missing saw live frescoes doing the catwalk and people drinking beer which is prohibited within this area very high priced for tourists

We climbed with our kids aged 9 and 5 and were able to climb in about an hour with breaks. The climb itself is not difficult at all and it is encouraging that the site has been improved to ensure that there are different pathways for people climbing up and down. It is a truly magical experience and the views at every level are breathtaking especially at the summit. The frescoes are indescribable and you have to see it to believe it. The place to buy snacks at the lion's paw has been closed . So please make sure you take adequate water and snacks if you are climbing with small kids. Also be mindful when snacking on food as monkeys watch you from afar and can pounce on whoever who has the snacks. A couple of them actually growled at us so feeding them is definitely not a good idea ! There isn't much of a crowd early morning and the rock is also not hot so this definitely the best time to go. You also avoid wasp attacks at this time as apparently they get irritated for noise. You are not permitted to park near the entrance unless you have a permit so you need to park at the three wheeler park and take a three wheeler to the entrance . (Note - Locals please carry your NIC with you, this is checked at the entrance )

Unless you have researched Sigiriya's history both recent and past, like me you might not have much of an idea of what to expect. If you go expecting a tall rocky outcrop with the remains of a fort on top, like me you'll be amazed at what's actually there. It's past history is quite incredible, the scale of the whole place and the amount of work involved is mind boggling. Yes it's pretty expensive at R3900 per person to visit but to really get the most out of this site you need to hire a guide (R1500) to tell you the story and point out the detail otherwise you'll just be another day tripper who enjoys the panoramic view from the top. As others have stated, you need to be reasonably fit to make it to the top of the rock as well as having a fair head for heights. We saw several people who decided against climbing the perfectly safe but quite open stair ways to the top

We climbed with our kids aged 9 and 5 and were able to climb in about an hour with breaks.   The climb itself is not difficult at all and it is encouraging that the site has been improved to ensure that there are different pathways for people climbing up and down. It is a truly magical experience and the views at every level are breathtaking especially at the summit. The frescoes are indescribable and you have to see it to believe it. The place to buy snacks at the lion's paw has been closed . So please make sure you take adequate water and snacks if you are climbing with small kids. Also be mindful when snacking on food as monkeys watch you from afar and can pounce on whoever who has the snacks. A couple of them actually growled at us so feeding them is definitely not a good idea ! There isn't much of a crowd early morning and the rock is also not hot so this definitely the best time to go. You also avoid wasp attacks at this time as apparently they get irritated for noise. You are not permitted to park near the entrance unless you have a permit so you need to park at the three wheeler park and take a three wheeler to the entrance .

Pictures do not do justice to this world heritage sight. The first look is breathtaking ! you walk through the elaborate garden towards the rock and climb through a maze of steep stairs. The climb can be taxing on a hot and humid day. advisable to go a little early in the morning or late in the afternoon. Halfway to the top there are some amazing cave paintings almost 1600 years old. At the top the view is stupendous of the area around and the top has some remains of the palace and the pools of this 5th century fortress. The entrance fee sets you back by 30 US $ , however if you are from a SAARC country , the fee is half. A must visit sight in Sri Lanka.

I really didn't expect to have to climb 1200 steps up the side of a big rock out in the middle of nowhere but i did!  Took about an hour to climb up and 20 minutes to climb down.  I did have the guides with me and i thought that was very helpful.  For the few US dollars that i gave them, it was well worth it for me.  Be prepared - i didn't really know what to expect and didn't really plan to climb all the way up but you really don't have much choice once you get started.  Bring water with you and rest when needed.  Thankfully we had an overcast day and a good breeze blowing so it wasn't bad at all. Well worth the trip to go and hear the history and see the views!
Just great!! Absolutely recommended to visit. Nature and views are amazing! Was so surprised that some people dont find Sigiriya Rock an interesting place to visit..............

Visit the museum first to get a sense of what it's about. You shouldn't need a guide although as we didn't have one, maybe we missed out. The usual hassle from the guys near the entrance is off-putting and we witnessed a youngish Aussie getting serious grief re his payment to a guide. The entrance fee is steep enough as are the steps, so save your money and your breath, it's obvious which way to go and the museum can tell you everything you need to know. The climb is arduous but ok. We're a pair of 60 year olds and the whole thing took us an unrushed 90 minutes, with a fair few photo-breaks. Take some water as the café is inadequate and on a hot day, you'll need it.

Breathtaking in both meanings of the word - the walk/climb up was not what we really wanted after a number of hours on Sri Lankan roads (an experience in itself) but the view from the top was totally worth it. If you get the chance then go. Take plenty of water, wear good shoes and if you are scared of heights then be warned some of the climbing is a bit exposed. But bear in mind that my better half is scared of heights but she made it - down is probably worse than up!

I climbed all the way up to the top of the rock. Despite the rain and fog, it was simply magical. The stairs were not easy for someone with fear of height. But I was so glad that I made it to the top. Wear good shoes!

I was not prepared for the sighting of Sigiriya Rock which  is a huge rock rising about 500 ft. and can be seen from a distance  it is home to a 5th century fortress  on the summit are the remains of a palace with gardens and  pool  .It is a. reasonably  strenuous climb on a very hot and  humid day   There are amazing frescoes on the way up. But the climb is not for those you do not like heights as part of the metal stairs cling to the side of the rock

Just breathtaking. And it is a wonder as both a natural landscape and a site of historical and cultural significance. Take it at your own pace, as it will be challenging to those who aren't inclined towards regular physical activity. We went in the afternoon and found that this was ideal because you still get the sun illuminating the various sites surrounding Sigiriya rock, but you avoid having direct sun on you for the majority of your climb, as opposed to going in the morning.

It is a long climb up Sigiriya, and there are many things to see on the way up that you could easily miss out on. We didn't get a guide, but it might be a good idea to be sure you don't miss things. I was there during the off-peak season, but it was still full of other tourists. The best bit by far was the painted damsels. The top of the rock was also quite interesting as you could see some of how the palace would have been. However the views were no where near as beautiful as the views from Pidurangula Rock, which is just 5 minutes from Sigiriya Rock.

Enjoyed the rewarding hike up the famous rock.  It's a cross between Edinburgh Castle and Pompeii, truly remarkable.  The ticket is a little pricy, but you couldn't really visit the area and not see this.  With the interesting history, amazing frescoes and spectacular views it is an unmissable site.

The rock itself is so distinctive to look at and whilst you can see it without going inside it is definitely worth doing so. You can explore the gardens as well as the museum (interesting to give you the background to the site) but the main attraction is climbing the rock itself. The first bit involves going up to a cave high up in the rock where you can see some old cave paintings - it's a fair climb requiring some fitness and a head for heights. Then by the lion's paws there is a route to the top if the rock. Again you are quite exposed but the views from the top are impressive and there are some interesting building remains up there as well. As with a lot of these sights they are not cheap, but definitely with seeing having travelled so far.
One of the most interesting places we visited in Sri Lanka.  We recommend a guide as they are very informative on the features but make sure you agree a price before proceeding.

This is quiet a climb but worth the scenic views. Lots of steps all the way, carrying water is essential. Beautiful gardens too. I recommend u take a guide if u want an explanation of the full history behind the rock. Our tour guide (highly recommended) Rushaan Cassiere (rcassiere@gmail.com), explained the basics to us before hand.

When we got to sigiriya the price to enter was so expensive at 3,900 rupees and as I am a volunteer it is too expensive. After abit of arguing they still never put the price down but we still decided it would be worth it hopefully. We got a guide and it was so good as he was explaining everything to us and the history behind sigiriya rock and the gardens and boulders etc. Worth it to get a guide! The climb itself was tiring but when we got to the top the views were amazing and breathtaking. Totally worth the money, the sweat and tiredness!

The Sri Lankans call it the 8th wonder. I'm not sure I would go that far but it is very good. A guide is essential otherwise your looking a stuff and don't know what it is. Steps at the beginning get your heart rate put but it not all that hard. If you don't like heights then a couple of places might make you worry a little (just don't look down!) the frescoes have been touched up but it will make them last. Takes about 2 hours tops less if your fit! Enjoy it

This definitely ranks as one of the most beautiful ancient sites i have visited around the world. We left our hotel at 6.45 am and returned by 9 am for breakfast !  Ticketing office opens at 7 am. Recommended to start early morning to beat the crowds and the heat.  It felt like we had the whole place to ourselves on the way up. On the way down by 9 am, the crowd was starting to build up and there was human traffic jam at the spiral staircase. The entrance fee was LKR 3900 - not cheap but well worth it. The entire site is very clean and well maintained. The climb is 1200 steps so bring lots of water, a cap and comfortable shoes. There will be "assistants" wanting to help you up the steps but you can politely decline. The view from the top was breathtaking . The ruins and architecture was awesome . Not to be missed !

This is hard work going up to the top but completely worth it when you are half way there and see the paintings in the cave. And stunning when you get to the top and see the ruins of the king'scastle. Treat it as a work out so wear comfortable shoes such as running shoes or trekking shoes and comfortable pants such as something you will wear to the gym or cargo pants. Jeans and sandals, not recommended. Also keep quiet while going up as there are hornets around and they will come after you if you are noisy. And also it's also good to keep quiet to allow tourists to enjoy the wonderful setting. Just a personal preference.

At 30$ this monument isn't cheap but is not to be missed.  It was our first day and we got trapped into having a guide, he wanted 45$ but got 20$, to my mind still outrageous but we didn't make that mistake again - also don't let anyone help you up steps unless you need it, they will follow you and expect a big tip.  The whole area is well maintained and is quite different to other monuments.  There are 1200 steps to climb (and another 1200 to descend), so it is heavy on the knees and hot work.  The work that went into creating it is awsome, the rock itself is quite beautiful.  There are good informative plaques everywhere so if you care to read them a guide isn't necessary.  Take your time at each level, the cave paintings are really interesting and the engineering that was used to build it remrkable.
Despite climbing in the heat of the day, Sigiriya was well worth it. The grounds, the view, the story were all incredible. Get a guide, it was well worth learning about this amazing site's history.

My husband and I visited Sigiriya and found it fascinating. We began by exploring the grounds where you can see how the water works and gardens were landscaped. We walked through the boulders and began an assent to the top of the rock. About midway we toured the Aspara paintings which are in shallow caves on the face of the rock. These 5th century paintings are awesome. We then climbed on up to the Lion staircase, a spectacular plaza about 3/4 the way to the top. My husband, who loves to climb to the top of all sites, proceeded up the stairs to the top of the rock. He said that the terraced palace site and the view of the surrounding area was spectacular. The sunset as we made our descent was very beautiful. I recommend this site especially for those visitors interested in history.
Start early in morning or in the afternoon, beacause of the hot weather. Just plenty of water and you are ready for the beautiful climb 'til the top (1200 steps circa)

I began an early morning hike. Though it looks difficult, it is relatively doable as it has many attractions on its way, so you don't get tired. Entrance fee: The entrance fee is whooping Rs.3900 LKR. Tip: For Indians (not sure for rest of the SAARC countries, by showing your passport, the entrance fees get reduced to half. Photography Tip: In morning the sun is behind the rock hence would get a good silhoutte (+ plus you hike you in shade) and evening its behind you (while climbing the sun strikes but it is not as harsh as afternoon sun )..hence the pictures come good.

fabulous ancient palace built ontop of a rock surrounded by crocidile filled moats, a feast for the imagination and a great museum swell.  Climbing the rock gives one a sense of achievement, a great view and a justification to go wild on the buffet dinner.

I have visited many ancient ruins  around the world.  Sigiriya was a standout up there with Pompeii and Ephesus. My partner John had not visited any ancient ruins until we visited Polowannaru and Sigiriya in two days!  Both of us preferred Sigiriya and wished we had spent more time there to explore the site. Polowannaru was 41 degrees and we visited between 12 and 3 pm which was just insanely hot. So this may have figured in our preference for Sigiriya. Sigiriya is just a spectacular geographic site with a large rock dominating the landscape and providing a view over the plains.  THe rock itself is surrounded by water gardens and crocodile filled moats.  There is a museum which assists with videos of how the ancient palace and gardens would have looked .  Sigiriya was a tourist attraction when it was the seat of the king in Sri Lanka because a palace atop a rock that commands a view of the plains for miles. Tips to enjoy Sigiriya. 1. Consider staying locally: The local hotels are over expensive but staying locally is a bonus as it allows you to come back and forth to the site.  We climbed the rock in the early morning and then went home to shower and change before returning to the museum.  We also enjoyed an elephant ride at the lotus filled lake at the base of the rock in the evening. 2. Climb early or late.  Avoid the midday sun .  We are hardy fit Australians used to the heat but we were very glad we set off early.  Secondly wear comfortable shoes eg sneakers, takkies , trainers.  Take a hat, wear the hat, and take sunscreen and 1.5 litres of water each.  There is no where to buy water once you commence the climb. 3. Consider the government souvenier shop at the museum.  Alas we were new to Sri lanka and not yet prepared to buy.  That hand cast bell I loved was made locally and I didnt find another on our trip. 4.  the museum has a video of sigiriya in Sinhalese, tamil and english.  We watched it twice in Sinhalese waiting for it to come onto the ENglish version before I discovered two more TVs around the corner.  THe last one is in English.  I suspect a lot of tourists make this mistake. 5.  Consider an elephant ride in the cool of the morning or evening.  We loved it.  And our elephant which we fed two kilos of bananas and 1 kilo of pineapple seemed ok with it aswell.  Our elephant ride lasted 45 minutes probably because we paid $50 US for the two of us without bargaining.  We also tipped the mahouts $10 US we were just so estatic to be that close to the elephant and feeding her. Reasons to Go;  it is easy to imagine the kingdom and ancient society that occupied Sigiriya, the moats are stupendous and the whole site offers a feast of exploration.  We were advised that the site is at its most spectacular in November when the rains have started, the moats are full and the birds arrive. Disabled:  if you are in a wheelchair or unable to climb steps the museum is accessible but most of the rest of the site will not be.  You can hire sri lankans to physically assist you with your climb and descent if you are able to walk but unsteady.  If you are older and unfit, take your time, stop for rest breaks and drink plenty of water.  THere is no need to reach the top.  Even one third or two thirds of the ascent will give you a wonderful experience.   An elephant ride around the base may give you a very special experience.  I am sure the mahouts would figure out a way to get you on top of the elephant.  There is a secure padded seat on the elephant with a safety rail.  We climbed a platform then stepped on to the elephant.  We were also invited to sit on the elephants neck but found this very hot.

OK you are only once in a lifetime in Sri Lanka so you have to see all the highlights but this one is way overpriced. 25 Euro to climb a rock and see some frescos. For that amount of money I can also go to a theme park in the Netherlands.

The very glance of of Sigiriya Rock challenges you, the awesome view of this gigantic rock is nothing but mesmerizing. The day was sunny, we were rightly advised to visit the Rock in the late afternoon.You would easily require 1-1/2 to 2 hours to go around the place.  Be careful while climbing the steps, they have turned slippy. The passage on top is narrow and cantilevered,those who fear heights should be looking in the direction of the nose. The ultimate joy in the endeavour is to reach the pinnacle, the 360degree panoramic view of the surrounding turns you speechless. It is an adventurous tourist destination. Don't forget to carry drinking water you will badly need it. I wish authorities spare some thought on few basic amenities for tourists such as.....
The view was amazing and worth every step. Even the walk to the rock through the gardens was a great experience. Don't forget to bring a lot of water.

Shady trees were welcome in the humid heat. Easy access with a driver who asked us if he wanted a guide. We elected to go on our own allowing us to frequently break our visit to read and marvel without interruption. The climb up 1200 steps is safe, even in the rain which poured down as we climbed down from breath taking views on top of the rock. Take time to look into caves, nooks and crannies at carvings, paintings or ancient features hidden away there. Guides were available, as were all the usual trinkets, but nothing was pushed on us to the extremes of some places we have travelled in the Americas, Middle East or Africa. Min. 2.5 hour drive from Kandy, cave temple, spice garden stops will increase this time.
Extremely interesting part of the country`s history. The gardens are very well kept, and a steep walk up to the top can afford great views.
Well worth the climb - first of all for the Sigiriya Damsel cave paintings, then right at the top - the views.  Go early though

Considering when this place was conceived and built up, the construction and project planning are astounding - especially when you consider the relatively short reign of the king who made this place what it is.  Incredibly detailed planning and execution on an impossible piece of rock make you wonder what they could've done elsewhere.  The climb can be slightly demanding on you (depending on physical condition), so plan to go early in the morning before the sun starts beating down on you and the humid air extracts every bit of moisture from your body :)
Take good shoes, go in the morning, enjoy the walk...and the view. Give yourself time to walk around, explore the nooks and crannies, and have a good day of it.
We loved the rock. We went early in the morning to do most of the climb in the shade. It was 2,000 steps in total; take your time and some water. It is well worth the climb.

The Sigiriya site itself has seen much improvements over the past few years. But the problem lies with guides and touts. The guides and touts don't swarm round you like years ago. But the Guides wait near the entrance or on the way and approach you without informing you that they need to be paid. Tourist think its  FOC and part of the services offered for the US$ 30 they pay. But when the guide demand Rs.2000 for a 2 hour assignment then its too much,. then there are also a bunch of young men who come along and hold the hand of female tourists pretending they are there to help them to climb the steps.

The history and new museum was just being built when we went so I look forward to seeing that next time.  The stone lion entrance and climb is not for the fainthearted so carry plenty of water and wear a hat. The summit has some very old ruins and the view is spectacular.

A ruins of a kingdom on top of a monolithic rock which is accessible by a metal staircase and an hour or more of climbing.  The view is worth the climb and the best way to enjoy this is to find out the legend and history of this king.  Beware the sellers in the area trying to intimidate you into buying their wooden boxes and the price for this attraction is high $30.00.  There are some original rock paintings half-way up.  Beware also the bees which can be disturbed by loud talking and noise (see the sign).  Monkeys are all around as well so keep your distance and enjoy their antics.

Nature, history and good exercise up the steps. Best to hire a turist guide to show the Gates, tell stories and see it all. The frescoes in the upper cave are of woman from different parts of the World. One  of them has three hands. Old times fountain with holes to be seen in the pond area. gorgeous gardens and pools.

I'd seen photos and read about this place for years. Arthur C. Clarke's Fountains of Paradise is based on this spot. It was more spectacular than I imagined. The climb was tough going at times but worth it. The paintings were beautiful and worth the climb in itself. The whole experience was great, especially the views.

The Sigiriya rock complex has 3 gardens before the Boulder garden from where the climb begins. Two thirds up the way is the famous wall paintings of the Sigiriya Damsels, the mirror wall and the Lion's Paw. From there there is another climb to the top. It had been raining from the morning and the path was slippery. I am an elderly person, with poor eye sight. I had decided before hand that I will climb upto the Lions paw and see on the way the frescoes and the mirror wall. Apart from my guide I hired a local guide and with one man pulling from the front and the other pushing from the back, I could climb up quite quickly. In some places the steps were very steep and at others the stairs were hewn from the rock. The insteps were quite high where the stairs have been cut from the rocks. Near the end of the climb to the Frescoes there is a spiral staircase several storeys high. However, there are separate spirals for going up and down and there is a protective cage surrounding the spiral staircases, making it fairly simple. I suffer from vertigo but here I had no problems. On seeing the magnificent frescoes, the climb was worth it. After reaching the paintings it was a level walk to the mirror wall and the Lion;s paw. The descent is by a seperate path and this makes it much easier. I was lucky as the rain had become a drizzle during the climb. One compensation was that the overcast afforded shade and the temperature had come down appreciably. There ws no burning sun.

What a wonderful place and the view from the top is spectacular. We went early to avoid the heat of the day which was always helped by the main steps up the rock being on the shady side early in the morning. Also note, similar to other government owned sites in Sri Lanka, there is a very steep entrance fee for foreigners so be prepared!

We were there at 7:00 when the gates opened and were the only people there. It was amazing to have the entire space and Rock all to ourselves. Made it more special not having hundreds of other tourists around. When we climbed down around 1 - 1.5 hours later, there were loads of people streaming in, so I recommend you go as early as you can.

It's best to climb early in the morning before it gets too crowded with the staircase otherwise your knees start hurting really bad but enduring the pain till we get to the top is all worth it because of the view that simply takes your breath away.

Stunning views from the top. Fascinating back story and very knowledgeable guides to take you up to the top. Climb is a challenge, but provided you have a very base level of fitness it shouldn't be too much of an issue. Thesweat is well worth the reward!

To get to the Citadel, you have to climb Lions Rock - all 1262 steps. This is made easier (not by taking a helicopter or a lift!), but accepting the services of a very fit young man who helps you up the steps for a small fee. It's well worth the effort, the view is amazing
Although you have to put a little bit of effort to climb the sometimes steep stairs, you will be rewarded with amazing views from the top of the lion rock.

Truly Magnificent and for $ 30 it should be (for Indians $ 15). As you enter the long walk to the 200 meter high rock with almost vertical sides you wonder how could men in those early days carry so much material to construct a palace on top of this. The walk goes through a dried up water garden and a boulder garden, all the while ascending. Mid way through there are frescoes which you reach after climbing a spiral stairway. If you have seen these frescoes in the museum save yourself the climb and take a shortcut below the spiral staircase. The mirror wall is not so shiny any more more of a smooth wall finish. Some more climbing brings you to a escarpment with lion's paws hewn out of the rock and some more stairs between the paws leading to the summit. Finally after climbing these stairs you reach the top. It is not an easy climb and those with heart problems could face difficulties as the climb is very steep. The summit is a plateau of sorts with the ruins of the palace in view. The swimming pools, the king's throne and other remains of structures transports you back to the the 3rd and 4th century AD.

October of 2013 my travel  buddy and I visited Sigiriya Lion Rock and were surprised but the extensive climbing, however i persevered even though I hate heights and was not disappointed. My friend however having a balance issue due to a Lazy Vestibular Nerve, had to give up 2/3 or 3/4 the way up and go down early. The last portion after you reach the Lions Feet, is very much on the stair wells on the side of rock more or less, I passed one guy along the way as he was coming down and said, "will I make it"? His reply was very true and helpful, he said: "absolutely, just keep looking down at the stairs, and not out  all around you". This was so true, as long as i focused on the next step, and didn't look around the fear of heights stayed away! I think i was too busy thinking how out of shape I was to think about the heights as well. Definitely needs a bit of a fitness level, which i thought i had, till put to the challenged. I persevered and made and glad i did, cuz the view was worth it!!  Our guide bought the tickets and then seemed to have another guide he hired out of the money we paid him to drive/ guide us for our 2 week S. Lankan visit,  at the sight who took us around, this guide was just at the sight and was fantastic with information, but he seemed to struggle with the climb himself as he had a bit of a tummy, i was worried he might have  problem more than my friend with the balance issue! But he made it!

We were there last week. This is a must see attraction for anyone visiting Sri Lanka. It is a UNESCO World Heritage site and you will see why once you experience the place.  There are tons of descriptions and photos of this place on the web so I am not going to write descriptions. But here are some tips for the tourists. As an expat Sri Lankan, I am ashamed of the ridiculous charges that they have.  RS3900 for foreigners vs Rs50 for locals.  However, most tourists that I spoke to said that the place justifies the charge. Get to Sigiriya either very early or late (around 4 PM for us). This will get you out of the killing heat and humidity and the crowds.  4PM start will give you enough time to go up and start the descent as the sun sets. If you get there during midday, visit the museum (included in the entry price) and wait for the midday heat to go down a bit.  The museum, I am told, is very good and will give you lot of information to understand once you enter the ruins. Take plenty of bottled water with you. Nothing is available once you enter the site. Wear comfortable clothing and walking shoes are a must. A local guide at the site will be of much help. However, there are many "guides" at the entry that will try to tack on, so if you can arrange a guide through your travel agency before reaching Sigiriya, it will be better.  If you plan to visit the museum first, you may not need a guide. Wasps.  They are a real danger, however, our local guide told us that they are present on the rock only during the cooler season - during rain. The rock gets too hot for them at other times.  Warning signs of wasps are everywhere but do not get alarmed.  People say that strong perfumes will get them agitated and so will loud noise. If you stay in one of the hotels in the area overnight, you can do both Sigiriya and Dambulla Rock Temple (another World Heritage Site in the area) easily.  The top end hotes in that area are really good - comparable to top end hotels that we have experienced in Caribbean and Latin America. In the near by Minneriya National Park (one hr drive from Dambulla), you can encounter one of the largest heard of Elephants in the world. Spoiler alert:  Here are some photos from our visit. https://picasaweb.google.com/106724093066537855605/SriLankaSigiriyaAndDambulla?authkey=Gv1sRgCLzE2ImaidHvVQ

First thing you should do before you start is visit the Museum it contains artefacts and information that will make more sense of this place and the computer generated representations of what it used to look like were very informative and interesting. We were driven to the entrance by our guide via the old road which passes by the outer walls and moats that used to surround the rock. After some History about the rock and the museum visit we were basically left to our own devices, which was fine by us. This is an impressive Historical site even from the ground with points of interest before you even begin the breath taking (in more ways than one ) climb to the top. On more than one occasion I found myself marvelling at how this place was constructed with such basic tools or was it just to have a rest from the climb? The remains of the Citadel at the top are impressive too, the site is almost like a mini Machu Picchu in appearance and the views are incredible and make the climb more than worth it, as is the cooling breeze. It can get very windy at the top so literally hold on to your hats. We saw a couple of guys making batwings from their jackets and leaning at almost 45% angles into the wind without falling. Great photo material from almost every angle and probably one of the most impressive places we have seen since Angkor Watt in Cambodia (possibly the pinnacle of all Historical Sites). Take plenty of fluids and don't expect your drink to be cold for more than a few minutes, take the climb steady as it is quite taxing in the heat ( I cycle 5 days a week 50 - 100 miles and was winded on more than one occasion ). When you get back down to the bottom watch out for the people offering to show you a short cut back to the car park, we unfortunately being curious went the wrong way and fell for this, our "guide" decided that the $2 I gave him for showing us the way was not enough and wanted $5. I told him $2 was plenty and that was the end of it, thankfully. If you are in Sigirya you simply have to do this it's a must, highly recommended.

Fighting off the insistent man who wanted to be our guide to the sight, we bought our tickets (Rs3900 for foreigners, Rs50 for Sri Lankans). These were expensive by UK standards, let alone Sri Lankan and our Sri Lankan friends felt shamed by the difference in prices. We were a little taken aback. Understanding we earn more than Sri Lankans do, put in a system of concessions for schoolkids and the aged then find ways of presenting the experience that wealthier European or Asian travellers would pay premiums for rather than out-and-out gouging. There was no guidebook to the site and no audio guide on offer. There were no official guides and little evidence of any attempt to structure the experience as a value-added one beyond 'pay up and go'. In some ways, this adds to its charm - it's not slick and over-developed. But then in others it detracts - the pestering tour guide, the lack of any facilities. Even the availability of cold water. That apart, the site itself is splendorous. You travel through the ruins of glorious water gardens and what once must have been an amazing citadel towards the rock towering above you. You can see the steps climbing up to the foot of the rock, then the gantries and walkways stuck to the side of it and vertigo already cuts in. We chose a hot, sunny day and it was warm going. There are charming signs all over the place telling you to stay silent to prevent hornet attacks. Shame they weren't in Korean or Japanese. The hornets, presumably unable to speak Korean or Japanese themselves, let it pass. The climb up, taken with care, is not onerous if you are relatively fit. Many choose to go as far as the 'lion's feet' and leave the final - and most vertiginous - part of the climb to more foolish folk. It's only when you're traversing rock a couple of hundred feet from the staging point below looking out over vistas of Sri Lanka's forest carpet that you realise you're standing on a structure maintained by the Sri Lankan Office of Public Works. On the way up you pass the Mirror Wall, a porcelain wall once apparently so burnished the king who built his palace atop this 200 meter-high boulder could see his face in it. You also get the chance to clamber up a spiral staircase to look at the remains of the frescoes some experts believe once adorned much of the rock. We passed, it was too hot, too busy and none of us much liked the look of the buttressing holding the viewing platform together. Struggling to the top (not because of the climb, but negotiating the press of people coming down - even a section which had two walkways was so busy that people were pushing past going and up down on both), you're rewarded by an amazing view of the lush countryside, as well as a scramble through the stepped ruins of the palace, complete with a huge cistern and water pools. Apparently yer one had 200 wives and liked to disport with them here. You can't blame him. It didn't do him much good - he was defeated and fell on his own sword in AD495. Delightfully, once you've struggled to the top and wandered around a bit, you come across a sign that says 'GOING DOWN IS DANGEROUS'. Thanks, wish you'd said that before... Suck it up, cough and pay the inflated fee. Give this at least half a day. Do not, under any circumstance, pass it by.

This is located some 40 mins from Dambulla. You need to purchase a ticket of LKR 3900 per person. You can hire a guide if needed at extra cost. We did not. There are descriptions mentioned in all necessary locations. The climb to the top can be tiring if taken in the afternoon. We reached at around 9am and reached the top before 11am. This way we climbed in the shadow of the rock, hence, it was easier. Very breezy at the top too. The first view is of the paintings of women in the cave. It is very beautiful. Probably the only thing that justifies the high cost of the entry fee. On top of the rock are the famous lions paws carved out of stone. Atop the rock, there are just ruins (low brick walls) and a pond. If you cannot climb, there are people to either carry you or hold your hand and take you. We heard from someone that you have to pay $25 to each person helping you. There are proper stairs and handrails for the rest.

The world heritage centre at Sigiriya is a place not to miss, but be warned it is not an easy climb to the top with over 1400 steps, most of which have risers taller than average and some cling to the vertical rock face with nothing more than fresh air below you. Take your time and stop for breathers at regular intervals and the climb will be more rewarding with stunning 360 degree views from the top. It is quite mind boggling that at some time in the past an entire palace adorned the top of the rock, and to have to go up and down daily must have been a daunting task. Take plenty of water with you because once you have left the museum at the base there is no opportunity to buy more. Yes the price is expensive at 3,900 rupees per adult especially as you seem to be doing all the effort, but there were not many visitors at the time we visited and the place is probably quite high maintenance and requires such a fee to keep it in a safe condition.  There is also a stark difference in the price the locals pay, but on the basis that they earn considerably less than your average tourist, put it in perspective, they should not be denied the opportunity to visit their own heritage.

We (children 20-22, parents) had a private tour guide that was as well our driver. The rock of Sigiriya as part of our roundtrip around Sri Lanka was for sure one of the highlights. We arrived when it was a bit rainy and of course the walk up the rock was in this hot and sticky air totally sweaty. But never mind, it absolutely worth it because the view is breathtaking and unforgettable. Altough it is not for free it shouldn't be missed!

Definitely the highlight of my trip. I really enjoyed the fascinating story behind this historical site. It really is not for the faint of heart, so if you're afraid of heights it might be best to skip out on going all the way to the top, but I say it was well worth it. Decent footwear is a must and if it's raining, be sure to ask your guide for an umbrella.

Woah amazing from bottom to top!  It’s 370m high and looks unbelievable as you walk to it.  Entrance is $30 each so quite steep for Asia but worth a visit.  Guides at the entrance will offer their services but these aren’t needed.  You need some level fitness to ascend but you can take breaks all the way.  Plenty of water is needed and good shoes/ walking sandals.  We started around 2.50pm when temperatures were decreasing but still very hot.  The views from the top are breathtaking.  All you can see is green – like nothing we’ve seen before.  No buildings at all – beautiful.

Sigriya itself is an amazing experience. Huge in scale, wondrous in nature. Great experience if a little scary i almost gave up but my lovely hubby encouraged me and i got to the top ( and he is the one withe the fear okf heights!) I would have liked a better guide though to learn more about the history. Helpers attach themselves to you and we though they were part of the steep entry price. They were forceful and rather than fight we just let them help. At the bottom we took money out to give them a tip but they refused and demanded more money quite an exorbitant rate actually.

One of the most impressive historical attractions that I have ever seen. Although nothing too alarming is encountered, for those with a major fear of heights it might perhaps be necessary to avoid the final ascent (even though the structures on and view from the top are excellent) and the picture gallery - the latter reached via a spiral metal staircase. The rest could easily be done - and IMO would still be worth it. The walk up is moderately energetic - but with appropriate pacing it seemed quite easy. Reasonable shoes, a hat and bottle of water would be wise - one cannot get any such items once one has entered the attraction. The amount of labour and engineering expertise that must have been required to create this structure are hard to comprehend. The entrance tickets are quite expensive - approximately £19 per person (October 2013). However, it seemed quite good value as everything seems so well organised and maintained. We opted for a local guide - this made things easier/better paced & sequenced (even then, the total time for our unrushed visit was around 2 hours). We paid the guide ~£10 - which included a generous tip as he was so helpful. However, one could have managed very easily without a guide. There were only a handful of people selling local merchandise on the route up - they were all very polite and were not too persistent. We made our visit as a very long day trip from Hikkaduwa (which is well south of Colombo), combining it with Dambulla Caves. We hired a car and driver (which one can do at a very reasonable  price in Sri Lanka - for this 600km round trip we paid - opting for a reputable company - £135). We  started at 4am and got back to the hotel at gone 7pm. It was an easier and more successful trip than we could have hoped - but we did it the hard way.  There is no doubt that the trip from a town much nearer to Sigiriya (such as Kandy) might have been rather easier! Our trip was still well worth the time and money involved.
A good walk.. Well organized...  Beautiful views.  Went up there with a 4 year old, 7 and 11 year Olds...  Some areas were not very safe but we're manageable.

A stunning historical site - make sure you wear decent footwear.  My vertigo got the better of me half way up but my husband and daughter made it via very precarious steps.  Well worth the effort if you're braver than me!

My son (13) and I had two spare days while recently in Colombo. We booked a tour with Upendra De Silva. He met us at our accommodation in Colombo and took us to the main train station. We caught the train to Kandy (which was fantastic). Upendra drove up to Kandy while we were on the train and picked us up. We then saw many of the sights in the area over the next 3 days. Upendra was a fantastic guide. We was very informative and took time to explain things to my son. We climbed Sigiriya which was well worth it. Best done early morning to avoid the heat. I would highly recommend Upendra.

We got there early in the morning and it was already very hot! The 1,000 + climb was def a challenge but worth it. We had to stop a few times to catch our breath (most other ppl had to do the same). I'm glad I did it and do recommend it to others. Wear comfy shoes and take lots of water. Tip: Do not ride the elephant in the lake you will see below when you get to the very top. We saw it and being excited, went to ride the elephant after our climb. It's overpriced, the owner was very rude and I can tell he doesn't treat his elephant well. The poor thing :/. Go somewhere else to ride an elephant.

Well worth the climb although being a bit older it was fairly hard work, we had our own guide So did not get pestered by people offering to help you climb etc. glad I made it to the top views Are fantastic and the site can be really appreciated from the top, a must if you are nearby

Despite the site's heritage and fame, this place has been on my list for quite sometime although I am generally not in favour of climbing places and travelling too far. This time I decided to go ahead with my wife. The site opens at 7 am. Entrance fee Rs 50 for locals and USD 30 for foreigners. What I understood was if a local fails to present his or her Sri Lankan identification (even if they are truly locals) by means of National Identity Card (NIC) of a Sri Lankan passport, they are required to pay the fee of a foreigner. However a reimbursement facility is given to claim back the fee (I think within a week time) if the local produces any of the above identity at the Site's office in Bauddhaloka mawatha in Colombo-7. Entrance tickets are also sold at this office. We reached the site around 7 am in the morning and started the climb. The climate was bit of a concern earlier but fortunately the time we went (3rd week sept), was perfect, partly cloudy. The area is generally known to be high in temperature most parts of the year and I heard a local say that there hasn't been rain since the year began. The steep spiral steel steps did make the climb harder but it was worth it. When we reached top, the view was absolutely spectacular. We sat by the rain catchment pool and glazed above as the unpolluted air swept away our tiredness. Stepping down wasn’t a big deal and didn’t in fact realize when we reached the ground in no time. A day would be more than enough for a return visit but if you consider a rest necessary after the climb, Guest houses and Hotels on Dambulla road and nearby the Site would be a better option. As we planned to visit the Golden Temple the day prior Sigiriya climbing (climbing both places same day could be disastrous), we checked-in at a Guest house on Dambulla road. Many others have written in detail about the Site reviews therefore I’ll skip that part but a friendly suggestion will be to keep your hands free as much as possible during the climb and avoid carrying Back-packs. Whatever you carry will just add more weight during the climb. The scorching temperature could also slow you further down if you do not start early. Many visitors from Colombo seem to have trouble making decisions on how to reach this place when it comes to distance and means of travel. Majority book through Tour agents and some through Vans or Coaches and they do cost quite a lot. We travelled this way from Colombo on our own: Day 1 - Colombo Fort to Kandy by Express train (2:30hrs) : Start 7am, reached Kandy at 9.30am. Costs between Rs 300 and Rs 500 per head depending on Reservation Class. - Breakfast in Kandy (45min). A tuk tuk to Kandy town (to a decent restaurant) would cost Rs 100 but while returning walking is preferred because of one-way routed traffic and all-time terrific traffic. I mean it! - Kandy to Dambulla by ‘Anuradhapura Intercity (Air-conditioned) Bus’ (2hrs). Costs around Rs 200 per head. Frequent buses available one after other. Dont forget to remind the Bus-Conductor to tell you the place you need to get down. - Arrival and check-in at Guest house by about 13:00hrs. Refresh and lunch. - 10min walk to Golden temple. Climb takes around 1 to 2 hours return depending on whether you wish to see the Tallest Buddha statue and visit the temple’s museum. - Return to Guest house. Refresh and dinner. Day 2 - Took a Tuk Tuk at 6.30am and reached Sigiriya site at 7am. One way costs around Rs 800. - Reached Guest house by about 10.30am. - Refresh, lunch, 2 hours rest and check-out. - Dambulla to Matale by Cab (1hr). Costs about Rs 3000 - Matale to Kandy by Intercity A.C bus (1hr 30min). Costs Rs 130 per head. - Kandy to Colombo (Pettah) by Intercity bus (2hr 30min). Costs Rs 290 per head.
this is a must visit if you visiting Sri Lanka. This place has great value when it comes to ancient architectural and technology.

The guide book told us the ticket office did not open until 8:30 a.m. this is incorrect. We got there at 7 a.m. - just as they opened and glad for it. It was a comfortable and quiet climb up the stairs. Was we were coming down, met up with a lot of people who were struggling with the heat.

I recently spent two weeks in Sri Lank with three friends.  It was one of the best holidays I have ever had.  We toured around visiting many of the ancient world heritage sites, such as Sigiriya, Historic Polonaruwa, Anuradhapura, the Caves of Dambulla, as well as having days at Kandy with its beautiful botanical gardens, Hunnas Falls and beautiful beaches such as the Camellia Resort, Nilaveli Beach and wonderful Marissa Bay.  The country was so beautiful and the people so friendly. What made the visit absolutely perfect was our wonderful guide Siri and his driver Pria, who kept the minibus clean every day.  They could not do enough for you and were great company. Siri planned a brilliant itinerary for us, but was flexible. He was extremely knowledgeable and interesting in explaining the country’s history. We had so much fun  So if you are thinking of visiting this country, do visit Siri’s web site http://www.srilankalegacy.com/

We visited Sigiriya during our honeymoon in Sri Lanka. Such an interesting part of Sri Lanka's history and so beautiful. We ignored the advice of our tour guide, who said we wouldn't need the help of the Sri Lankans who work their helping you climb and my husband and I were very glad of their help. Well worth spending a couple of pounds and that's all it was. 1200 or so steps to the top, stopping to send some amazing ancient frescoes on the way to the ancient palace on the top and the most amazing views of stunningly beautiful Sri Lanka. Definitely recommend visiting Sigiriya! Wow!

A great place to visit an amazing piece of engineering a good climb to the top but well worth it. I would suggest doing it with out a guide as your not going to get lost and the guide book tells you all you need to know. You will be approached by many helpful locals but I suggest you politely decline any requests they offer

This is really a amasing experience to see the rock from far and then the next moment you are on top of it. The walk and climb is not difficult at all because the steps are well planned. Really a must do fro anyone visiting Sri Lanka

Yes this place is expensive by Sri Lankan standards to get in - $30 - but the view from the top of the rock is worth every single penny. A stunning climb up steps and stairs - we felt secure and safe and loved every single minute. Take your time at the top - theres plenty of room to wander around - find your own spot and take in the views. Top Tip - go EARLY!! It is hot and sweaty making that climb - and that was at 8am!

Started our climb at 8 a.m. and along the way we left 4 of our party behind. Started off by crossing the 10m deep moat and ramparts, then walked through the once magnificent 'Water Gardens'. Walked past Monk recluse caves before climbing our first set of stairs. (Stopped for a breather.) Climbed the next set of stairs. (Stopped for a breather & admired the view.) Walked along a catwalk, then climbed a spiral metal staircase before entering a rock chamber to view the stunning rock paintings. Back down another metal spiral staircase, then walked along the 'Mirror wall'; check out the ancient graffiti. Up another set of stairs that overlooks the 'Reception / Seat of Government Hall' before stopping opposite the magnificent 'Lions feet'. (Stopped for a long breather, enjoyed the wind, amazed at the size of the hornets nests well above us on the rock face & admired the view.) Walked up a seriously long set of stairs to almost the top. (Stopped for a long breather and enjoyed the strong gusts of wind.) Walked around to the huge swimming pool! Then proceeded to the very top for our "Toyota moment" (jumped for joy). Very strong gusts of wind and stunning views, on the way down we saw 2 different species of monkey. (The oldest member in our party is 80 and she made it to the top . . . ) The whole Sigiriya Rock experience is well worth the exertion.

I first saw Sigiriya from above while flying over it when in 1971. Thereafter I have climbed on to this many times. I was fortunate to meet a historian/archaeologist once while viewing the frescoes of the 1,000 wives of King Kashyapa. He was able to identify that King Kashyapa had wives not only from Sri Lanka but also from Mongolia, The Middle east, Africa, India & Bhutan. He was able to differentiate the races. I have been intrigued by the dynamics used in the hydro systems to pump water in the mega structure. This was not only a palace but also may have been a Royal nightclub at 1,000 years ago. The view is stunningly breathtaking. Be careful not to talk loud or shout as it would upset the hornets nest. The attacks from hornets is not wanted.  Take a super wide angle lens with a large aperture to photograph the frescoes. No flash is permitted as it damages the frescoes. Best time to Photograph is early morning before 8 am.

We were a bit worried about climbing Lion Rock because of steepness, and wasps around it. But it turned to be fine. It was a perfect day for hiking, not too hot, and not raining. The only drawback was that it was a Poya day and there were too many people climbing rock that day creating traffic jams on stairways. try to do it on week days for more peace to enjoy on top of the rock.
A real climb but worth every step! The Sigiriya paintings are wow! The view on top is great and was real cool after the heat of the climb. Do it early morning or late afternoon to avoid the heat.

I was slightly anxious about the climb as I don't get on well with heights but it was not at all scary (apart from the prospect of the bees swarming). The views from the top are breathtaking and the feat of building a palace on the summit more than one and half millennia ago is awe-inspiring notwithstanding the fact that slave labour would have been used. A holiday to Sri Lanka without visiting here is like a visit to NYC without ascending the Empire State Building.

Besides admring the view from top of Sigiriya rock, there is one more thing to admire on this rock. Visit the cave gallery located about half way up the rock. There you can find a series of fresco paintings depicting topless female figures bearing graceful motion of offering flowers and fruits suggesting their spiritual existence. The fresco here are one of the finest example in the world, withstanding 1500 years of gushing wind.

My mother is a sri lankan (with sri lankan passport), my father is a german, so i have a german passport. Still i am half sri lankan and also lived here for several years.  At the ticket counter my mother wanted to get 2 local tickets because i am also under 18 years old, after a long discussion in sinhala they said it was ok. Then at the security checkpoint they started making a fuss again telling us to get somekind of signature to accept it! We were so pissed off! And also there is no equation between both prices 50 rupees < 3900 rupees, of course we left then. They expect way too much money and exploit the tourists (which are so stupid and pay all the money) Dont let yourself get ripped off! In europe, the us and australia we also don't charge local and foreign prices! In situations like this it is really a shame to be half sri lankan!!!!
Even if you are afraid of heights go up as far as you can. Guides will come and assist you but you will have to pay them. The view from the top is breath taking.

Be prepared to do a lot of stair climbing if you want to experience the worthwhile views from the top of Sigiriya rock. On the way up you will stop and see the wall paintings as well as the mirror wall and the lions feet. The climb isn't difficult but can be crowded, which can give you a welcome rest. Make sure that you have enough cash to pay for $30 entrance fee (around 4000 rupees) as they don't accept cards - paying was probably the most unpleasant experience with locals pushing their way to buy a ticket.

You cannot miss this. Brave the climb and the heights and experience this world class attraction. Words can express how amazing this site it. Crowds were not too bad and up on top it was easy to get away from the groups. The school groups (there were a few of them) were full of smiles and letting them past was the way to go. I was never keeping up with those young legs, besides as they went past you got to see all the smiling faces. Our kids, 7 and 11 made the climb easy, even with the elder one's fear of heights. There are a few scary moments but it all just adds to one of the best travel experiences I have ever had.

Sigiriya is a must for any Sri Lanka itinerary. It's a huge site - with lovely 'water gardens' at the base. (shame it wasn't raining as the water to 'power' the water gardens comes off the top of the rock! The main focus is on the rock - which entails a fairly hair raising climb. It looks worse than it is and for the majority of people is definitely achievable. Just keep on going. The view from the top is stunning. The murals on the way up are stunning. The palace, perched right on top of the rock must have been majestic in its time. Definitely worth it. Spectacular

The climb is not as hard as I expected.  My main tip is to go as early in the morning as you can.  We went up at 7.45 and it only took us 25 mins to reach the top.  We spent another hour up there and already to go down the crowds were thick and slow.  It is really a worthwhile thing to see, great views and the brick work is spectacular. It is easy to picture the buildings when they were whole and we were in awe at the work that had gone into the construction. It is a highlight of our holiday, it is up there with Anchor Wat in Cambodia.

You cannot miss this site if you're visiting Sri Lanka. One think to remember, your fitness levels should be up  to date, because is a good workout. Don't give attention to locals trying to sell anything or everything. You're there to climb this rock. Don't accept help for locals , they normally try to push you up the steps. Just say NO firmly . You need good sun protection, we had and small umbrella each and a large bottle of water. Take your time to climb and do in 3 or 4 stages. Once up there just enjoy the view . Great place
It wasn't my best experience ever.. I don't like to climb this unsafe place.. A cable car can be more interesting for me.. Could be an idea

As you approach this rock it is truly a site to behold. We walked up to the very top, up hundreds of steps including a spiral staircase that is fixed onto the rock itself - very scary! Once at the top the view is amazing, and has the remains of a palace that the king at the time built on the top. The colours in the rock is truly startling.  Well worth a visit!
I used a local guide and I'm glad I did, I learnt so much more. The climb up the rock was not so difficult and the views from the top were amazing. It is worth a visit.
The machu picchu of Sri Lanka, grab a guide book, brush up on the history of this ancient site and climb to the top. Its worth every step.

The site itself is a lovely place, it was part of our overall holiday package so I'm not aware of how much it costs but its a nice afternoon out. We spent a few hours here and a small group of us managed to get separated from our tour guide. We new what time the coach was leaving so attempted to find where we had parked. We walked back to where it had dropped us off and we were told by locals / Staff how to get back to it, evidently the easiest way was to walk round the perimeter to the opposite site where all the coaches were parked. As we approached the car park there were some armed (Guns) guards in a small Hut. They immediately stopped us and demanded money as we had 'left the grounds and needed to pay' we tried to explain that we had already been paid for and were simply trying to get to our coach at which point they became agitated and aggressive. We could actually see the car park as not that far away but they refused to let us by. By this point it was getting dark and in Sri Lanka it goes from light to dark very quickly, so rather than be stranded we paid them about £100 between us to get back to our coach. An unpleasant and unnecessary experience that soured our trip and demonstrated a greedy and hostile side to an otherwise pleasant and helpful tourism industry in the country.

If you want to understand the story of Sri Lanks this a spot that you can't miss. Be prepared to climb "some" steps and be amazed by the work done by Ceylon ancestors.  From the hotel get a tuck-tuck and a local guide and explore this wonder of the world.
we went with a guide who explained the story behind this marvel and it was truly amazing,i cuoldnt believe that long time back they had this much of technology

This 5th century palace is well worth the visit.  The walk is tricky if you have vertigo, but the view from the top is worth it, especially the lovely pool there.  The surrounding gardens are also impressive. My 5 year old managed the walk to the very top, but it proved too much of a challenge for my 7 and 8 year old. There are many local men, who try to help you on the way up, hoping for a tip.  But we ignored their attentions. The cost was around USD30 for adults and USD15 for children.

This was an amazing experience, would recommend very highly to anyone. We weren't to sure when we arrived and even having to fork out US$30 each, we questioned is this really worth it? We got an excellent guide who spoke good English and explained everything very well. Would highly recommend a guide , we learnt so much more. The views from up on the Rock were exceptional, the sheer scale of the site was extraordinary , the Frescoes amazing.The climb not too challenging but not for the faint hearted or one with vertigo! Just don't look down whilst climbing the steps. Even the few sellers were not a problem they did not hassle. Well worth the money. The Museum was good, also part of the ticket. Worthy of an 8 th Wonder of the world status.

A great day but do it first thing in the morning before all the buses full of tourists arrive. It takes awhile to get to the top but it is worth the 1200 steps up and you can do it at a leisurely pace

My girlfriend and I were already in Sri Lanka when another friend emailed me and recommended we visit Sigiriya.  We made arrangements with the hotel's driver to take us there.  I am 66 and my girlfriend is about 10 years younger.  Reviews here had me a little skeptical as to my chances of making it to the top, but we both made it.  Worth every step!  The view was amazing.  Just before the final climb are a troop of monkeys, which we were advised not to feed those extra bananas we had.  I am sure that would have led to a much different review if I even had hands left to type.  The big cage is a reminder of the large honey bees that have their nests alongside the mountain. The cage is available to take cover in should the bees become disturbed.  Myth has it that the bees are incarnations of King Kasyapa's soldiers.  We had a guide, but did not need him.  A little reading before the trip would have eliminated the need for one.  Along the way, "helpers" grabbed at our elbows, but we were aware of their intentions to extract more money from us, so we pulled away.  It is expensive, around $30, to get in.  Tourists pay dearly for their stay in Sri Lanka.  The only negative comment I have is that we were led around quickly and missed the museum entirely.  The guide made sure we were diverted through a pack of hungry gift sellers.  One even chased us to the car trying to make a sale.   I am sure this is a day trip, but our driver was on a schedule so we had to leave after we arrived back at the car.  It is certainly a beautiful place for a picnic.

This is a must do attraction in Sri Lanka. Yes it's a long steep walk to the top, but is absolutely amazing. If you are scared of heights, you will not make it to the top as the stair ways are steep, open and very high. Also if you are not in good health I would not attempt the climb. If you do make it to the top you will be amazed how this was built in slouch a location. The vision of the designers such a long time ago is sensational. Top tip, as everywhere in Sri Lanka, tips are what people live on, so if approached by someone offering information on the attraction, either stop them quickly or use it to your advantage. Won't cost much but can be annoying if you want to be left alone to take in sights.
Sigiriya is not to be missed! Well worth the climb, only moderate fitness required. The views from the top were spectacular and the ruins amazing...... Loved every minute of it.

Sigiriya was one of the highlights of our Sri Lanka tour. The walk up was thoroughly enjoyable. We are not particularly fit but didn't find it taxing, and the views are absolutely amazing. We went on a cooler day in November - it was spitting for most of our downward journey - and I think that helped. In the roaring heat it may have been a much tougher walk.

My driver took me there and dropped me off. I had read on Lonely Planet to be careful as a woman traveling alone and it sited guides cannot be trusted in certain tourist sites. Well, I think this was one site they were referring to. I ended up getting a guide, I thought it was better than being alone in this huge space with a lot of local men milling about. The guide added context which made it more interesting for me, they expect around $10, if you choose to use one. It was beautiful and I did not think the climb was too bad (I have been climbing a lot of temples :) and definitely worth it. While we walked around there were locals everywhere and they would talk to my guide and it made me really uncomfortable as they stared, etc. The guide told me there are 120 guides and they can't all be used everyday so they rotate days, so I think it was guides hanging around on their day off? I was constantly on guard and at the end the locals exit to the right and the foreigners exit to the left and next thing I know we went from being around many people to none. And it was close to closing time. My guide stopped walking and was looking behind us, it seemed to me he was looking for an opportunity, so much so, I got my phone out to call my driver. I walked ahead and thankfully we saw people and I got to the driver okay. I met two women who had a guide and they felt uncomfortable too. I do not want to scare anyone, it is definitely worth visiting, it was one of my favorite sites here. If you are alone, especially a woman, I would just highly recommend joining others to see this site.

Great climb to the top. Make sure you take plenty of water to drink on the way up. Even first thing in the morning, it's a hot climb. We did get approached by guides but they weren't persistent. One guy at the paintings suddenly started pointing out features which was useful but we made it clear we didn't want a guide although he still asked us for money. We didn't realise we were walking past the mirror wall as its not sign posted or obvious so we missed that bit. More guides at the top who just look like they're sweeping the area. They point things out and then, once again, ask for a tip. Didn't hassle us though. The way down isn't sign posted and we just followed other people. Eventually we got to a point where a guy told us which way the car park was and which way to the museum which we wanted to visit. Really enjoyable way to start the day.
The climb to the top is not that hard and well worth the effort. We didn't use a a guide and found it easy to navigate. Views from the top are great.

Definitely best to go in the early morning, when the steps are in shadow, because it gets very hot as the day goes on. I did wonder before we started whether I would cope with all those steps (I'm fifty-something, and not particularly fit) but I had no problems at all, and it felt like an achievement when I finally arrived at the top - and the views are spectacular!

We visited Sri Lanka on our honeymoon in May 2013, Upendra De Silva was our tour guide for the nine days we spent in the country. Upendra provided excellent service and fantastic commentary on all the sights and history as we made our way from Colombo to Habarana to Kandy to Nuwara Eliya then onto Bentota Beach. The Sigiriya was one attraction we attended throughout our journey and was an amazing piece of history steeped into an architectural masterpiece. Visiting Sri Lanka for the first time accompanied by the friendly and wise Upendra was an uplifting cultural, historical, natural as well as spiritual experience. We highly recommend visiting this country and having Upendra as a guide to any would be travelers looking for a new and uplifting experience .

As you approaches the site, the rock emerges reaching 200m vertically above the vast plain of Sigiriya reminding you the movie Close Encounter of 3rd Kind. A entrance fee of $30 is really expensive for getting a experience of walking up and having a 360 degree view of the vast plain. You need to be fit to walk up the narrow limestone stairway and at the Lion Platform last stage of ascent where a narrow flight of metal stair in single file leads up to the summit. The plateau is crowded with people and can be very windy so ensure your hat and stuff is secured with you otherwise it will be blown away.

The Citadel of Sigyria is a must for anyone who travels to Sri Lanka. It was one of our highlights. It is an amazing place with the ruins of a palace and magnificent views for miles around. The climb looks daunting, but despite the heat we made it to the top OK. There is no need to hurry and you can rest along the way, particularly near the Lion's feet. But remember to take water with you! There are plenty of local guides who will undoubtedly offer their service, but you really can do this on your own. Just take a copy of the Lonely Planet and read it as you go. But beware when you are climbing back down. When you get right near the bottom turn left towards the car park rather than go back through the gap in the two boulders, where you would have entered. There is a con job going on here. There were three men sitting there who we think removed the exit sign or covered it. They wait for you to go through the rocks and then offer to guide you out. Despite us immediately realizing what we had done, we couldn't shake them and they demanded a fee for their "service". They were taking it in turns to shake down the tourists. It left a bad taste in our mouth, but the wonder of Sigyria overrides it.
Great views at the top, good hike to get there, interesting gardens at the base. Be ready for the daunting spiral and end staircases, especially at crowded times.

The museum is ordinary but the climb to the top of the rock and the view is exhilarating. There is not much that is intact by way of ruins and one wonders at the originality of the art work on the cave walls high up on the face of the rock. The hands intrigue me. The colours are quite reminiscent of art work I have seen in Italy from the 15th Century. Beware the steep winding stair case, the heat and the wasps.
