We hired a van -cheaper than a car and more comfy than a tuk tuk with a very polite quiet driver who didn't quite make the bowser at Sigiriya and had to go in search of diesel in a nearyby village to get us there. I hitched a ride on a motor bike and started the climb before the heat set in.

We spent the day in Sigiriya. we took a local train from Dambulla for just 30 rupees and arrived within 30 minutes. The entrance fee is 30 dollars per person which includes an entrance to the museum as well. The gardens surrounding the mountain are beautiful and if it is a nice day the views are incredible. The walk up isn't hard at all and doesn't take long. Although the museum was only built two ago it is a bitrun down which is ashame. By the way a deffinite highlight is the monkeys who are very cute and friendly. They aren't aggressive like in Thailand or china. A day well spent. In our opinion you don't need a private driver. Just do it like the locals and take the bus

Sigiriya is a world heritage site full of culture and history. Climb the rock to be at the top for sunset. It is an incredible view any time, but the sunset on a clear day is the icing on the cake. The climb can get a bit overcrowded, but at least that means that you are not exhausting yourself getting to the top. The frescos and mirror wall on the way up are interesting. The ruins are really intriguing. How a community could live in palatial surroundings on top of this rock is beyond imagination. Our driver ensured that we were there at the right time. Finding a good driver in Sri Lanka is not always easy, but I would recommend Nishan at countrytravelclub.com. We have used him twice and he ensures that you do not miss out on seeing attractions at the right time.

Go early in the morning to avoid the queues on the climb. Liked: the views, the history, the climb itself. Disliked: the queue later on as people arrived in numbers - it's single file, so the ascent is at the speed of the slowest person.
Beautiful grounds, stunning views. Lots of steps so good footwear needed. The climb to the top is fantastic.

Totally amazing palace ruins perched at the top of the rock, an incredible feat of engineering from the 5th Century AD. The climb is quite hard work but broken up into sections, the final third being the hardest. Would certainly recommend getting there early morning to make the ascent in comparative cool, and fewer crowds.

Seriously $30?! Expensive ordeal if you're going to take the family. Site itself is interesting and reminded me at times of a little Siem Reap. Climb I expected to be a little more arduous and into right mindset most people won't have any problems doing this walk. Lovely views and interesting history just not for $30 a pop. Add this to the other sites of Sri Lanka and you've found yourself a couple hundred bucks out of pocket just for cultural triangle and the activities within.

Lion Rock was among the highlights of a fascinating visit to Sri Lanka.  Climbing was challenging for me but stopping periodically and drinking water made it very possible.  I did not need to hire one of the local guides for the climb up but I did have to tread very carefully.  We climbed at the end of the day when the heat was not as intense and that helped as well.  In addition to spectacular views of the countryside, the sense of accomplishment at the top was well worth it.  It also felt great to get some exercise after spending a good portion of the day on a tour bus.  Those in our group who did not want to make the climb were able to relax at the museum.  I highly recommend including this on your Sri Lanka itinerary.

Tickets USD30 for foreigners (Adult) but it is worth it and do bring your passport. As you enter, you will pass a really peaceful moat, reportedly filled with crocodiles when the city was flourishing. Then you will come upon the gardens where you can still see how the water is channelled in. Then you will start an easy climb where you will see how water is harvested with water ledges. Guard posts on bolders with steps carves into the bolders. After the fall of Sirigiya, the city was handed over to the monastery whereby many of the water ledges were used as meditation locales for the monks. Next stop will be the paintings of the King's ladies. The 18 paintings that are still visible are in pretty good condition. The paintings were done on wet plaster where by natural dye is injected into the plaster. If you look closely, you will find that some ladies have oriental and afrikan features. The space here is really small so the earlier you go, the more space you have! Then you will come down to the mirror wall. It looks like any normal wall but if you have the patience, you will find some singhale inscription. They are small & was informed that there were poems written in ancient times by people who were so impressed by the city. Then you will get to the Lion's paws. Good place for a rest. Then the hard climb  starts but when you get to the top, the view is fantastic! And it is extremely windy up there too. There you will find a swimming pool carved into the rock! Just imagine being King and you have all the views and the wind! Tip : Might be worth it to get a guide if you didn't have time to research before going. Bring water and hat (make sure the hat can be firmly attached to your head or else it will get blown away!). All climb is on staircase so hiking boots not really necessary. Go as early as you can, I think they open at 7am. We got there at 7.30am. Reasons being the heat and the crowd. Not suitable for people with movement difficulties. My knees and thighs were turned to jelly when we got back down! But kids seem to enjoy the climb. Probably not suitable for those with fear of heights too.

My kids aged 6 & 11 yrs climbed it fairly easily however my wife quit midway. Make sure you go in the early morning or late evening hours as the heat can increase the difficulty tremendously. There are a few stretches where it gets very crowded and have to walk in a file. Overall , we had a adventurous climb , the kids enjoyed the thrill of making it to the top from where the views are really good. Well there is nothing really exceptional , but if you go to Sigiria and dont climb the Lions rock then its pointless.

Climbing the Lion Rock Summit has been the most amazing experience.After buying the tickets and showing the passport( which is mandatory) you have to to walk through gardens to reach the summit. Its better to go in the morning and carry water. Its advisable to wear comfortable walking shoes because the climb is steep.We took our own sweet time to climb, resting and gazing at the panoramic view.The rocky steps are  chipped.Finally reached the Lion's paws.The climb from the Lion’s Paw to the top was difficult, along very nar­row metal stairs with rail­ings attached to the side of the rock. Finally reached the top.. “Wow - well worth the climb to the top!” and what a magnificent view this place has to offer. I will always remember my climb:):)
It's an amazing place, a history, a great example of eastern sculpture and construction technology. Afternoon time is a better time to climb up.

Looking at the ruins one can tell that what an amazing place it must have been at it's peak. With ponds where 500 concubines used to bath for the pleasure of their king! Breathtaking panoramic views from top. We/all the tourist looked like a plague though ... littered all over the place.

It's hard to imagine any visit to Sri Lanka being complete without a visit to the ancient city of Sigiriya, a network of moats, pools and walkways ascending through giant boulders and terraces to the sheer face of a giant volcanic plug, the rock fortress, rising the best part of 500 feet above. The ascent of the rock fortress, via a series of stone and metal stairways, is recommended for anyone of even moderate fitness, and leads upwards through the gallery of famed frescoes and the Mirror Wall to the large platform, the Lion's Paw Terrace, at the foot of the Lion Staircase. Ascending between the two giant stone paws, an iron stairway then rises steeply to the summit, the site chosen by King Kasyapa for his palace. The panoramic views from here are well worth the climb, and there remains much to explore at the summit itself, where a network of paths, stairways and terraces lead around various points of interest, including the king's stone throne and the large pool, both hewn with ancient tools from the rock itself. The descent, on which - it goes without saying - care should be taken, follows a different route down from the Lion's Paw Terrace and skirts the wooded base of the rock before reaching the walk's end point, an opportunity to refresh and refuel and, should you wish, to purchase Sigiriya related merchandise. All in all, Sigiriya offers the visitor a richly rewarding experience, combining stunning views, an exhilarating ascent, culture, history and lore...well worth the entry fee, and surely a must-see for any visitor to Sri Lanka.
It seemed daunting at first but what a view and what a feat of engineering it must once have been - magnificent!

So most here write about how this is not a problem for those of moderate fitness.  But what if you don't think you are?  Or have bad knees (where stairs are an issue).  Yes, you can still climb the rock.  Think about your fitness and levels of heat tolerance an make your own decisions.  So first of all - allow about 3-4 hours if you aren't sure of your fitness.  it will take you longer.  Morning is better as you will feel less rushed and it is cooler.  But if you don't mind the heat - try after lunch.  Lots of people come first thing in the morning and it is much more crowded (but if you aren't fit you aren't going to be rushing up to the top anyway).  If you are less fit - hire a guide.  They will carry your backpack - your water - your camera etc.  Also there are places where the stairs are steep and there is no handrail (in the beginning).  The guide will help you up these stairs (lend a hand or shoulder).  Also if you are less fit and walking along slowly - every guide will run up and pester you.  Just get one at the beginning and negotiate a price up front.  Offer a little extra if you get to the top!  My guide was super encouraging and suggested the obvious - take your time - stop and rest - and then keep going. A little over halfway up - at the lions staircase - there is a flat area where people can stop and take a break.  This is also a good place for a snack if you brought one (and your guide carried it!).  After this the staircase is metal and some found it steep.  But it has handrails so it is much easier to navigate.  Also the metal staircase has several landings - so there are places to stop and pause if you need to.  Finally at the end of the metal staircase - there are more steps (another 50-100) to get to the top (these do not have handrails).  So if you are less than fit - you will not be up and down in 1-2 hours but it should not take all day either.  Allow about 3-5 hours.   When coming down - you will come down the metal stairs - but then there is a path downhill with few stairs.  Again - my guide showed me the way to this path and I'm not sure it's that obvious without a guide.  The path can be steep as well - but was easier than going down stairs.  For those with knee (or hip or whatever) problems - I'd also say take an anti-inflammatory before you start and then take more about 4 hours later.

We really enjoyed Sigiriya. Initially I was looking forward to the trek with a mix of anticipation and slight dread because all anyone seemed to talk about were the zillions of steps.  In reality, it wasn’t that bad.  Yes, the Lion Rock is 200m high and there are more than 1200 stairs but there are plenty of places to stop for a breather while you enjoy the amazing view or the small group of surviving frescos.  There were four of us climbing, plus our guide Sumedha, but we just went at our own pace.  Our two kids (11 and 14) charged on ahead, my travelling companion went next and I puffed along behind whilst Sumedha kept track of all of us.  We met up at the lion, and then again at the top. My friend and I agree that if we had the same day to do over again, we’d take a (light) backpack and stop for a mini-picnic when we reached the lion gate.  It’s easy to lose yourself in the climb but it really is essential to pause and appreciate the mastery of your surroundings on the way up, too. The view from the summit is incredible: one of those vast, lonely landscapes that make you feel tiny and insignificant and totally exhilarated all at the same time.  It was only slightly breezy at ground level and the lion gate was protected by the summit, but it was howling an absolute gale up top.  We spent ages wandering around just taking it all in while Sumedha told us about the regions amazing history (I should probably mention that Sumedha wasn’t one of the ‘guides’ from the car park; he was our guide/driver/nanny for the whole trip, which is the only way to go in Sri Lanka if you ask me) My friend didn’t overly descending enjoy a couple of the metal flights of stairs near the top, but he was fine.  The stairs are sturdy, there are handrails and the ‘bad’ parts don’t last long, as some others have also mentioned. I know a lot people climb the rock early in the day but we chose late afternoon and it worked really well for us.   By the time we arrived it had cooled down a lot and most of the crowds were gone.  A few school groups were making their way down as we climbed up but we shared the summit with only a couple of other people.  The trip back was quick and easy because we pretty much had the steps to ourselves.  Dusk was falling by the time we reached the car park.  Late afternoon is a fantastic time to visit Sigiriya but keep an eye on the time because I wouldn’t want to descend those steps in the dark! This was one of the highlights of Sri Lanka for us.

This lesser-known wonder of the world was created by a volcano whose sides have long since eroded, leaving a gigantic igneous tower in the middle of the beautiful, green Sri Lankan jungle. Named Sigiriya, or the Lion Rock, by the early Sinhalese inhabitants, it was thought to be built on by King Kasyapan in the 5th century, though archaeological insight suggests it's most likely always to have been a Buddhist monastery. Either way, 1) it's incredible to comprehend the layout and presence of antiquity from as soon as you step into the ancient city at the bottom of the rock, and 2) once you're at the top, the citadel and the views are utterly mind-blowing. People, understandably, gush about Machu Picchu, and while I wouldn't draw a competitive comparison between the two, it instantly struck me as somewhere that shares the same qualities - remote and naturally dazzling setting, millennia-old character, evidence of ancient design, incomplete historical understanding - and all of these to a spectacular extent. A brief practical note if you are afraid of heights (like me): it is not too bad, so please don't be put off. At two different points on your ascent, you walk up 20th century iron staircases that give a slightly precipitous view. You are quickly past them, you have sturdy handrails to hold on to, and you'd shoot yourself if you missed the reward of an outrageously good view which is only moments away.

Much has been written over the centuries, on the virtues of the imagined splendour of the ancient fortress of a besieged and paranoid monarch and the sensuous enchantment of the drawings of alluring celestial damsels on the several cave walls. What is hardly ever mentioned, are the series of works along the "mirror wall" in script that predates modern Sinhala which a Sri Lankan scholar attempted to decipher during the last century. The many inscriptions on the wall extol the visitors' impressions of beauty of the maidens in their naked innocence. The scenic views are hardly ever mentioned, as the ancient travellers had not seen anything remarkable about the vast stretch of jungle, with lakes scattered at random. The symmetry of the architecture is mind-boggling as a work dating at least fifteen centuries. One wonders what technological equipment could have been used to design the structures (moats, gardens, ponds) exactly the same in proportion and exactly the same distance from their opposite member. Similarly, how did ancient technology enable water to be pumped up several hundred meters from ground level, to the king's palace? It is quite impossible that rain water was the only source despite the existence of reservoirs hewn from the rock, in what is part of the "dry" zone of Sri Lanka. The fact that the site also had metal industries (foundries, furnaces, smiths) needs more study and investigation with modern technologies. When climbing the rock, do dwell on these issues and pause along the way to reflect. That will make your visit more thrilling and educational if not entertaining. Lasantha Pethiyagoda Melbourne, Australia

Best time: Start morning. Tickets: $15 for SAARC countries (Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, Maldives, Nepal, Pakistan and Afghanistan), you have to carry your passport to prove nationality for discounted tickets. Wear comfortable shoes. Guides: If you are interested to know about the history, it would probably a good idea to hire a guide who are easily found. I had come all the way to Sri Lanka to see this once thriving medieval city and decided not to consider the alternative, to not see it. My Sri Lankan friend and I started the climb after visiting the museum (included in the ticket price).   It took about an hour for us to reach the summit. On the way up, we saw the cave with the graffiti maidens and the mirror wall.  Once we reached the top, the ruins of the palace were in full view along with stunning panoramas of the water gardens and Mount Pedro (the tallest peak in Sri Lanka).  One can only imagine the scale of the summit palace from the ruins. Recommendations: We went during a very hot month (early May) and were soaking in sweat by the time we reached to summit before noon.  Next time I visit, I would go to the museum after climbing to the summit, as the museum is air-conditioned in many of their exhibit rooms.  To have avoided the heat I probably should have started the trek up much earlier. It helped to be somewhat fit and also not acrophobic.  The stairs going up during the second half of the trek (passed the Lion Paw’s Gate) is quite narrow and pressed against the rock.  There are many, many stairs to the summit.  Generally, I have no problems with heights, but when taking photographs of views during a pause, I found my hands trembling while holding the camera. Big Tip! If visiting Sigiriya without a guide, watch out for the guys trying to sell their services as a guide.  I regret that I allowed one man to follow me up all the way to the foot of first flight of stairs.  He was so bothersome and didn’t seem to take no for answer. I had missed viewing the water gardens just trying to get away from him.  Only until I expressed, emphatically, my displeasure and annoyance of him he turned away.
excellent place to break journey while climbing Sigiriya rock castle and proceeding to Anuradapura

I echo all of the positive comments made about this attraction.  I truly loved my time here and wish it could have been longer. If I ever go back it will be a better experience because I learned the following: It is good to arrive early to climb but the museum doesn't open until 8:30 (the park opens at 7).  Once you get done climbing you are exited down the other side of the rock so to go back to the museum is not at all convenient. There are numerous "helpers" all over.  They are as aggressive and pesky as everyone says.  If you are a woman traveling alone, hire one who looks agreeable and tell him you'll pay him "x amount" to do nothing more than take pictures of you in front of cool things and keep the other "helpers" at bay.  It will be the best money you spend there. If you are afraid of heights, you won't like climbing the rock.  I am not at all afraid of heights but with the high winds and small stairs, I felt a little nervous. Just because you can make the climb in sandals doesn't mean you should.  Wear good shoes to minimize your chance of stumbling. Give yourself the time to enjoy this amazing place.  You're going to spend $30 to get in, you may as well get the most out of your money. There is a lot to see (much of it at the base of the rock) and it could be a very peaceful place to sit and rest for a while.
it's a nice place to visit, but does not worth the 30 USD entry fee, anyway you can have nice photos in that place and enjoy the view from the top of the rock.

I believe there are over 1500 steps to the top, but it is worth it - just take some water.  Wonderful view and lots of monkeys. There are guides available if you wish and some local handcrafts at the base. The entrance is a bit pricey with that;s Sri Lanka these days.  At least it goes towards preservation.

Hi All! This year january we been sigiriya and also we did 7 days tour with Uplanka Tours.They gave us to excellent service. also I have never seen like sigiriya it is wonderful place to visit any travelers. sigiriya is a ancient kingdom and it was build by king kasyapa. It was amazing place. this is a best place to visit.

Amazing site and was named as one of the world's natural wonders. A must visit if you are in Sigiriya and well worth a visit. Its amazing to see that a kingdom has been built up on the rock and how huge it may  have been in the historical years. This is Sri Lanka's most visited tourist attraction which has a very rich history.

At $30 for foreigners the entrance fee is quite high, but I'm so glad I went and, to justify the high fee, the site must need constant finance for maintenance. For local people this is a 'must see' as the entrance fee is pennies. It's a fairly easy climb up and down (even in flip-flops), but best to start early to avoid the heat of the day. Having said that it's an easy climb, I don't mean that you shouldn't take water and wear appropriate shoes; but that there are steps and railings which take the fear out of the descent for me. It is an extremely well kept site with absolutely beautiful views, well kept gardens and water features. Truly amazing! Definitely worth a visit!

Lions rock is a must see destination when visiting Sri Lanka. Best time to climb the rock (stairs) is early in the morning (I think they open at 6 am, but please check in your hotel or with your guide, driver etc.). Yes, there are many stairs, but it sounds worse than it is. We (2 parents and 2 teens) are not the worlds best sporstman, but we managed with no troubles. You just take enough water with you and rest here and there. Climb leaves you speachless, specially considering only a part (the first part at the bottom)of the stairs were there originaly, the other part were the ones you see carved into rock. View on the top is worth going there, history of the rock is owsome. The only down side are (too) high etrance fees for forign tourists (100€/4 people), without a guide.
It was amazing, hard work and very hot. The views even from half way were breathtaking. Be prepared, take a sun hat, suncream and water.

I am of a certain age, not as fit as I could / should  be and seriously terrified of heights, yet climbed Sigiriya and could not be more thrilled. Here are my tips. Go early before it gets too hot and before the sun is on the rock, and to beat the crowds. We started at 9am but it opens at 7am. Wear your joggers. Take water and a hat. Our driver recommended a fab guide. He encouraged us to rest regularly and not rush. He also reassured us that we could turn back at any time. He then encouraged, advised and lent a supportive hand under my arm when needed. Told us to focus on the back of the person in front during the hardest parts. Also explained the history and significance of what we saw.  I will be honest, there are times when it is very scary if you have any fear of heights. But I made it through all the gardens, up all those stairs (including the spiral staircases up /down to the painted frescos of the apsaras) and across the scary landings, along the mirrored wall, up more stairs, as far as the lion's feet. Decided to not push our luck, and gave the final ascent a miss. (The wasps were buzzing around the final staircases and we had to retreat to the net enclosure for a minute or two.) Thrilled to have climbed. It was a highlight of our trip. If I did it you probably can too. But get a recommendation for an experienced guide and don't forget to tip him well when you get down. (Well worth 3,000 rupees to us, as we would not have done it without him.) Still can't believe I climbed!
The fort rock was worth a climb (1260 stairs as we were told). Very beautifully & neatly maintained site.

Amazing experience, make sure to take a tour guide with you to explain all the amazing history and events that took place hundreds of years ago when the king lived here. It's a great sight but be sure to wear proper shoes as the climb (mostly all stair steps) is high and extremely lengthy, approx 12032 steps to the top The grounds around the rock are equally interesting and steep in historical value.

This was one of the highlights of our trip, but not for the faint hearted. Neither me nor my husband are afraid of heights, but this climb made us nervous! A real sense of achievement at getting to the top and great views, interesting frescoes not to mention great exercise! Be careful not to attempt the climb if it is raining though, can imagine the small metal steps nearer the top of the rock can get very slippery when wet.

As others have said, this is an impressive sight.  It makes you really understand the scope and scale of the history in this area.  A must see!  Take sunscreen, water, a hat, and be prepared for a little work.  Snacks and drinks available on the site are limited. The Museum is remarkable.  Quality exhibits, great explanations in multiple languages.  The water and fountains running throughout create a great atmosphere and a cool breeze.

If you love rock painting go to see Sigiriya frescoes. Their smile will remind you many Monalisas. If you love rock climbing , go to Sigiriya summit. You will witness the grandeur of the Sri Lankan Heritage. If you are an architect, lover of Gardens dont miss this heavenly place, as it is one of the best garden lay outs of all time. If you are a traveler with a will to comment, search more about the graffiti on the mirror wall. You will experience the taste of the travelers of yesteryear's. If you are in Sri Lanka DONT miss this place. IT is one of the best sites Sri Lanka can offer.

If not for its colourful history, Sigiriya is definitely worth the visit for its ancient artistry. Sigiriya is a rock fortress/kingdom that is unique to Sri Lanka if not the world. History records it was built by King Kassapa in the 4th century AD. Apart from the remnants of his palace on top of the rock (that commands a land area of over an acre), the palace gardens, moats etc extend over a wide area from the base of the rock. However the famous fresco's and "mirror" wall are what attract most to this place and are worth reading up on prior to a visit. I have climbed this rock 8 times and never tire of it. Happy climbing.

It starts from the very bottom and ends on the very top, inbetween a steep climb that can make you breath: a unique historic experience, worth every minute, every mile and every dollar (the UNESCO has to maintain its sites!). We went in september: no rain (global warming changes monsoon), but as well nearly no people. Enjoy the girl's frescoes, the gate with the huge claws (half-way to the top) and the view from the top. Walk around the garden, pools, irrigating system..... If you suffer from dizzyness of a hight, the climb might be some kind of a torture. in any case: carry a bottle of drinking water with you - and a camera (respect: no flash for the frescoes)!

Our guide/drive Amitha was very good on this trip as he was on all the others because he took us first thing in the morning. After buying our tickets 7000 rupees we walked through the kings pleasure gardens with pools and fountains, which I'm told are still working but weren't that day, while Amitha went to park the car and met us at the boulder garden where the steps to the top of the rock go. Must admit seeing the rock from a distance I couldn't imagine how one could get up there but it wasn't half as hard as I had expected from what other people had written (and I'm 65 not a twenty year old!). The first steps are carved into the rocks then there is an iron walk way and stairs attached to the rock face. Halfway up is the "mirror wall" with beautifully conserved wall paintings of women, preserved from the weather by an overhanging rock. The last part of the climb, entering through lions oaws,  was in the sunshine but it didn't take long and we were on the top looking over a fantastic 360° view of forests with an occasional stupa or statue of Buddha shining white in the distance and the lay-out of the gardens below us. There are only low walls left as remains of this palace fortress but enough to get a good idea of what it must have been like. Going back down was a lot quicker and on the way back to the car we walked through other parts of the gardens with caves and strange rock formations, the most noticibale the cobra's head. It is well worth the money (which goes to it's upkeep) and the walk up. My advice is do it in the morning when you will find most of the climb in the shade.

Sigiriya is an icon of Sri Lanka and I have been there twice. Nowadays an extortionate charge of 3750 SLK is made, 75 times what the locals pay and this is a part of a "soak the tourists" mentality that we have found widespread in Sri Lanka. Having said that we climbed it in the heat of the day taking plenty of water. The advantage was that we avoided the crowds which appeared later in the day. There are steps all the way and half way up there is a gallery of rock paintings of very nubile young maidens reached by a steep staircase.. Fortunately their somewhat inaccessible location meant that the escaped the destructive attentions of religious extremists through the ages. The view from the top is magnificent and well worth the climb. The gardens at the bottom are worth a leisurely stroll past ornamental lakes and gardens. Allow about 3-4 hours at a leisurely pace. Ignore the guides who will help you up[ for a very large fee and feed you misinformation about the place on the way up.

You have to go here as it's pretty unique. It's similar to Ayer's rock in that it appears to have been dropped there from outer space. It's slightly higher than Ayer's rock however. The cost is high 3750 rupees for tourists, but I think it was worth it because of it's rarity. You first go through the walled gardens up to the rock. There's then a climb which starts off ok, and then get's genuinely scary. The climb involves walking up a metal spiral staircase to a cave and then up another metal staircase to just below the summit, then things get seriously scary. The metal staircase from there up has small steps and 2 handrails but is otherwise exposed to the sheer drop below. The steps have gaps between them so apart from looking straight down at the steps, anybody who suffers from vertigo isn't going to have a good time. On the way down, I could see that if you slipped on the steps, you could fall down the steps and through the gap at the bottom to certain death. What you do have to avoid this fate, are 'guides' who are there looking for nervous prey. To be fair, the guide was useful not only at getting me up and down the steep bits but also taking me on a tour of the top and pointing out the water tanks, the dancing hall,the king's palace etc. The going rate for a guide is 500 rupees but they don't mention a price when they first start assisting. I knew the rate beforehand, however. When I'd go past the worst bit on the way down I thanked the guy for his time at which point I suggested 300 rupees and he said £20 was the going rate! I moved to 500 rupees and he insisted on 1000 rupees. I said tough luck and gave him 500 rupees and he went away muttering under his breath. I don't feel sorry for the guy, I'm sure he's got £20 from somebody in the past, but not specifying a rate straight up and then demanding what is a fortune for a Sri Lankan is not an acceptable way of doing business.

bring your own water, umbrella and wear lots of sun screen! if you guys dont eant to climb there are pictures and videos of the rock itself that you can enjoy. the paws are the only things thats left and they make great pictures. you can pass this climb if you like. not for the feint of heart!

Not for the faint hearted! Unfortunately that turned out to be me. A long climb to the Lion's paw with spectacular views. Amazing to think the stairs had been carved out of solid rock all those years ago. From the lion's paw it was a sheer climb up the side of the vertical rock via a metal stairway. Many of my colleagues did however make the climb to the gardens at the top.

Went up the rock at 7AM. It was an easier climb then I had imagined but take water and remember some parts have a huge drop with not much holding you in, although I would still say it was safe. We were the only people on top when we got there so this may affect our review but It was stunning and highly enjoyable. Entrance fee was high but when you are the only ones there its well worth it.

It is worth making a special trip to see Lions Rock, easily one of the top attractions in Sri Lanka. However... Beware the guides. As we went through the gate a guide was hanging out and kinda joined us. We asked him how much to take us through and he told us what ever we felt was fair. At the end we gave him 1000 LRK, which was too much but we enjoyed ourselves. However he told us it was not enough and wanted 1000 LRK more! I would say skip the guide, there is lots of informative plaques all the way up. Also beware the angry hornets. There is several huge nests of them as you climb up the Lion entrance. They come out of their hive and sting the climbers when it gets hot (after 12pm and especially in August). Note: there is a safe net house at Lions Entrance that you can get into if the hornets do attack.
The rock is amazing, and the climb (up stairs) is not nearly as challenging as we thought. The museum (which adds another $15 to your ticket) is not worth it, no matter what Lonely Planet tells you!

Sigiriya is magnificent and well worth the walking and climbing to get to the top as the view is magnificent. I would highly recommend this not just for the ascetic outlook but also for the cultural experience. One of the highlights from our recent trip to Sri Lanka!

There are no words to describe the magnificence of this rock. It looks much better in real life than on any pictures you'll see. The view from the top is fantastic. The stairs can be a bit scary if you have vertigo but they are very very very safe. Just beautiful.

The site of Sigiriya is one of the great ancient sites of the Asian continent. The many rock shelters and caves here were occupied by Buddhist monks from the 3rd century BCE onwards. In the 5th century, a beautiful royal palace was built here by King Kasyapa, atop the towering Sigiriya rock, nearly 200 meters high. Around the rock, are the remains of the magnificent capital which the king made at that time. It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The Sigiriya Cave is a heavenly place. The paintings carry forward the tradition of apsaras, celestial maidens who carry offerings of flowers for deities and venerable beings. The paintings of the Sigiriya Caves, of the 5th century, in Sri Lanka, are very similar to those of Ajanta, in India. They have the same inward look and a lyrical grace, which reminds us that there is an end to the sorrow of the world. The painter’s gentle touch shows us that his eyes are filled with sympathy and compassion for humankind. These 5th century paintings display an exquisite rendering of volume and form. The skilled painter persuades the eye of the softness of human flesh. Above all, the expressions transport us and take us to a realm of peace and beauty. The painter’s gentle touch shows us that his eyes are filled with sympathy and compassion for humankind. These paintings carry forward the tradition of apsaras, celestial beings who carry offerings of flowers for deities and venerable beings.

The concept of a fortress of such grandeur being built on top of a towering rock is astounding. The climb is steep but worth seeing the beautiful frescoes on the face of the rock as well as the ruins on top. The museum does an incredible job of visually recreating what the site would have looked like and documenting the treasures recovered from the area. Well worth the effort and price.

I went on a rainy day and it was a little tough to go all the way up. Lot of walking and climbing stairs, but every moment up on the rock is worth the effort. Take half a day for this trip and have a night stay in Sigriya. You can cover Anuradhapura or Kandy the next morning.
It's a solid 2 hr ascent/descent. Make sure you're fit. Probably not worth the entrance fee for what's there.

A visit to Sri Lanka will not be complete without visiting the Citadel of Sigiriya. The grounds massive, the climb tiring, but it's an experience not to be missed. We did this together with our 6 and 8 year old on a wet day. The wind was strong, the stairs were wet, and my youngest wanted to give up after reaching the Lion's Mouth but we encouraged her to push on. It was such a great feeling standing on the summit, and experienced how the King Kashyapa must have felt looking down from his palace. The frescoes of the Apsaras were very vibrant even after all these years. It's absolutely worth the climb and worth the money (entrance fees is not cheap, but it was worth it).
people, culture and food just amazing. I enjoyed my whole trip, meeting friendly people, eating amazing food and the scenery just breadth taking - will be returning in August for the Kandy Festival

hi ! The ancient rock fortress of sigiriya is a stunning site for any enthusiast. Surrounded by the lush green forest where wild elephants roam, the rocky mountain is visible from many miles away. We could see it from our hotel. There is an ancient garden with ruined buildings on the bottom of the rock. the rock is surrounded by a man made ancient canal. on the top there is this fortress of an ancient king. but guys you have to be careful as there are hornets in the area. sings were there advising to be silent. Up with Tikal (Guatamala) in the ruins stakes. Insanely built complex on a vertical rock. Marvel at how they built the stairways up (bearing in mind the King had vertigo). Be there at 7 am as you will have the top to yourself. Sit down as we did for 2 hours and contemplate the feat of engineering. Sri Lanka must do.

Really is a site of outstanding beauty. Take the guidebooks advice and visit very early or very late in the day, not just to avoid the heat but also the queues. I'd made it to the top in about an hour (08:30) and there was hardly anyone around, ideal for taking in the views and getting some quality photographs. It is a bit of a trek but if you're able-bodied it well worth the graft. As others have said $30 is steep and the local touts are annoying but once you're on the climb it's breathtaking.

Nice to visit lions rock. it is very beautiful place & amazing place to visit in Sri Lanka. In that tour my driver "Calli" was very friendly and kind experience person to explain my tour for me. he show me lot of important places. i never expecting to see places like that. he is a good driver for visit in sri lanka for tourists. i recommend for him to any one like to visit sri lanka. His email is callisrilanka@gmail.com
Very nice to visit. Go early !! We did this at 7am. The most of the crowd comes later. Don't take any advise of 'guides' that want to show you the way. They only want money for nothing.

On a scorching day we slogged up the 1200+ steps; however it was well worth the effort.  The cave paintings were exquisite, and the views along the way and from the top were exquisite.  And we bought a beautiful carved "magic box" for $10 for our daughter from one of the sellers (his initial asking price was 4 times that.) A wonderful morning, even at the admission price of $30 each.

This was a fascinating thing to see. Walking through the gardens, toward the massive rock, I couldn't believe that I would soon be climbing it, let alone that a palace was built on top such a long time ago. Expensive, yes, but forgettable, no. Go with a guide, so that you understand the complex, as signage is lacking.

As a heritage it worth visiting and see how intelligent people were that time. As per  me admission of 30 usd is slightly expencive.  locals irritating on the entrance  with too insistive offers of help are not adding charm to theplace. I would suggest of eldery and people with heart of joint deseases not attempt climbing as it was not very easy even for a very fit person like me. AVOID HEAT. as its unbearable. And busiest hours have got too much traffic so get ready to que all over. it reallyworth visiting at 7.30 am as its good weather and not much people. Don't  forget to see the museum as it will give you appropriate feeling how impressive the palece was.

The downside is the cost. At 3750 rupees, this is expensive for what is a ruin. However, the whole place is really four places in one, so I have to say, I really would pay again. The water gardens are stunning and apparently a real treat after rain. Then there is the boulder garden which is great to wander round. The steps up the rock are broken by the caves where the paintings really are as amazing as you think, and when you get to the top, the view is tremendous and well worth the climb.

early morning is the best. if possible, get your usd 30.- ticket the evening before and start before seven in the morning. take a guide for another usd 20.- and bring something to drink at the top. feel the rock, touch it and experience the energy. the rock was worshiped by spiritual people long before it was conquered by the usurpator in the fifth century. in the end, he killed himself, because - in my opinion -, he didn't worshiped the energy and spirituality but misused it for his own grandeur... that's a great lesson to everybody visiting: not to conquer, but to submit to the spiritual energy emitting from this place.

We weren't sure what to expect having read all of the reviews. However, we really enjoyed the visit. Maybe we were helped by our driver who ensured we bought our tickets and entered the site without attracting a "guide" but once on the climb we only experienced a few "helpers" and others keen to sell a souveneir or two. A polite "no thanks" was all that was needed for them to smile and leave us alone. The walk itself is challenging but relatively easy if you are moderately fit. I have had mild instances of vertigo in the past so had some worries but I was fine on all sections of the climb. The view from the top is fantastic. Yes the price of a ticket is quite high but its so worth doing and compared to other attractions across the world Sigiriya is a unique experience. Others have said the site is poorly maintained. That was not our experience, with the grass tidy and no obvious litter.

This was one of our favorite attractions we saw and would do again.  Our guide recommended to do it in the morning, but it actually should have been as soon as it opened as it does get hot quickly.  Not having a head for heights, it was actually okay with lots of handrails and stairs.  We quite enjoyed the frescos and the view from the top, great.  It gave you a picture of the lush countryside that was beautiful.

The ticket price is extortionate at 3750. The visit started with a man guiding us as if it was what you get when you buy your ticket. Of course he was a chancer as were his helper mates. However he was very good and his helpers did push us up the many many steps. This is best done when it is cool. It is not so much the climb as the heat which will get you. The guide informed us of several collapses going up the steps. The whole thing is wonderful. The top is just more ruins so if you wanted to chicken out of the last leg you will not miss much apart from the view and of course there is the shame of not doing it.

We are in our mid sixties and we decided to climb to the top with our tour guide.  It is certainly manageable if you take your time in the heat.  Wear thin clothing and a hat.  There are plenty of places to rest on the way up. About half way are the famous frescoes but at the very top are the remains of a complete palace!  How they got the building materials up there is incredible.  The views from the top are amazing and well worth the effort to get to the top.  Actually going down is almost worse as you need a good head for heights and strong knees! The water gardens at the foot are very extensive and one can only marvel at the manpower needed in the construction.

Take the time to do this. Stay in  close accommodation and do climb of rock early before heat and crowds. It is a challenge but pace yourself and you will get there but a lot of stairs. Read the history  and pay for the guide or go yourself what ever you prefer ( we went solo and  did " big ears " on guide group when we wanted to know something  And this suited us best - about 2.5 hours round trip .Don't miss the frescos  And do some selfies at the top lol. You can negotiate reasonable car/ taxi rates from Kandy  ( near the markets/ rail station - too expensive through hotels )  and worth combining  with great migration of the elephant Safari or other cultural triangle attractions. Drivers seem happy to stay and drive you back to Kandy ( they have to go anyway) and they show you other things  along the way. Suggest taking the train to Kandy from Colombo as cheap and a great experience and view . Take water and wear walking footwear and cool clothes

Incredible views from the top and the whole site is astonishing, it is a long hot climb though, fine if you are fairly fit but we did see people struggling.  Take plenty of water and wear a hat. We cheerfully read the warning signs about hornets and carried on, it wasn't until we reached the last point before the summit that our guide explained the cages were for people to escape into in the event of a hornet attack!!! The final climb was worth the effort, it really is a special place and despite the crowds it still felt peaceful and calm. Tip - as with all attractions in Sri Lanka there are a fair few hawkers, don't touch the magic boxes if you don't intend to buy them and make it very clear that you don't need help or will not tip any local who is prepared to virtually carry you to the top!!!! If you aren't going with a guide and would like to know the history then it's worth buying a guide before you visit. After our holiday we asked the children which was their favourite attraction and this was the one they all wanted to revisit (10, 13, 14yrs)

Hi, Just finished my nine-days tour of Srilanka and this was on my list. I took a local guide with me to tell me the stories behind the rocks. I always find it interesting to take a local guide when visiting the historical ruins though I do bit of reading before going to a place of attraction. The climb is worth a do; its a bit strenous if you are totally out of shape. Age got no limitation; I have seen both nationals and visitors of many ages climbing to the top. Spend some time when you reach the top; worth a sight and your tired muscles will love the cool breeze. Yes, get some water with you as the weather is humid and you may need it. The paintings are worth looking at; interesting interpretation of the paintings. Worth a try!!!
really good experiencem 1202 steps a good work out. worth it to see the paintings and the view from the top, also the lions paw stair  case is impressive!

This defensive citadel is worth the climb just to see the stairs carved into the rock wall.  The size of the steps are an indication that these people were short and had very small feet.  The climb is doable for most if you take your time and bring water, especially with the humidity.  I loved the refreshing breeze at the top, the throne overlooking the bathing/water reserve and the sheer drop we just traversed to get to the top.

It is a nice place. Good view from the top. The museum is useless. But it is really too expensive for what it is. Eiffel tower, british museums, etc are less expensive. There were works close to the stairs framed by part of the lions. The workers had the great idea of leaving their equipment on one of the lion's leg!! ruining everyone pics!

Do not attempt much of this if you are unfit. The ruins of the gardens and museum are good without the climb. The climb can be done in stages with an opportunity to stop and return after each stage. All climbing is with steps but they do not all have had rails. The 1st stage is to see the rock paintings of topless ladies. As out guide said, they are well endowed - perhaps with some silicon help! Also the mirror wall with ancient graffiti but this is not clear to see. The 2nd stage is to the lions feet. If you stop here you can sit down and admire the view. There is a small kiosk selling water etc. The final stage (which my husband did) is to the top of the rock for amazing views. Go early - it is very hard in the heat of midday. Do take a guide with you - there are plenty around. Good - but I preferred Dambula.

Very costly for the foreigner but worth the climb. Leave early as the humidity is taxing on a steep climb but doable at most fitness levels. It's an amazing feat of construction given there was no machinery to assist in the build. Once at the top, truly spectacular 360 degree view

We arrived at the Rock at about 9 a m and steadily climbed for an hour to reach the summit . A most rewarding experience . The views are stunning . Take plenty of water ! . After a good look around we spent the rest of the day relaxing at the pool of the Sigiria Garden hotel

My wife and I were treated to a personal guided tour of the Sigiriya Citadel complex. We spent an unforgetable 3 hours exploring the history and beauty of this beautiful place. It's difficult to put into words the 'whole experience', but for me the place was brough to life by our very knowlegable guide and I would recommend this to anyone wanting something that little bit different. The story of the place was fascinating, the views along the club to the top of Lion's Rock were beautiful, and the overall impression captured our hearts... so much so that we hope to go back to Sri Lanka just to return to Lion's Rock once again.

Climbing the rock is a fantastic experience. To enhance the experience, remember the following a) Carry sufficient water with you. It is a tough climb and water is not available on the way anywhere. b) Carry candies, energy dink if you feel lack of energy c) Dont go if you have problem with heights and Vertigo

Beautiful, beautful, beautiful, from the bottom the whole way up so much to look at, we had a tour guide who gave us all the background history, the last part of the climb is quite busy but the view from the top is worth the claustrphobic ascent. Anybody that did Adams peak, lions rock is a walk in the park in comparison.

history, climbing, adrenalin & disco legs. We were approached by the usual 'guide for hire', and in this case it was well worth it. He recomended another chap to assist in getting our 3 year old to the top. It seemed a little extreme to hire a porter for him, but it proved invaluable. Both hands are definately necessary! This place will kill or cure you from any vertigo! rickety spiral staircases up the cliff face, rusty walkways bolted onto a sheer cliff, and a total of 1,200 or so steps to the top, where you are greeted by breathtaking views. Not a bad place to defend yourself from your brother, who is trying to kill you! I'm not sure which is worse: being the king getting carried up the cliff, or the porters carrying him - fairly precarious in the days of bamboo and rock-cut steps. It would be nerve-wracking today! If you do anything in Sri Lanka, climb Sigiriya

This was one of the highlights of our two week tour of Sri Lanka and the views from the top and on the route up were stunning. We went quite early but it was still incredibly hot and humid, carry plenty of water and wear light clothing. The climb up was easier than I had imagined, particularly for someone with vertigo, as the steps are enclosed by rails each side - they are rather rusty though! It was interesting to see the difference between the half that had been excavated and the other, they are obviously still working on this too. We had a very interesting guide and didn't find it too busy and were not hassled by 'helpers' perhaps because we were with him. There are no bathroom facilities that we saw and it's a long climb up and down!
A bit of a climb and rather busy, especially up the spiral staircase to the painted caves but a must see and a terrific view from the top.

I failed to get any further than the lion's feet but would not have missed the climb for anything. The views were fabulous and our guide was brilliant. A must-do and younger people will achieve the top with ease. Just beware of the vendors that haunt the base

We made this climb in the late afternoon a couple of weeks ago. We had hardly anyone around us which made the climb much easier. I think all of the "helpers" had also given up and gone home for the day, we were not bothered by anyone. It is worth the climb for the views from the summit alone, even for someone like myself who has mild vertigo! The only part that I found daunting was the metal stairs, especially as it was very windy. Going down, i made sure that my companion walked directly in front of me! It has to be done, I am no spring chicken and managed the ascent much more easily than I thought. But I agree with previous reviewers, bring plenty of water, it is very humid.

The entry is US $15( for Saarc nationals). From a distance it looks impressive and you see so many people climbing it and think it will be pretty easy and exciting but the climb is really tiring if you do it in the late morning and afternoon as we did around 10am in the last week March. When you reach near the Lion Paws the Panoramic View it gives of the city is just amazing. One needs to carry lot of water and be careful with touts and guides ( if you take we paid him SLR 1000 and was asking us 2500).

My advice : Go there early! It is physical and people who suffer vertigo, or seniors should refrain from going. Now , get ready to sweat ! When you get in the park guides will approach you, in my opinion they are not needed, in the end its about climbing and enjoying the stunning views of the forests, mountains, lake etc... It is a bit pricey ( 30 dollars) but it is a must do!!!

The climb wouldn't be so bad, but it was 35 and blazing sun the day I did it, with the humidity sky high too. Unlike Cambodia, or India, Sri Lanka hasn't done a lot with its ancient monuments, so, apart from climbing the rock itself, there isn't a lot here.  The museum is fine, but so dimly lit it can be difficult to make out what you're looking at.

The climb to the top is worth the effort because the view is spectacular Unfortunately the touts trying to act as guides, the huge numbers of visitors and the poor condition of the spiral staircases on part of the climb diminished the experience.
This walk needs to be done before it gets too hot.  The monkeys were very entertaining. The view from the top of the rock was magnificent.
Sometimes the best view isnt from on top of the mountain, its from in the valley.

Read up on your history - this will make your visit here so much more worthwhile - although you can hire a guide as well. Yep, it's expensive to get in. What are you gonna do? Not go?  You've already made it that far and it's absolutely stunning throughout the grounds, and especially at the top! It's a decent hike, but totally doable - just bring lots of water.

This was my second climb of the rock and was even better than the first due to me having done a litle more research on the place since I first conquered it.  I do however think that the entry price is an absolute rip-off and would be a huge deterrent for others to visit the place. It will be the last time I pay to go in and only did so this second time as I had a group of family and friends with me.  Some did refuse to pay the shocking price and waited it out. Perhaps to justify the exhorbitant price, they could employ some of the touts to escort a group of climbers. If tourism is to really take off in Sri Lanka, the government needs to step in and regulate the pricing of attractions such as Sigiriya. I would be happy to pay 1000-1200 LKR but 3750 LKR is enough for me never to bother going back again, particularly when the money is really only lining the pockets of whoever reaps the benefit and is not going back into the attraction.  You can only really do so much upkeep on a rock.
Really enjoyed this climb, we were there as the gates opened and took it slowly. Well worth the climb. Fascinating insight into the history of this marvellous island.
It is daunting from the bottom and the heat doesn't help with the climb but the views, the frescoes and sense of achievement when you reach the top are worth it

The Lion Rock is a must see. It is a wonder on its own. With the little tools people had back then, this places makes you appreciate and wonder human mind and skill. The climb wasn't bad at all, but it gets really hot as you walk up. Best to take water and some wet wipes. Sunscreen and hat would be helpful. We didn't take a guide because that would be extra charge. If you are from one of the SAARC countries, make sure you mention that (they will ask to see your passport) and get 50% off your entrance fee. We paid $15 dollars each. (Only wish we had done the same for Anuradhapura. We didn't know at the time). I would highly recommend this place.

Sigiriya rock was really incredible.  From our hotel, we looked out over the lake at it, and it looked very high, steep and imposing.  But once we got there, there were a lot of stairs, but it wasn’t as difficult as we thought it would be (it was easier and shorter than the World's End hike in Nuwara Eliya, which had been described as moderate and mostly flat). It does get hot and humid, so it's always a good idea to start early, wear sunscreen and bring water. It was the most exepnsive Sri Lanka site we visited (at $30 US - 3 times more than a first class 6 hour train ticket from Colombo to Nuwara Eliya), but totally worth it - wouldn't miss it. We had to repeatedly decline help from the "helpers," who would grab our elbows, and try to help us up the stairs (for a fee), but saw several people who were taking advantage of the "helpers" and seemed quite grateful, so it's up to you. Enjoyed all of it – the gardens, the frescoes halfway up, the “mirror wall” w/ ancient “graffiti” on it, the lion’s paws (very cool - wish we could have seen it as originally designed), and of course the stunning view from the summit.  While we were on the top, a German tourist decided to try to climb the ancient steps built into the rocks and slipped into the green murky pond, so wouldn’t recommend that; he was fine, just a little wet and embarrassed, and made a joke about his little “swim.”

Just one of those must-do tourist things... But hey, it is pretty nice and memorable. Admission price (March 2013) was LKR 3.750 per person (young children free), about 23 Euro or $30 at the current rates. We climbed the 1200 steps in the morning and it took us about 45 minutes (including a 15 minute wait standing in line for the stairs to the cave). We took plenty of water, it's always hot and humid and we sweated a lot. We had our own guide and were not harassed. The rock is impressive, both from far away and close by. The main thing is just climbing it, which feels like an accomplishment and the views from the rock are great. Cave with some paintings and the ruins on the very top are just ok. The lion's feet are cool though, as well as walking up via his 'throat'.

This is a great place to visit, but is overpriced as with all Sri Lankan sites. I would recommend reading up on the history of the rock before going as there is no information there and after paying approx 4000 lkr to get in we were reluctant to pay a guide as well. It is 1202 steps and extremely high up so if you suffer from vertigo I would not recommend it! In addition,  be careful when coming back down the rock as many touts will be trying to guide you back to the car park- for a small fee of course!

Taking the time to hike up to the summit will be the best way to appreciate the beauty and history of the Sirigiya Rock. It will take about one and half to two hours to hike up and down, sometimes it could be longer depending on the visitors.  The best time to start the climb is as early as 7:00 am with less crowd and the sun could be scorching hot towards the middle of the day. There are concrete trails and strong metal staircases to use in climbing.  The view at the summit is outstanding plus the wall ruins of the fortress. Plenty of local guides surround the area and they will try to get you, just be smart and it will be your call to hire one. I did not hire a guide and I did it myself and it was even better. As per my experience, you will not get lost since there are many tourists and you just follow the crowd.  The trails up and down are pretty direct and easy to follow.  Be patient when climbing up and down and it's a one lane "traffic" for the most part. This activity is not suited for young children due to the intensity and heat. Bring bottled water for hydration. A good workout shoes or light hiking boots  will be great. I saw quite a few wearing beach slippers which seems not to be well-suited with this kind of activity. On your way down to the parking lot, keep eyes on the sign "Foreign Vehicle " Parking, otherwise you will get back to the ticket counter area where you start the hike and it will be a very long walk under the scorching hot sun to where the car or tour bus are parked.  Pace yourself and do not be in a hurry in your hike and it will be easy and fun. I recommend a half day excursion to the Sirigiya Rock fortress. It is a must-see when in Sri Lanka. It's like the fortress of Massada in Israel. Don't forget to wear good eye shades protection, hat, and sun block and you are good to go. Enjoy the history and hike, Lots of fun!
great historic site that is worth the visit, advise to go early or late as a lot of steps to the top

Start early..as early as posible as it is very hot there and humidity makes it even worse. I'm usually ok with heat, but going up there it's a lots of sweating...Looks more difficault than really is. Views are very nice and it's worth to see this place. Even price of ticket shouldn't scare you away - it's just one of must places to see. On our way up there was like hundreds people going up, so again to avoid it start early. If you want to buy something at the parking from vendors bargain hard as everything is 3 times more expensive than you can really buy it for.

Sigriya Rock Citadel is in the Central Province of Sri Lanka, located about 3 - 4 hours drive from the Colombo city. It is an important archaeological site and declared World heritage by UNESCO, it is a must see for the persons visiting Sri Lanka for cultural interest. On the western side of the rock citadel is the entrance and also a small museum explaining the history, making of the citadel and also displaying the ruins & articles recovered from the excavation of the site. The pictures, paintings and the articles in the museum briefly explains the history of Sigriya. The citadel has an outer moat and an inner moat to act as natural barrier from the invaders. Inside, is a symmetrical garden having water tanks of different sizes and a complex body of water channels based on hydraulic system. Our guide Beni, informed us that in ancient times the rain water stored on the top used to be pumped into the underground ceramic channels for the fountains. To reach the top of rock citadel, one has to climb about 1270 steps and the top is located about 200 meters above ground. The steps leading to the top, are narrow and slippery/ worn out due to usage, so be careful. Loose sandals and slippers needs to be avoided and also loose clothes. Families with small kids can safely climb upto half way and should avoid climbing the other half to top, as the way to top is narrow and sometimes gets chocked due to frequent visit by the school trips and other group excursions. After the garden is a rock pathway/ steps which gradually climbs upto citadel. While climbing the citadel, one can see the famous frescoes painted on the walls, which as per our guide were made from bee wax, egg whites, rice husk and other natural ingredients. The large size frescoes on the wall are wonder, as it seems impossible, to create such large paintings on the rock faces in ancient times. On way up, can also be seen mirror wall, which was polished to reflect the frescoes painted on the rock face. After the half way climb, the main entrance to citadel comes, which is shaped like a sitting lion. It is said that in ancient times, the shape of citadel used to resemble a lion and the entrance was created in such a way to resemble a lion couching. The main entrance is on the north side. The view from there is beautiful. Advised to catch some breath and be ready for the next climb which is steep. It can get difficult, when its windy. After the climb of the second part, the top/ summit of the citadel is reached. There one can see the ruins of the old palace having the living chamber of the royal family, court room, auditorium, water supply etc. On the descent, you can see the cobra cave (shaped like hood of snake), where the monks use to meditate, after King Kashyap (the occupant of the citadel)  vacated the palace in a coup/ revenge by his brother and other entrances to the rock citadel. It takes about 2 - 3 hours to completely visit the place. Take pictures from the top, the view is magnificent.

Recently made my second visit here with a group of friends.  Simply put, I am no longer young or sprightly enough to contemplate climbing the Rock in the heat of central Sri Lanka so my views on the place are perhaps atypical.  Sigiriya is quite a special place but foreigners are charged a pretty penny to get in and then subjected to the persistent attention of swarms of 'helpers' who profess poverty and then sting you for outrageous sums once they have 'helped 'you up or down a few sets of stairs.  Usually these guys attach themselves to you when you have gasped your way up a lengthy set of steps and are at your lowest ebb.  In my view, the government department responsible for the upkeep of the Rock need to do something about these leeches.  You get a fantastic view of Sigiriya from nearby Kandalama Lake and that's as close as I'll be going in future

We took the advice in our guide book and decided to visit here in late afternoon so it would be a little cooler. The gardens on the ground level are green and lush with plenty of plantlife and a couple of ponds. As you walk through the gardens the immense size of the rock strikes you: it seems almost infeasible that anyone could have built a citadel on top of it. As others have said, the climb does get a little easier the further you go up, so it is worth persevering. There are plenty of vantage points to take photos from. Not a visit for those who are nervous of heights, although you are protected for the most part. The spiral staircase to reach the cave paintings at the midpoint is a little unnerving as it feels like it's held on by pieces of thin wire and not much else. The view from the top is quite spectacular. Entrance fee for adults was $30 per person as at Feb 2013.

We began the climb at 9am after a short visit to the museum which is situated just behind the ticket office. If you don't visit the museum before you start you will probably not have the energy to walk this far back later. Cost is included in the LKR3750 (US $30 ) ticket. It is a good place to take photos of the maiden ladies as you can not use a flash up the rock. The walk begins with a long walk thru the gardens to the base of the rock. After many steps you reach a metal walkway leading to the mirror wall which on a clear day you should see your image. Really just looked like a wall touched by many hands to make it smooth. Next is the spiral staircase to admire the frescos. A few more steps brings you to the first large resting spot at the base of the lions paws. We saw the cheeky monkey's here. Once we had rested it was up the most dangerous looking part of the walk. What a relief to make it to the top and see the wonderful view. We went on a busy day when there were hundreds of university students doing the climb. We just had to pass them as didn't want to take all morning at Sigiriya. We were back at the car at 10.30. Had no hassle from any locals wanting to assist as guess we were lost amongst the crowds. Take water as it was 34 deg in March.

if you want to visit a monument in sri lanka, this one is awesome, combines both natural and cultural heritage, it is very high, and takes you lots of energy and strength to get to the top, but when you ultimately climb on the peak, you will find the scenes of your surroundings are stunning, and mot mention the ancient painting on wall is incredible and is a "just can't miss" type. One more thing, the juice is so so good, when you get back on land !
If you have to choose one place to go to see the historic Sri Lanka, maybe this is the place. The way up is easy, not a problem. The view is fantastic, and the paintings on the caves are a must.

Go early on in the morning when it is cooler - Once you have walked through gardens and rocks /caves there is the first steep climb - the steps are not too easy to walk on but worth carrying on as steps get easier - There is a steep spiral staircase leading up and again down  to/from the gallery showing the paintings of the Damsels - you then walk along the mirror wall (disappointing) with ancient graffiti on it - more steps and eventually come to the base of the lions foot platform - Your walk up through the lions paws along metal steps that are cut into the stone face - perhaps worse coming down them than going up !! - There are lots of "guides" to help you up the stairs, but if you do not want one - be strong on saying no -  as they keep trying to help you climb - then obviously  ask for a fee once they get you to the top - go at your own pace and you will not need a guide - just take care on the uneven steps But eventually reaching the top the view is amazing - worth getting a guide book to see the aeriel view of where you have walked up to - take the walk back down slowly and praise your self for having achieved a well worth it journey
Everything was excellent - go early in the morning, afternoon sun is very strong and rock also hot, take a lot of water, museum small but interesting .

The remnants of a once great fortress is the foundation for this breathtakingly historic monument. The climb - ***MAKE SURE YOU CARRY DRINKING WATER*** make sure you start it before the sun is at its highest. The heat will be a factor in the climb. As it is an old relic, there are no lifts, ramps, wheelchair access etc ... and believe me when I say that any of those things would ruin the monument. Also be aware that the steps you climb are not even, so if travelling with friends, you will need a helping hand for some parts. There are people available to assist you, as well as guides, but remember these people will require payment at some point. To get to what is called the Mirror Wall, there is a metal walkway that you have to cross. If you are scared of heights, DON'T look down as you will think the walkway is rusty and will break away, which it won't as it has been used for many years without any problems. It is here that you can also climb up to see the frescos of the topless maidens. Again, it requires navigating metal spiral staircase (said to be from an old Underground station in London) in a single file. Since they have added another spiral staircase, getting up and down to and from the Frescos is a lot easier. By the way - flash photography is NOT allowed where the frescos are, so be prepared to be spoken to by the tourist police if you insist on ignoring the simplest of requests. The Mirror Wall - it's not a mirror!! Well, there's a surprise, considering that the fortress was built centuries before mirrors existed. The name has been given because, in the right light, you can see your reflection on the wall. Don't expect anything spectacular as you will be disappointed. The Lion's Paws - this is the first real resting place that accommodates lots of people. Prior to this, if you stopped for a rest, you would inevitably be in the way of others. Some years back, you would be able to purchase drinks and trinkets at this point but due to people's failure to keep the place tidy this facility has been removed, which makes the place all the more beautiful. The final ascent to the top of the fortress requires some stamina and faith in the metal stairs which is stuck in the rock. When my father was younger, he climbed this section holding onto a rope and using foot holes in the rock to get to the top! Trust me, the metal stairs will hold you up. But again, those with a fear of heights DO NOT LOOK DOWN as you climb. With the limited space, sometimes the final climb can be chaotic, but when you reach the top, you will appreciate the beauty of the whole piece. The view from the top, on a clear day, is spectacular. You can even see Dambulla's Golden Buddha, which is quite a distance away. The climb down - you will have to traverse the same set of stairs attached to the rock.  The way down is somewhat different, with other views to take in. The Cobra's head (rock) is just one of the things you will see. Near the bottom of Sigiriya, you will encounter a snake charmer.  You do not have to participate, but if you do, payment is required as this is NOT included in the fee to enter Sigiriya. It is at the very bottom, as you return to the car park, that you can buy trinkets and holiday memorabilia, but be aware that the prices are much higher, and you can be taken for a ride.  This is when you should barter. The fee for tourists is very high, in comparison to the local rate, somewhat similar to prices you would expect to pay in the US or the west, which is wrong. There is no bartering for the entrance fee. Be prepared for the various guides offering their services, because they can be persistent. Please note- I say I was last there in 2012, only because Trip Advisor doesn't give an earlier option.

When we saw the rock I was not really sure if we would make it up to the top. So we started with the goal to reach half height, seeing the fresco as well as the mirror wall. We left the car and walked up to the entrance of the rock itself. Seeing waht people did approx. 1500 years ago, stunning. We had to wait a little because right before us arrived a huge group of monks which were also on their way up. Then we started and the beginning is really hard. But when you made the first 300 steps you get used to it and it's getting more easy. The frescos are very nice, the mirror wall quite disappointing. Finally we reached half height where again we had to wait for the monks. We were sitting, looking up and decided we'll go all the way. The second parts is quite easy, much easier than the first one. I wouldn't say it looms very secure - but so many people make it. Up at the top of the rock you've got some fundaments - but that's not the main thing. The main thing is the VIEW - and this view is out of this world. I've seen many places, Australia, New Zealand, Argentina - but I would rate the view from the top of the rock as one of the best I ever had. It's just WOW!!! Until now this has been the best experience I had in Sri Lanka!

Left my wife at the hotel for my early morning ascent of Lion Mountain.  The thought of 1200 steps to climb did not appeal to her.  Started at about 08.30 on a partially cloudy morning for which I was later glad.  It took me about 60 minutes to get to the top with a brief rest at the lions feet stage.  The views from the top were definately woth the effort, although I never did find out what the large Budda that could be seen was all about. My photographs were that bit more special than I expected, as a group of Monks in their bright orange robes were also ascending - just like in the guide book pictures!  The ascent was not too bad but certainly to be avoided by those with medical issues or dissabilities.  Many people were assisted by their guides but alas a few could not make it to the top, with just a small distance left to cover. One thing I did not appreciate was that the fresco's are located on a separate landing.  You do not just pass them on the way, but descend back the way you have come a little before continuing along to the lions feet stage for a rest.  Access to the fresco's is via vertical spiral metal staircases. Signage is non-existant and I missinterpreted something overheard from another guide regarding the exit from the mountain.  I did not return along the side of the mountain the way I had come up and instead descended some steps and a pathway back to the cobra stone.  This was probably not the best way as I was engaged by opportunist guides and wood carving sellers who were hard to shift.  probably would have been better to have returned the way I went up!  That said I bargained for a wooden elephant and my wife was delighted with it. Had no aches or pains the next day and concluded that it was actually 600 steps up and another 600 down.  Highly recommended but take plenty of water and a hat.
Brilliant views from the top well worth the climb but go early as its a hard climb in the heat. Not for people who have a fear of heights

Well, climbing Sigiriya is one of those things that has to be done on a visit to Sri Lanka and we did it! Over 1200 steps in 34 degrees C was hot! Beware if you don't like heights as the climb in one or two places is pretty scary. The worst part was the spiral staircase half way up to see the frescoes, only attempt if brave! But the view from the top is magnificent. How several stray dogs managed to get up there is a complete mystery!

We started our visit from the car park. It as long walk through the gardens to the base of the rock, this shows just how extensive the place was and the variety of areas built as part of the citadel. Once at the base of the rock it is a steady and hot climb up uneven rock steps through passages etc until you get to the actual rock. From here it is more of the same up the outside of the rock until you reach the spiral staircase to go and look at the cave paintings. These are amazing to see and strange being able to see the mistakes e.g. the person with six fingers on a hand.
