Still more steps brought you to the terrace where there was a chance to sit and rest plus being able to see the views back across the plain. For those intrepid and still with some energy metal steps (much more even and smaller) led up to the top of the rock. From the top the views all around were stunning, they would have been better if it was not misty. If you go up make sure you take plenty of water.

Went there with my family and fiancee. I have heard so many legends and stories about Sigiriya, and have always wanted to go there. The ambience when entering it is amazing, seeing the lovely large rock just the way you've seen it in pictures and nice gardens and ponds of water that make us forget the heat of the day. I must say the local authorities are doing a great job in keeping it clean, despite the thousands of tourists and locals that go there daily, and the very nominal 50 LKR they charge from an adult and 25 LKR they charge from a child. However, it was very strenuous to climb it, with the very narrow and steep steps, and near the katapath tower, winding stair cases. Thank God for the occasional empty floor areas where we could rest every 10 minutes or so. I was out of breath and in tears multiple times, and from what I saw I was not the only one. But once I reached the top, it was surreal, the feeling... I cannot believe Sri Lankans that lived that long ago were so skilled and had this much of architectural and engineering skills, without formal colleges or degree programs. Also loved the mango, pineapple, guava and maniyoc sellers on the way back - gave us back some of the energy we lost while climbing. The total journey of climbing up and down took over 3 hours - Great workout! Some tips: If you have a weak heart or are scared heights, Sigiriya is not the place for you, cause there are so many places where you have to see directly down Aged people low in stamina or have weak legs or knees, this is going to be tough! Once you get to the top, there are no resting places and specially if you go on a peak day (I went on a public Holiday), there's gonna be 1000 people behind you screaming go go go.... whenever you stop to catch your breath for 5 seconds ! :) Beware of some local guides, I heard myself one particular guide taking about 3000 LKR from a tourist for a ticket that was just 50 LKR. My only suggestion to the local authorities would be to have a parking space at the entrance available at low costs for locals.. We had to walk about 2 km from the main road to the sigiriya site since they said it would cost us LKR 4000 if we wanted to take a vehicle there, and a 3-wheeler would also cost 300 LKR (occupying only 3 people) - so it was not very cost effective.

This is a very impressive attraction that was, for us, totally spoilt by so called 'helpers'. The people of Sri Lanka are warm and friendly but don't let these parasites anywhere near. Some have official badges on but most do not. Best advice is to completely ignore them especially if you are older. If they reach out a hand to help or you find a hand on your arm as you climb the first steps, politely but firmly remove it. If you don't you'll find anything up to four of them talking to you and holding on to you as you climb following steps and then you'll find them all demanding money later. If you decide that you don't want to climb the steps they will still try to talk to you and later demand money. Don't speak to them, don't make eye contact and definitely don't let them touch you. Their behaviour anywhere else would be regarded as harrassment and it is a mystery as to why the Sri Lanka authorities allow this.

I would suggest going to the museum before you climb the rock. There is an interesting video about 3 minutes long but also a video showing an artists impression of what the palace may have looked like. Also a lot of history. A beautiful building blending nature and light. Lovely gardens to walk through and take time to look at some of the caves. The climb is not too strenuous and is definitely worth it. Start early and avoid the crowds and enjoy the view. Once you have seen the museum it is far more impressive.

This is an impressive attraction albeit one with a lot of steps to climb including a rather hairy metal spiral staircase, it was two way when we climbed it in February.  Its  one worth visiting providing you are reasonally active but beware of  touts who try and help you at all stages. They can be useful if you are finding it hard going but negotiate a price first, say 2000 rupees and stand firm at the end.  Otherwise be very firm and decline their help.   Puzzle boxes and snake charmers were also on offer, at a price.  Given the cost of the tickets some official policing of the site would be useful.

On of the most spectecular places i have ever been to. Starting with the parc w the rock and ending with the great ruins on top - including a spectecular view over the surroundings. Be sure to climb the extra stairs to see the wonderful wall-paintings. Lots of monkeys around, no scam recognized. And keep smiling to the people: You ask to take a picture with them and they will surely be more than welcome to take a photo with you! No place for people with fear of heights though (stairs to top)!

Despite the heavy rain the rock is worth a visit but the facilities and interpretation of the site were very poor for the excessively high entrance fee. The way up to the rock fortress is not for the faint hearted, particularly the final metal staircase in the wind and rain!
As we are getting on in years and I suffer from vertigo, we didn't attempt the climb to the top.There is plenty to see and do in the gardens at the bottom so we didn't feel that we missed out.

We went all the way up to the top of this giant rock to see the ruins of the palace of king Kasapa. Approx. in the middle of the climb you can see the 1.500 years old fresco's of the half-naked courtesans and goddesses, beautiful. The climb is all by stairs, sometimes in stone, mostly in metal. Not dangerous at all, can be don by everybody that is in normal health, just have a little rest in between. A must see while in the area.

We decided we wanted to go to Lion Rock ever since we saw it on the t.v. once and it is definitely worth the effort. Unfortunately we turned up at midday and the temperature and the heavy climb combined nearly made the whole experience unbearable so I'd definately recommend anyone to climb it early morning or late afternoon. The climb itself can be very unnerving in parts especially when you see there's nothing between the metal step your walking on, jutting out of the side of the rock, to the ground hundreds of feet below. The paintings on the wall halfway up are amazing and well worth climbing the creaky spiral staircase to see and, when you get to the very top of Lion Rock you really appreciate the effort that must have went in to building the citadel all those years ago. The views from the very top are spectacular also. It is on the expensive side but its well worth it.
one of the seven wonder,and evry body must climbed and watch the nature as well as ancent pictures beening drow n in rock serface,one of the amazing in the world

I went early morning just as it opened before it got too hot and too crowded. This was a good idea as I was coming down a lot of tour parties arrived to climb up. Length of time depends on how able you are to climb with out rest and how long you want tostop to admire the views and how the place was created.It is an amazing thing well worth the climb,and  it's a lot easier coming down. It is possible to rest at different stages of the climb but this takes time

We arrived in the rain and climbed the rock during a torrential downpour. The steps turned into miniature waterfalls and balance was difficult while holding umbrella, camera and railing. The climb is steep and an adventure, still easy enough for most people to do. The simple fact I couldn't see the ground since we were in a cloud made probably made for an easier climb and lots of fun.Overall it was an absolutely unforgettable experience. Lots of touts hang out by the entrance and around the rock offering up their services and lecherous comments in Sinhalese. I'd be cautious if I were a female traveler and opt for an older  more professional guide. Also if you are foreign the price of a ticket is quite expensive by any standard which most people fork out for since you just can't miss this amazing rock.

Spectacular natural landmark with huge historical and engineering significance.  Agree with most reviewers that this is a ‘must do’ - provided if you do not suffer from vertigo and are fit enough to cope with the climb (estimates of number of steps varies between 1,300 and 2,400). The site can be easily reached by bus from Kandy but it is better if you have your own car; better still to stay overnight in Sigyria.  Entry cost is 3750 rupees or approx. US$30 including a mini DVD.  You can get pestered by guides, helpers, carving sellers, snake charmers etc (more noticeable here, probably due to the limited employment opportunities in the local area).  Just say ‘no thank you’ firmly if you are not interested. You should plan on spending at least 2-4 hours to climb the rock.  If you can, allow extra time to stop by the museum (to see the reconstruction of how this inaccessible rock was transformed into a royal citadel - a truly amazing feat) and to browse for a bit in the water gardens.  I would do this before you start your climb as you probably won’t feel up to it afterwards. The first half of the climb up to the level of the Mirror Wall did not seem too bad though the humidity was a bit of a challenge.  There were plenty of passing places to stop and rest; steps are mainly stone but were narrow and uneven in places; there weren’t many handrails.  At this point we had the option of seeing the 'Damsel' frescoes. I really wanted to see these but, as I struggle with crowds and enclosed spaces, I was put off by the very narrow spiral staircase and enclosing safety netting. We went straight onto the Mirror Wall (which left us a bit underwhelmed). From there it was a relatively easy walk to the Lion Platform (once a immense recumbent lion carved out of the rock and whilst only the paws remain these are awesome).  After this the steps were really metal ladders which looked steep and flimsy.  In all honesty I was glad to see the rain coming in as this gave me an excuse to wimp out on the rest of the climb up to the top. Tips.   Go early in the morning, or even better late afternoon around 1600, partly because there is not a lot of shade on the climb and partly to avoid the crowds from the tour buses (which will really slow you down and distract from the tranquillity).  Wear sensible footwear and go at a sensible pace, taking time to rest and enjoy the views. Take plenty of water and maybe some snacks because there is nothing after the first ticket gate.  You will get more from your visit if you take a local guide who can better explain the history and show you the sights down the side trails (e.g. Cobra Hood Cave, Audience Hall platform). Avoid June when hornets can be a problem round the Lion Platform.  Finally, even if the weather seems fine, take an umbrella if not a light raincoat!

we stopped by this site as part as our long backpacking trip.  The rock itself was absolutly stunning and the site is interesting but we really found it difficult to justify spending almost 8000 rps (60$) for 2 people. It is the most expansive site we've visited ever and not necessarly the most rewarding. For the travellers counting the rupee, before you go to the rock, take a nice walk to the temple of Pidurangala and go to the top of the rock. the view is stunning, much less crowded, very interersting and only 200 rps entrance fee.

We climbed Lion Rock early in the morning and were glad we did....Don't think I'd have managed it in the midday heat! There are stopping points on the way for those that need a break, the terrace with the Lions claws had spectacular views. I'm not scared of heights but parts of the climb were pretty scary, especially on the higher staircases where people would just suddenly stop mid-way up for a break....not a lot of room for overtaking on the staircase when this happens. It was hard work, backs of my legs really felt it...but boy was it worth it, the views from the top were truly spectacular! One negative - I found the 'helpers' who kept grabbing our arms trying to help us up the stairs (for a fee) really annoying....especially as we hadn't asked for their help and being as it was on the lower terraces really didn't need it. We had to ask our tour guide to tell them to leave us alone. A sight not to be missed, water bottle and decent footwear recommended!

You need to be quite fit and not faint hearted it you want to climb up to the top.1202 steps! Part of the climb are open metal stairs - I choose to look up, not down! We had our driver to arrange for a guide, well worth the fee of 1500 rupees. His english was really good and his knowledge made the visit even more memorable. Lovely frescos and breath taking view. This was one of the high lights of our trip. We did the trip with driver and car from Kandy (arranged by our Guest House), which also allowed us to stop at a Spice garden, a Hindu Temple and most importantly, to see the Dambulla Cave Temple.

Locals pay Rs 50 . Tourists pay, wait for it, seventy five times that amount: a whooping Rs3750. The flow of tourists is such that the place is an obvious gold mine. That combined with its UNESCO status as a World Heritage Site, you'd imagine you were getting something of the calibre of Machu Pichu for your money. Alas, no. Okay, so the site is interesting, and if you let your imagination really get to work, you can just about begin to visualize what it might have been like in its heyday. In truth however, the main benefit of the rock climb was to absorb the lovely views from the vantage point at the top. Even the climb is overrated. All the talk about fitness is patent nonsense. Old grannies were doing it, and a few younger women were walking in heels which defied gravity. My main grumble is that the entire site is unkempt. With all those dollars rolling in, you'd think some would be ploughed back into upkeep and improvement. Again, no. There is litter everywhere, and we could spot only two old guys sweeping (and not making a very sustained effort to lift stuff which is offensive to the eye). The grounds at the very top of the citadel are overgrown with long grass and weeds (again the contrast with Machu Pichu, which is immaculate), and in my humble opinion the SL government should be doing a lot more, in tandem with UNESCO to justify both the World Heritage Site status (for example with a programmer of sympathetic restoration of the few remaining ruins), and the exorbitant entry fee. Still, if tourists continue to file in like lambs to the slaughter, one can perhaps understand why those responsible for the place, do the bare minimum. The adjacent museum is equally disappointing. Constructed as a gift from the Japanese, it is a typical piece of inappropriate (and non-poverty-relieving) aid. Only a few years old it is already looking neglected, and is in any case, far too large a building for the few exhibits on display. In summary then, my assessment is that if you fancy paying $30 for a steep walk up a cliff face fitted with some steel staircases, to then enjoy the views from up top, then go right ahead. But I wouldn't go again. My wife is less critical, but then she isn't propelling herself to write this review!

Sigiriya rock is about 3-4 hours drive from Kandy. One needs to go to Sigiriya via Dambulla. There are plenty of public/private buses available from Kandy to Dambulla. The frequency of the bus service is about once every hour. Any bus going towards Jaffna, vavuniya, polonnaruwa, anuradhapuram will go to Dambulla. Again, from Dambulla to Sigiriya, buses are available every hour. The last bus available from Sigiriya to Dambulla is at 5:30 in the evening. From Dambulla, one can get buses back to Kandy till late in the night. Ideally, one should plan for the entire day if you are planning for Sigiriya as the to and fro journey and the climb at the site can be quite taxing and time consuming. One should really be cautious of the tuk-tuk drivers at the main sigiriya rock stand as they all charge hefty amounts to drop you to the ticket counter. It is a nice 1 km walk from the main road. so we preferred to walk. There is a small water body running all along the road. We were told that it had crocodiles in them. However, given the shallow and clear water with no boudaries/grills, it was difficult to believe that. The entry price for the rock and museum is a steep USD 30 per person. There is a special concessional price for tourists from Saarc nations (USD 15 per person). However, the same is not displayed or openly communicated. One needs to display the passport at the counter and ask for the concessional tickets. The ticket price covers the rock, museum and the mirror wall. Quite frankly, even at the reduced prices, the ticket charges seemed exorbitant (particularly if you compare it to entry charges at key tourist locations in India). The climb to the rock top has more than 1000+ steps and can be quite challenging for some. The site essentially has ruins from a srilankan dynasty and it has now been declared a world heritage site. Unless one is looking for a tour guide, it is best not to get into chit-chats with the locals. Most of them ask you few friendly questions and force themselves on you to hire their services. It is best to smile and politely refuse them. One of the key attractions here is the mirror wall (which is essentially a light yellow coloured wall whose colour has come off over the years and has become plain and shiny at places. Hence, the name mirror wall). The wall graffitti (scratches, scribblings) are similar to what you see on most of the Indian monuments' walla. we were told that the scribbling were done centuries back by visitors, locals etc to the king's court. We did not found it too impressive. Midway to the climb, there are circular iron steps projecting out of the main rock leading to the frescos. We felt that given the available funding and cultural importance of the site, there was complete lack of monitoring in terms of safety arrangements. For example, throughout our climb, there were so many iron steps that were shaky and coming loose. For a iron climb drilled into the rock, it is important that no. of tourists allowed at a time are carefully monitored. There were at least 40+ tourists jostling for space on the iron climb. The lone guard standing at the entrance was shouting instructions and was conveniently ignored by all. This looked certainly dangerous to us. We quite liked the historical paintings. Me managed our climb to the top in about 1.5 hours. there are a lot of monkeys at the top and one should be careful about their bags/eatables as some of the monkeys tried snatching the same from few tourists. The journey to the top can be quite taxing. However, you will love it once you reach the top of the rock and see nothing but lush green cover in all directions. The view is very scenic. The whole gush of fresh, cool air with with interplay of sunlight with lush green vegetation in distant horizon was definitely the highlight of our day. As we were getting late and were planning on returning to kandy the same day, we did not sat there too long. We did not have much time to see the museum but did not regret it as it has not received rave reviews from fellow tourists. There are jungle resorts/cottages available within 10 mile radius of the rock and can consider staying there for a day or two in peaceful settings. Locals informed us that there is an elephant corridor nearby. Overall, it is a good place to visit near kandy but definitely needs to be managed properly given its popularity among tourists.

If you hesitate climbing the 1500 or so feet pretty much straight up a 'staircase', there are "helpers", young Sinhalese men who take each of your arms and do indeed help you to climb to the top and back down to the car park. These helpers are part of the 'staff' but they work for themselves and you must negotiate the cost as with much else in Sri Lanka. I agreed to 1000 rupees for each man but on arrival at the bottom, they wanted more. And they were pests, following me, insisting on more money, meaning that they did not get more because they had agreed to the cost before starting the climb.  As long as you know this will happen, do not hesitate to hire helpers should you be hesitant about making the climb with aging arthritic knees.

Fab experience but you need to be fit to do the climb in the heat. Lots of steps some of which are uneven. There are so points for resting although its a must its not for the faint hearted. Amazing frescoes and views reward you at the end.

A huge citadel built on top of an immense rock in approximately 417 AD. The walk up is challenging and not for the faint-hearted or those scared of heights. Much of the stairway is open metal stairs with thin railings. The views from Lions Paw Terrace are breathtaking so do not feel shortchanged if you cannot make it to the top of the plateau up the last steep, open stairway.

If you only see one historical place in Sri Lanka, this is it!   I have been wanting to see and experience Sigiriya since watching Duran Duran's Save a Prayer Video in the early 80s.   Sigiriya was not disappointing. A fantastic hike to the top which takes an hour plus if you're in good shape.  Your hiking is slowed down by less fit and big tour groups.   It is nice to walk off and explore some of the side trails on the way up.  You must stop and enjoy the views too.  The stairway climb to the cave paintings is a must. Before taking the last set of stairs to the top, make certain you stop to see the lion paws guarding the stair entrance.   The top was green and breezy when we reached it.   Amazing views too.  Spend time walking around the whole top area with the multiple layers.   You do come up and down the same stairway from the top. Don't forget to drop by the museum to see renderings of what is assumed the fortress looked like when it was in use.  I'm amazed thinking how they got materials and supplies up to the top. Everyone goes in the morning because that is the coolest time.  If you can deal with the heat, locals said go mid day for less crowds.   Bring lots of water and snacks because there is nothing once you cross the first ticket gate.

For 30 US$ you can walk round and up to the top of this historic Lion Rock considered by some as the eighth wonder of the world.  Interesting and far reaching views if the weather is clear.  You are given a mini DVD with a few minutes of pictures and commentary to take home but unless you wish to pay more for a guide there is no information on site.  Good shoes required as water  makes some steps slippery and you need a head for heights.  You need to take water with you as few facilities.  The site can be easily reached by bus from Kandy for a day trip.

I went to Sigiriya at my friend's suggestion. It's an expensive visit (cost of travel and entrance fee) hours away from everything, but it makes for a good day trip from Kandy. Despite my fear of heights and dislike of being in hot sun for long periods, I enjoyed seeing the frescoes, completing the climb, and taking in the views at the top. Overall, it takes at least two hours to complete and requires some degree of fitness. Bring plenty of water as there is nothing to sustain you until you return to the bottom.

You have to go through 2 barriers before you even get in the staff are rather impolite and if there is a large group ahead of you they only have one gate open,  so I stood in the blazing sun while I waited for them to stamp 30 tickets. Go in the morning and just say no to all the guides inside who are waiting to pounce on an unsuspecting tourist. The walk up is fairly steep with lots of steps I enjoyed it though but you need to be fairly fit.

WOW! I read the book Sigiriya - The Real Story (Senani Ponnamperuma) (available on Amazon) before stepping onto this extraordinary site. What an insight it gave me! Having a little knowledge made a big difference to my perception, understanding and enjoyment of Sigiriya, as of course it would any historic site. The Frescos are breathtaking as is the view from the summit and the feeling you get when you realize the entire site was handmade 1500 years ago.... I took an entire day to enjoy, as it certainly gets hot and steamy in the forest. Pace yourself and really take it in, its a beautiful place and definitely worth the $30 USD entry fee.
You must going up at early morning or afternoon, but at 6. p.m. is dark. Entry cost 3750 rps=30 USD.
The feeling of history and serenity, a pilgrimage in honor of our father.  Hard Steep climb many stairs but worth it.  View and the grounds are just breathtaking
Loved the whole experience - strolling through the gardens, the walk up the stairs and the views from the top. Wonderful!
A must vist place in Sri Lanka. The sigiriya arts were great. Greatview from the top of the citadel. Its really amazing how this citadel was build on a rock.

We were two couples with an age range of 64 to 69 and frankly approached this with trepidation the more we heard about this climb. In the end we need not of worried . The climb is well broken with obvious stopping places if you need them and its well worth the effort. The views from the climb and the top were spectacular and the paintings and the ruins at the top extremely interesting. I tip though it worth listening to your guide and getting up early to make the climb early morning.  When we were coming off the sun was getting up and people were noticeably more uncomfortable climbing up at that time. Also remember the water.

Absolutely fantastic - disliked nothing! We were nervous of the climb but in actual fact it was quite easy as one could go at one's own pace. It was amazing to think that it was inhabited for a comparatively short time. It is mind blowing to think that this was built wihout the modern equipment we take for granted now.The views fantastic as were the paintings.

I hadn't visited this for about 20 years, and it was still as amazing as when I first went. Although it was raining pretty heavily, and I did feel sorry for my friends who were visiting for the first time from the UK. They had to imagine the view from the top of the rock as the weather was bad with a lot of mist hanging low over the forests. Ah but it was an experience to cling for dear life to the metal handrails as the rain pelted down on us! We didn't have much choice in terms of dates, but if you're time is flexible... then check the weather the day before you go! ; )
must visit, views from the top are amazing you could easily spend a good few hours exploring this site. We got there early morning, left around lunch time and went to polonnaruwa for the afternoon.

Go early in the morning before the sun gets too hot. And wear proper shoes. You can climb slowly but still feel the strain. The fortress is itself amazing considering how it was all done out of the natural rock. The sights at various heights are well worth the climb and price. As for the guide, either do your homework and do without one. Or check ahead for a good guide who will actually explain the history and significance of different parts. Some of the 'official' guides hanging around will just point to spots for you to take photographs.
Climb all 1202 steps to the top in the early morning to avoid the crowds and the heat of the day.  Not good to do if you suffer from vertigo but worth the climb if not!

Before you start your climb you have the water garden (ancient fountains) Suggest being in good shape to climb to the top of the Lion Rock because it is a challenge. But after your climb (more than 2000 steps…) you have an amazing view. Bring some water with you because you will need it (the combination of heat and humidity made the climb harder). Historical and architectural it is awesome. It is a must see location if you are visiting Sri Lanka

Never heard of this place until I arrange the Sri Lanka trip and after having been I seriously thinks this should be a close second to macchu picchu but as amazing a natural setting and wonder as it is it's terribly and shamefully maintained I could literally have taken pieces of the all away and no one would have cared I have no issue paying the hefty free in truly but that coupled with the  disrepair make you realise that someone is making money out of this place It's should be way more famous it is increable and a stunning place but at times on the way up the rock I actually felt unsafe - the staps shake and rock and it's a sheer drop Come on Sri Lanka - national pride please and make this as good as it should be Shame on you Sri lanka ( and I loved Sri lanka )

The rock is such a grandeur even from afar. It was nice seeing it from photos, but seeing it in real life was something very different! It is amazing! Climbing to and from, learning the way how things were years ago, and looking down at the equally amazing view is worth it's entrance fee! =)
100% worth seeing this magnificent site - you will remember this forever. Plan on at least 2-4 hours to visit. Bring some water and good footwear.

Sigiriya Rock is an impressive site worth visiting. Entrance fee is about $25, but it is worth it. I visited February with four friends, and we hired a guide recommended by our driver. The water system and architecture dating back to year 490 AD is remarkable, the ruins are well maintained, there is a great view of mountains from the top, and due to all of the steps you will feel a sense of accomplishment when you reach the top. Although it is easy to skimp on the guide, it was completely worth it. We paid about $30 and he was very knowledgeable, pointing out items in the rock fortress we would not have noticed, and sharing the interesting history of the King. February is apparently the cool period, and it was still very hot, so I recommend starting early in the morning. We enjoyed a good breakfast at the Sigiriya Guesthouse beforehand. There is not a lot of shade so be sure to bring sun protection. I would recommend 2-3 hours for this activity. I hope this is helpful and you enjoy Sigiriya.

Lion's Rock is amazing.  The breathtaking views from the three ramparts leading up to the great climb all the way up the side and then atop the rock are all worth every step.  Be sure to hire a tour guide as it will not cost much and is worth every penny as you'll learn much more than what your book will tell you. Tip:  Get there as EARLY as possible.  I'd recommend 7am or even earlier.  This way you will see the sunrise on top of the rock which is stunning and - more importantly - you'll get ahead of all the tour buses that will surely arrive all at the same time and make an easy, carefree 20 minute climb last 2 or more hours.

Although the most expensive in the Cultural Triangle, this amazing place is a must! Imagine how they build the palace at the top of this beautiful rock (the museum has an enthralling 3D video on this). The water gardens although not at it's original condition, gives a good idea of how beautiful this place must have been. The boulder and terrace gardens is pretty good. Of course, the frescoes painting are fabulous. The wind at the top of the rock is really strong and living up there must have been quite an experience for the early rulers. The lion paws are huge and makes one wonder how awesome it must have been with the missing lion head in the past. Must see!

We climbed up here just before sunset in january . It was wonderful to reach the top ( over 1,230 steps ) we had a tour guide for our trip to sri lanka who arranged for us to have a guide here to tell us about the ruins on this fantastic rock , he was great and im so glad we had someone tell us all about this as we climbed, as without one would have been completely different and we wouldnt have learnt anything. it was wonderfully interesting to be told a everything as we climbed and made it feel much easier to do. well worth the climb for the great views and a good idea to go late afternoon when cooler.
The weather was nice and that made it easy to go to the top. great to see the ruins. Fake tour guides can be annoying. It is difficult to enjoy the visit with the constant escort.

Before we left, an acquaintance who'd had a posting in Srik Lanka assured us this was the one sight we must not miss - adding thoughfully, "unless you suffer from vertigo".  As a life long vertigo sufferer, with a true fear of heights, this did not fill me with joy.  Unfortunately the weather on the day we went in January was extremely damp and overcast, with very poor visibility. On arrival, we found the whole site swarming with (apparently 700) students/future leaders under the aegis of the army.  They were amazingly polite & well behaved with no pushing, shoving or jostling, but there were so many of them that it took them a long time to make the ascent.  We went to the museum first, which was rather uninspiring, and then wandered around the beautiful lower water gardens, which I enjoyed.  Psyching myself up to make at least part of the climb, we set off, me with heart in mouth. By then the majority of the youngsters had bounded up the spiral staircase and on to the next part.  I had read the guidebook, which didn't really make clear how vertical the metal ladders were up the face of the rock.  My husband and our lovely guide/driver cajoled me up to the mirror wall and the frescoes, knowing that I was really keen to see them.  I won't say it wasn't an ordeal, and coming down was worse.  When I made it to the Lion Terrace and saw the almost static queue up the next lot of steps, which were not enclosed, but had only a waist high rail, I knew I had done my character building exercise for the day.  Conversation with several others at this stage confirmed I was not alone!  The thought of standing for ages looking out over nothing and not being able to flee back down was just too much, and sitting down and closing one's eyes wasn't an option either!  I suggested husband and guide went on up alone, but what with the enormous crowd and the very poor visibility, they declined.  We took a different, very interesting route back through the beautiful ruins & rock formations, and I feel slightly wimpy at not having gone on right to the top, but illogical though vertico is (you know you can't fall, but you feel you are) it is a very real feeling and despite years of trying to overcome it, I didn't feel absolute terror or making an idiot of myself was justified! Apparently the king  who built it did not himself  like heights, and after being taken up to the Lion Terrace in a litter, went on up by some interior route with high walls - I wish.  So, vertigo sufferers be warned - the guidebooks are rather airy about this aspect! It is not the physical nature of the climb (probably not much worse than going up to Dambulla caves) or the heat and humidity, it's the height, stoopid!
Fabulous views. Well worth the effort of climbing to the top. Some of staircases narrow but never felt unsafe. The gardens surrounding the rock are lovely
View from the top was fantastic after the 1236 steps climb. On the way up can also see some cave painting.

Lion Rock is an attraction that is not to be missed, even if the climb of some 1000 stairs is hard. We got a very good guide, who made the climb easier with his enthusiasm, knowledge of history and being very helpful in giving a hand to my wife whenever she needed pulling up over the stairs. Before and after the climb, the very functional and clean toilets at the base were helpful. The fabulous frescos are about half way up the climb. Reaching to the top of the rock provides lovely view of the sourroundins.

Great walk, great views - for us definitely one of the high points of our Sri Lanka tour. Seeing the parking lot we were a little afraid of being overcrowded, well actually the way up was overcrowded. Yet the views on the top have rewarded us enough!

During our first week in Sri Lanka the weather was a little mixed, but, the weather on the day we went to Sigiriya was perfect, perhaps a little too hot!!! Our driver arranged for his friend to walk us up to the top and to give us a good insight into the area and history of Sigiriya Rock. You start at the bottom where the moats used to be and ancient swimming pools before you start the climb up the 1300 + steps!!! There was a Japanese tourist infront of us in high heels.... enough said!  Pumps / trainers are your best bet for footwear. Our driver had warned us about sellers trying to sell carvings / "magic boxes" but apparently they are totally over priced, but as always with most Sri Lankans, say no thank you and they don't take offence. The walk up to the top was really interesting.  Beautiful views, paintings on the way up, and points of historical interest, you can really imagine how it used to be all those years ago.  We aren't really into history, but I thoroughly enjoyed the visit to this attraction. The steps are steep, but really safe, just watch your footing if it's been raining, in parts the steps are wet underfoot so just be careful.  The day we visited it was really clear, so the view from the top was stunning, great photo opportunities. When you leave, you are given a little brochure and a dvd to take away with you. I would definitely recommend a visit to the rock during your trip to Sri Lanka. Tips: wear sensible footwear and take a bottle of water with you, you'll need it on the way up!

As with many of Sri Lanka's heritage treasures, time, weather and monsoon rains have conspired to erode their structures and glories. But it certainly is still obvious just how imposing and beautifully decorated Sigiriya was in former times. Sigiriya is a fantastic huge rock that sits in massive isolation in its gardens on the plain, surrounded by jungle. By visiting the museum and seeing what has been uncovered to date it is clear that the whole site is massive and only a portion is fully uncovered.. Walking through the Water gardens towards the Rock (it deserves the capital 'R'), the planning and symmetry of the gardens attests to the huge importance of the entire structure. Just seeing the oldest working fountains in the world (?) is quite humbling. Climbing the Rock is a significant undertaking as the are some 2000 steps to be climbed in order to reach the top. In honesty, there should be a health warning about this as, most of the steps are in no way "gentle" and many are quite steep and eroded which, in rainy weather, can be quite treacherous. For young folks it is probably a pretty easy climb (maybe) but even though I consider myself a pretty fit 61 year old, it was a hot, humid, climb that needed a fair few stops for a quick "breather". Some folk that we saw who were a little on the 'well built' side were going to have problems, or more, with the climb. The first climb up to the level of the Mirror Wall is significant but achievable. At that point you branch off to climb a metal circular staircase enclosed in safety mesh so as to go up to see the "Damsels" paintings. This can be quite a vertigo inducing experience. Going up, the staircase is pretty OK, but the view back down is pretty freaky... Seeing the Damsels is beautiful and I am glad that I did that. Going back down the circular staircase is really not pleasant as the 'down' side is in much less good condition with missing bolts on the arm rails and splits in the rusty 'safety netting - upon which is managed to snag my arm and had a good bleed as a result... Carrying on behind the Mirror Wall is flat and easy until the next long flight of steps up to the major platform just below where the Lion's head entrance used to be. This long flight of steps is fine going up, but almost vertigo inducing on the way down as there is no hand rail and the steps are "straight down"! In any event, you "must" see the Rock and just go carefully and enjoy this fantastic sight.

I am a Sri lankan. I went to see Sigiriya all the way from New Zealand where I live. I found that locals were not allowed to park near the entrence, instead have to park outside on the road and walk about 1.5 k in the hot sun to the ticket booth. After talking to an employee of Sigiriya I was told that only tourists are alowed to park in the car park. After purchesing the ticket and going to the ticket processing booth at the entrence I was told I can not enter without ID. Non of this information was writen on any board leading up to the enterence.the beauty of Sigiriya is tainted by how disorganised the entrence is.Its not difficult to list all the rules and regulations before having to walk 1.5 to enter the attraction. It was a sad and extreamly disappointing experience. The tourists are treated like royalty but I felt as though I was a second class citizen in my own country. Sigiriya is a part of Sri lankan heritage but currently it has turned in to a business that caters mostly to tourists.

Amazing place, an absolute must in Sri-Lanka! Beware steep steps at top but still very manageable, take a guide as full of history! Beware people willing to help you on the stairs as they expect a hefty tip, our guide helped my wife anyway.
A must see in Sri Lanka (as long as you don't get vertigo!. Amazing scenery, great cultural, historical and architectural significance and superb views.

Magnificent site.  The Frescoes are amazing and the views from the top majestic.  However, strongly suggest being in good shape to climb to the top.  Some areas are steep and there are 2,404 steps up...some are also narrow so your footing needs to be solid.  Also, if you're afraid of heights, best to not venture all the way!

Sigiriya is located in the middle of wide gardens with many animals (birds & monkeys). In case you cannot go up the rock because of health, you may keep standing at the bottom and looking at the rock while imagining the life of former kings of Sri Lanka. Few guides who are very kind and do not bother you in case you decline their proposal.

You can climb to the top of the rock and there are some wonderful paintings in the caves!! An easy climb. A well preserved heritage site and the entrance fees is very nominal. A worth watching view from above.

Once inside the park we found ourselves surrounded by thousands of school children escorted by soldiers in endless lines with total disregard towards tourist that paid the hefty fees to get in. We where literally moved away from the trials in order for these children to go through and we never could.  A disappointment
A must see if you are in the area. Stunning views at the top, great history and beautiful gardens. Plan on a couple of hours to take it all in and make your way to the summit.

Sigriya rock is a 'Must Do'!! It's not considered one of the 8th wonders of the ancient world for no reason!! It is truly a wonder. We had a good guide who pointed out key areas of interest and detailed history. This was a good idea. It was  great workout getting right up to the top....then you are rewarded by spectacular views.

Sigiriya is a slight not to miss...and the tourist board knows this so be ready to fork out 30USD per person to get in. The museum is not very impressive, the building is huge but there is not much in it. The before and after renovations photos are fun but not really worth it. Once you have passed the water garden where ancient engineering provided the means to have fountains by a canalization system, you arrive at the foot of the rock. We did not find the climb too tough but in combination with the heat and humidity we were soon soaked. About one third up you arrive at the Sigiriya damsels. These frescoes are still in remarkable shape. Other frescoes lower down the mountain were in worse shape. There is also a mirror wall, don't expect a mirror. We were not too impressed with the greenish/yellow slightly shiny wall. When you reach the lion paws you're about 2/3rds up. The next part is steeper but still doable because it gets a bit more fresh up the mountain. On top you can imagine why Kasapa wanted to be here because of the strategic location and the views. There are still foundations up there from buildings but no actual structures anymore. Overall a recommended sight!

1202 steps. That's a lot of steps, especially if you're scared of heights as I am, but as everyone else says it's definitely worth the climb. It had been exceptionally wet in December when we climbed the rock, so conditions weren't great. Water was cascading down the stone steps on the approach to the rock, but the metal steps were a bit drier and at least there was a handrail to cling onto and "helpers" to drag you up whether you want them to or not. The spiral staircase up to the viewing gallery to the frescoes was particularly unnerving as it's very exposed. My advice would be to wear sensible shoes, take some water, a camera of course, try to get there early to beat the crowds and whatever you do don't look down till you get to the top! The views from the top are truly awesome, and coming down is a lot easier. Don't expect a cafe when you get to the bottom. By the way the toilets are basic but clean, in fact the attendant insists you wipe your feet before entering. When we visited there was no sign of the dreaded hornets nor of the monkeys. Entrance fee is $30 though you can pay in rupees.

We absolutely loved Sigriya Rock and think it a definite must see if visiting Sti Lanka. We thought it felt a bit like Machu Pichu in Peru as did my daughter who has actually been there!  We spent a whole morning here so definitely don't rush it.

I'm a pensioner, with sore feet and a dodgy knee - but this was worth all the pain!  To be honest, the ruins on top are pretty vestigial, but the views are spectacular - both the distant landscape and the adjacent water gardens, and the climb itself is exhilarating!

We were here a few days after New Year this year and we were nothing short of astounded by the place. What you find at Sigiriya is an enormous rock standing alone in the middle of the jungle. The rock could easily be 500m long by 500 wide at least, and then 400m high. This may not sound big but it is incredibly impressive. a walk to the top via hundreds of stairs will take about an hour to 2 hours depending on your fitness. The grounds and ruins at the base and surrounding are beautiful, but the ruins on the top of the rock fortress are wonderful. The view is next to none, you can see for miles and miles, we had a very sunny day thankfully.
It was a steep climb up to the top of the citadel but well worth it.  The views are amazing from up there and the carvings and history is incredible.  Make sure you don't miss this Rock
Go with a guide if you are not on a tour already. Don't stop/go back once you start climbing and you'll be rewarded with the memory of a lifetime!!
We had to walk up during a rainy day. That was really adventures. We had a guide who was very knowladge. Entrance fees for the tourists are Really Stupid!!!

The walk up to the top was both stunning and a good challenge (especially in the heavy Sri Lankan humidity). The views from the top were amazing, but two things detracted from the experience: 1. my partner is afraid of heights and the stairs looked a bit rusty so he had to be helped to the top and didn't enjoy the final climb. 2. we didn't have a guide to show us around so aside from doing the main climb we weren't really sure what other things we should look at (there were lots of sign boards). Make sure to take some water with as well, we went through 2 large bottles during our climb.
In Sigiriya we had a nice early morning walk up at lion rock. Bring your camera and water, and remember to walk slowley.

I remember Sigariya Rock as one of the greatest challenges of my life. I have two artificial legs and the climb was both exhilirating and exhausting. I urge anyone that is even thinking of visiting to do so. It was a beautiful setting and the views from the top are stunning. Take lots of water and start out early. If you're fit and well it will only take a couple of hours up and back, maybe less. I have very fond memories and the CD you get free with your ticket means you can look back for years to come.

I have visited that place on the 10.of january this year nearly 2000 steps to climb up is not just easy but when you are  on the top you have a wonderful feeling and it is worth to do it .The paintings of the cloud girls are amazing > However do it early in the morning.
Use a local guide to make the most of your visit. Worth every rupee! The views were spectacular, the layout of the grounds awesome. Go early morning and take water.

This location has lots on offer and the climb to the top is worth it.  However, spend time in the gardens at the bottom as well as that is rewarding. NOTE - they charge tourists USD 30 each - very expensive but this is how they pay for the upkeep.  The problem is that ONLY TAKE CASH.  Do not get caught out because there are no cash machines near by

The citadel of Sigiriya well deserves its reputation. Don't give up even when the humidity and the heat may make it difficult to climb up the 1000 stairs to reach the top of the rock. All the site is very beautiful and you have to take your time to visit it. The best moment to climb is early in the morning to avoid the hottest hours of the day and the winter months when the temperatures and the humidity are accetable. You will find some people that will try to up lift you and then will wait for a lift. According to me it is better to decline their help even if they will  insist a lot, they make the way more difficult as you can't keep your rythm and at the end of the visit they will insist a lot for a tip (we were asked for 20 dollars each and of course it is crazy considering that nobody asked for their help"), Don't forget water and if you suffer from low blood pressure, bring some salt or a supplement.
Though the climb is little difficult, it is well worth the climb. The view is amazing and the feeling when you take last two steps is simply great.
A most unusual stronghold set on an enormous rock. Strenuous climb so take it easy! Beautiful cave paintings and intersting history.
This really is an extraordinary place. Don't think about it unless you are up to the 1,000 odd steps to the top. Brace yourself for a thing of majesty and beauty. Look upon my works ye mighty.

A Beautiful and amazing palce. Feels proud of our history and it is a Wond of the world for sure. It's Amazing how people during those olden days could have done so much of development with such a little technology.

About a 3  hours drive from Kandy. It sort of is a must see attraction in this beautiful country and it is hard to grasp the dimension of this creation. Just the climb itself is an attraction, while most people would find the climb very easily I have a tremendous fear of vertigo but I got up in the end and enjoyed every moment of it. We paid 7500 rupees to hire a driver for a whole day (not sure if this is a good or bad price, but I'm glad we did). Keep in mind it cost another 3000 rupees to access the attraction. Museum is also much worth a visit.

This was a highlight of a very enjoyable 3-week family trip to Sri Lanka, and words alone cannot describe how monumental Sigiriya is. You must attempt to climb it - it is a lot of work for people not in peak physical condition, but well worth it (and there are plenty of stops along the way). We hired an excellent guide, which is a must - you can hear guides speaking in all different languages, so chances are, they will speak yours! We visited in the late afternoon, and reached the peak at sunset, which was breathtaking, amazing, romantic, and more!  You get a real visual spectacle and can imagine how it all was back in its heyday. The sheer number of lakes and water features in the surrounding areas is tremendous. * Families - you cannot bring small children up unless you wear them in a carrier / backpack chair. Anyone under 6-7 will be exhausted & it might be dangerous.  We ended up leaving our children with family members in our rented van while we climbed, which took over 2 hours. * Suggestion re shoes & clothng - wear closed walking shoes with non-slip sole, as the limestone steps are slippery, even in dry conditions. Try to avoid touching the sides or wear long sleeves, as we all got caught on rusted wire fence & bruised / bled.  Just keep your arms close to your sides! ** Note re Fees - the foreign rates are hugely disproportionate to the local rates, but the tourist dollar / Euro is what keeps the attractions going, so it's worthwhile to pay the $30 entrance fee so this amazing world heritage site will be preserved and maintained.

Started out with our guide Ranjit - what a nice well woken man - he helped us on the climb and knew a lot about the paintings and history of this ancient site. Excellent views, amazing frescos and the reflective wall is fascinating. The paintings are a must see. The idea that these people carried their king up this rock is awesome.

Were one of the first to climb. Arrived at opening time at 7 am.  Best time to start climb, you can avoid heat and crowds. The gardens, marble steps, frescoes, and the view from the top of the rock were just amazing. Unforgettable experience. So glad we did this. However, management needs to improve the site. Arrived at 7 and the gates were not open. Staff had not arrived. The road (or lack of )  is just a mud road. Descriptions and signs are not great. I hope the entrance fee is being put to better use in the future.

After some apprehension about the potential quality of this attraction we drove the 21/2 hours from Kandy to climb the mountain. It was fantastic. The gardens at the base of the mountain are well maintained and most water features are still in working order.  The climb up to the top is relatively strenuous but worth it.  What people managed to achieve in terms of construction in what we consider to be primitive times is amazing. In rating this attraction as fantastic you need to be aware that this is in the context of Sri Lanka. Don't expect slick organization, there are touts everywhere, the 'new' Japanese built Museum is already grubby, the steel stairs are rusted which leads you to question the ongoing maintenance but as a historic site it is truly amazing and the views from the top breathtaking.

The climb isn't tricky and the views during the climb are quite breathtaking. Yes, the ones from the top are even better. A bit of rain made it all the more pleasant as the humidity does take its toll. A wonderful memory from the recent trip to Ceylon.

not everyday we can visit a UNESCO  nor one of the eight World Heritage Sites of Sri Lanka. Splendid views from the top of the complex, the remaining frescoes are awesome and what most amazed me was that a fountain  built in the 5th century was still working...OMG...after so many centuries??? minus (not for me) the 2000 steps ascent climb to the place where the main house was said to be.

This was the stand out destination in Sri Lanka - have not seen anything like it anywhere. Uluru with history and culture! Definetly needs a guide to point out the details and explain the history. Note that there are about 1200 steps!

This would have to be one of the 'must see' places on anybody's Sri Lankan travel list.  It is a UNESCO World Heritage site (described by some as the eigth wonder of the world) and simply an amazing place. It is a large granite outcrop (approx 150m high) which dominates the surrounding jungle. It is both a palace and a fortress constructed in the fifth century. The roads into the park are a little rough and after paying your entrance fee (which includes a mini CD) you cross a moat through to the water gardens (whilst these are partial ruins you get an idea of the scale and grandeur of what they would have been). We were lucky that it had rained in the days before as some of the fountains were still flowing. Beware of the so called 'guides' throughout your climb who will 'try' and help/assist you as all they are interested is getting a fee from you. If you can organise a legitimate guide then it is worth the money as only then will you get a real understanding of the history of the site (luckily enough our driver was very conversant with the site). After passing through the series of water gardens you enter into the boulder garden, where you climb commences. The natural landscape here is spectacular, the climb then gets steeper as you enter the terrace gardens. Finally you get to the base of the rock itself. There is a spiral iron staircase which leads to a terrace halfway up the rock face, on the walls are these magnifcent frescos and a long polished rock wall (the mirror wall), you then have to back down the staircase and around the base of the rock until you reach the Lion Gate/Lions Paws which is the start of the final climb up the rock. Once you reach the summit you really appreciate the extent of the ruins ontop of the rock (particulary given the fact it all had to be carried up there in the first place). Again it helps if you have a guide to explain the layout of the ruins of the palace, the kings quarters, the swimming pools and galleries. The view from the summit is simply breathtaking. Try and avoid visiting during the hottest parts of the day, bring plenty of water ('cause climbing all those stairs is thirsty work), sunscreen & your camera. The climb down for some is just as tiring as the climb up but you'll be glad you made it to the top. On the way out you'll pass (if you're heading to the tourist carpark) you'll pass by a number of souvenir and drinks stalls - all of which are generally overpriced (so I suggest you avoid them). All in all this a real highlight of our trip to Sri Lanka!

This was one of the highlights of our trip to Sri Lanka. We weren't expecting much from our walk but we were amazed. The way up is breathtaking - beautiful ruins down the bottom, lots of stairs and then a narrow staircase to the top. The views and the ruins at the top are well worth the trip. It makes you wonder how did they get all those bricks up there.

The place is a natural wonder - a 587m rock rising straight out of the ground below. And the citadel/temple on top is also pretty cool. I really enjoyed this place. I see comments from other reviewers about it being too hard to climb, or unsafe - this is far from true. I can only assume these are pretty timid people who probably shouldn't be visiting Sri Lanka in the first place. My 2.5 year old boy climbed almost all the stairs without being carried. As for using the services of a guide? We didn't, instead relying on the guidebook descriptions. I don't think there is enough detail on the history/culture side here to require a guide, but others may see it differently.

This is quite simply a wonderful place. It stands out from miles around and when you get close you realise how amazing it is. The rock is simply huge and towers above the flat landscape surrouning it. The trip to the top takes about an hour and consists of pathways, steps, various gantries and small iron stairs pinned to the side of the rock. It is a great journey to the top and one which brings with it a sense of achievement. Once at the top the views are brilliant. Do not be put off by any comments about getting to the top. Yes there are some scary parts and it can be physical but there are various stages you can go through to get there and if you take your time it can be easily achieved. However, if you do suffer from vertigo then the last section pinned to the side of the rock may just test you a little. But if you can make it then press on because the place is wonderous. The story attached to the development of the fortress is also intriguing and to think this was constructed many many years ago just adds to the achievement. If you are visiting Sri Lanka then you really cannot afford to miss this special place.

A must do on your visit to Sri Lanka but not the best if you have any fear of heights. We went in the pouring rain in December and the steps were quite slippy but we did avoid any issue with hornets as referred to in some of the other reviews. You must have a local guide as there is little to no information on site and you need the guide to build the picture of how spectacular this once must have been. They also warn you about all the other hangers-on who will try and make money off you. Our guy was called Alec and was superb! Fantastic views from the top and to imagine what it must have been like but obviously Sri Lankan health and safety is not up to western standards and the stairways leave a little to be desired- thus, not for the faint hearted.

Sigiriya seemed like a nice little town.  It was overshadowed by "The Rock".  Personally, after the long, arduous climb, I didn't see the big deal.  Totally not worth it.  The small Buddha cave was dark and average.  The very top had an OK view, but only if the weather was absolutely perfect. It was a bit overcast when I climbed (raining when I climbed down), and other than the big white Buddha in the middle of town, the view was underwhelming. The ruins were just unidentifiable rocks.  If you don't like climbing up steps, you'll probably find this one not worth the climb.
The walk is worth it as the frescos, ruins and views are spectacular. Our family spent 3 enjoyable hours here and would recommend it as a must do activity
An exhausting climb up the rock - not for the seriously unfit - but well worth it to see the stunning ancient frescoes that are still vibrant despite their age.

Although it looked like just a rock and you wondered what could be so fascinating about it, my friends kept telling me it was awesome. And it was! Just being at the bottom of the rock and climbing up the stairs, you realise what a magnificent feat this king has done - to transform this rock into his fortress. It's a do-able climb up to the top, though just have to take note that some steps can seem quite steep, especially the iron steps towards the end. The view from the top is awesome!!! Go early (around 8am) before the crowds come after 10! It's definitely one of my favourite places in Sri Lanka.

What can i say about this amazing tourist sight. First of all dont listen to what people have to say about the climb as each person is different. Its high the steps in some areas steep but once you reach the top the view is spectacular and a photographers or happy snappers paradise. It took around 40 minutes to get to the top although for some will take longer and about the same to descend. The descent was worse than the climb and my shakey legs were glad to reach the bottom. It is best to do the climb either in the morning when it first opens and after 3pm. The reason being is that it is too hot in between 12 and 3 plus make sure you take water. The downside was being pestered by the so called guides waiting for the inexperienced traveller wanting to show and help you up the rock. My advice is to say no right from the start and be firm if need be as you dont need a guide to explore the rock. Plus you will end up paying them more than what there worth. When visiting Sigiriya this is a must place to go but just be mindful of your fitness level and if need be take your time. If you do that you will have no trouble making it to the top no matter what your age is.

The rock is big, theres no doubt about it. The walk to the top, easy! People seem to always comment on how difficult it is but it is not. My girlfriend had extreme diarrhea for the whole week before this and was extremely weak but managed to make it up no worries. There are heaps of places to rest and take in the sights. The fee is a joke at $30 USD and even their sneaky little conversion rate makes it cost more than this, 3900rs is not 30 USD (at time of writing). There are also some sights that look a little iffy. One as such is the mirror wall, claimed to be many hundreds of years old. I saw extensive restoration of this wall going on with huge chipped out pieces being re rendered and then probably re graffiti'd. Make your own mind up about the authenticity of this trip, government money grab.

We visited Sigiriya Rock Fortress as part of a Sri Lanka tour on our Honeymoon, and I would say that this was the most impressive of the sights we visited, and should be the top priority for anyone wanting to sight-see in Sri Lanka (though do bear in mind there’s quite a climb involved) We went fairly early in the morning as it’s cooler for the climb up over 1000 steps. Our Driver-guide dropped us at the entrance where we paid the entry fee and were assigned a guide to take us through this amazing world heritage site. Firstly you cross the huge moat that was originally the first line of defence there, then you take in the water gardens with the gravity fed fountains and pools, the boulder gardens with the huge rocks with little steps cut in which used to be the base of walls surrounding the fortress, caves with drip-rails cut in over the mouth to keep the inside dry.  Climb up the steps to the first level of the lower palace where you’ll see the plastered walls with frescoes of the concubines of the ancient king (he had 500 concubines and it’s reported that there were originally frescoes for all of them, but only a few paintings remain).  Then you walk past the ‘mirror wall’, once polished to a high shine but now damaged through age and ancient graffiti, to take in views of the terraced gardens before heading up to the lions paws either side of the entrance to the upper palace part of the fortress (the entrance used to be through the mouth of the lion, but the head crumbled in times past, and only the paws remain). A further climb takes you up to the remains of the upper part of the royal palace, safe at the top of the rock, with the ancient pools, thrones and the remains of the old buildings. A different route down takes you through the terraced gardens back to the boulder gardens and the reception areas where the king would greet other dignitaries. Finally you pass a number of hawkers and stalls selling souvenirs – don’t forget to haggle – we paid a fraction of the initial asking price for a clever little secret box which you can’t open unless you know the knack! The ruins are still an amazing sight to see now, and I only wish I could see what it was like in the 5th century, when it was all built to defend the king who reportedly killed his father and usurped his brother.

lavish gardens, stairs made of the whitest stone, flowers and tree roots creeping between the greenish filled of musk walls. A climb that literally leaves you breathless and upon getting to the top an amazing view opens before ones eyes. the energy of this place is amazing. worth every ache, every step, every minute. nature and man´s genious combined at its best.

My husband had this on his must see when we were visiting Sri Lanka, but I hadn't read much on this and so I didn't know what to expect.  What a pleasant, surprise.  Since it was raining when we arrived, we had the whole place to ourselves.  It didn't hamper our time here but we didn't get the fantastic views. Before going, know that there are many stairs but it is worth it. As we were leaving, the crowds came pouring in, so go early and beat the rush.  Although the fee of $30 is steep, the site is well maintained.

this is 3 hours from pinnawala Nice place to visit. If you like history then be sure to take a guide. They will tell you things about the place which you will not come to know if you just walk around. The climb is steep, but worth it. Make it up to the top and you can see amazing greenery all around. I would just go up to see this. highly recommended place to visit when you come back to sri lanka

As others have said, this is a highlight of the Sri Lankan experience. £20pp is what we paid on entry with another £20 to our guide.  If you have a helper its another tip for him. Best times to visit are at either end of the day: early morning is coolest but late afternoon you could find yourself one of the last people 'on top of the world' watching an amazing sunset.
A hard climb but there were lots of support workers to aid the unfit westerners. It was a fantastic view at the top, interesting history and a great experience.

Liked: landscape. Grueling climb but worth it. Disliked: local vendors a bit pushy. Ticket price (3.900,00 rupies) was high. I haven't seen the museum. Could make 2 separate prices for the museum & fortress
Climbing the rock in monsoon with heavy downpour was fun and challenging but worth it. The guides can be much of a rob but you need one.
At first we were shocked ,about the entrance fee (25 €,loc als pay1€). But once inside and you'll forget that . It's really a place one should have to do while in sri lanka.

Climbing Sigiriya, Lion Rock was a highlight of our Sri Lankan trip. The ancient garden with its landscaping, rock paintings, lion's feet and the views are just amazing. We went fairly early in the morning on a showery day so didn't find it too hot. Had to be careful of slippery steps in parts. There are young men who you may unexpectantly find on either side helping you, but a polite no thank- you was enough to have them gone. We used a local guide who was recommended by our driver and found this to be really worthwhile as he could tell us all the history associated with the site. His price was negotiated first at 4000 SLR and we felt for the information and insight given it was well worth it. The steps are steep in parts and the spiral staircase structure near the caves a bit narrow and rickety, but all in all the 1,200 steps are do-able; we saw them being climbed by all ages. There are lots of resting places and great views to enjoy along the way, making it manageable. It was a fantastic feeling to stand atop of the last two steps right up the top and to be able to say we did it!! Look for the two steps and have a photo taken, then enjoy the amazing view!
Great walk and beautiful views.  Even feasible with young children.  Well worth the efforts, would highly recommend to anyone.
We spent 2-3 hours climbing Lions Rock with our three kids aged 4,10 & 12. Nice excursion- beautiful garden, great view. There was quite a lot people, but it was all well managed and felt safe.

We loved the impressive mural cave paintings, the ornamental gardens and the incredible views from the top.  Our guide was excellent, but we would have enjoyed an opportunity to purchase a more updated guide book about the site (all those on sale seemed to be from the 80's).  Also, the entrance price is $30 U.S. Some of this money needs to be used to improve the spiral stairs coming down from the cave paintings.  The stairs were installed by the British in the 1930's and is rickety and scary in parts.  The site is at the top of the list in the world of cultural sites combined with amazing views.  Well worth climbing the 1,202 steps!  Make sure to get a photo on the last two steps.

Great place and a must visit if you are in the Sigiriya area. $30 entry fee includes the gardens, the rock climb, the cave paintings and the museum. Go to the museum only if you want to waste your time - it's poorly maintained. We went in the middle of the day on 20th December - no issues with the heat and we had blue skies. Our son is 4 and he walked the whole way up as he was distracted by the features, rocks, views, MASSIVE vertical spiral staircase. Our baby was on my back, no problems at all! $30 is fine for what it is however given the number of visitors they get through I struggled to see the re-investment to give the sites the next level of care (beyond the gardens upkeep).
I would recommend climbing early morning or late evening to avoid the scorching heat on the rock. Not an easy climb but stairs all the way and well worth it to see this amazing site.
We really love the place. They charge for foreigner US35, it is really worth it. Anybody going to Sigiriya, don't miss seeing this place. Have to see.

The rock is magnificent to look at but a nightmare to climb. The wall paintings and the entrance through the lions mouth must have been magnificent and well worth the visit if you can manage the climb. You should have a tour guide and helpers are on hand for those who need them (at a price!) even if you do not ask for one or two. Be careful about paying your guide and helpers as you may feel obliged to pay more than you should so seek advice on the going rate first.

Nice place to visit. If you like history then be sure to take a guide. They will tell you things about the place which you will not come to know if you just walk around. The climb is steep, but worth it. Make it up to the top and you can see amazing greenery all around. I would just go up to see this. Rock formations are nice and the fresco's are worth the watch.

Definitely a must-to-see when in Sri Lanka! Although the climb to the top of the rock is quite steep and maybe not recommended for the elderly, the view is breathtaking and the pure thought of old king residing there incredible.

A very unique place to visit- the rock fortress with the gardens, pools, lakes and steps is a must see. Truly worthy of being an 8th wonder. It is unlikely that you will come accross a similar site across the continent. Also a little background on its history will certainly fascinate today's traveller.
Really worth the trip. But a little expensive for a 3 hours visit. I'd advise everyone to climb the other rock beside Sigiriya, you'll have an amazing view on the Lion Rock.

We had a good view of the sigriya rock from our tree house room. The area is very well maintained and looked quite beautiful  as we drove around it. We decided to give the 1200 step climb a skip  to seethe ruins of the kings palace on top of the rock.

I fought it looks not so great on pictures. But if you go and see it for  your own it is a great experiance! The rock is very impressiv as well as the paintings in the cave. However if you feel unlike at heights think twice if you want to go upstairs! But if you made it, the view is boombasitc!

This is a great old fort.  The grounds are quite lovely.  There are several old walls, pools and caves.  The climb up is quite nice and the views excellent.  The cave drawings are supurb.  The lion feet are exceptional.  What a great way to spend a couple of hours.  The toutes are very expensive.  The guides are not worth their wage.  There was a serpent guy near the bottom that was fun.  He had a couple of cobras and a python.   The cost is a little high at $30 per person.

When you look up from the bottom, you can't tell there was a whole ancient complex built/carved into the top of the rock.  Unbelievable carvings, pools, and thrones cut into the rock.  Well worth the climb.

We went to Sigiriya Rock in August this year. It was a weekday, so it wasn't crowded while we were climbing  up. This place is very important historically and archaeologically in Sri lanka.  At the top of the site there is a palace complex. The ruines of various chambers, stairways, pools and breathtaking views can be seen at the top. The newly builted museum is great!

We got up early & bought tickets at the kiosk at around 7.30. There were only a couple of people around & we ran the gauntlet of the guides determined to wander up at our own pace & without distraction. I've no doubt that I need to bone up on exactly what I saw but this was more than compensated for by a leisurely climb in peace & quiet where we were able to enjoy the ambience & the views without interruption. It is a truly amazing place, & pretty straightforward to ascend. Saying that we might both be getting on a bit but are pretty fit. It really is just a lot of stairs, where a head for heights might be useful. I suspect the earlier you go the better as the temperature is more favourable & I saw no evidence of all the scare stories on here about wasps/hornets/bees. Throughout the ascent you are treated to fantastic views & when you reach the summit you just marvel at what it must have been like in its original form (though pity the poor buggers who had to build it). We sat with our feet dangling over the edge & soaked up the views & atmosphere chatting for about an hour whilst the place started to become more busy. Then when we saw the coaches arriving, started our descent. A must visit. Awesome.

I must confess to initally being in a state of shock at the entry price, at a whopping $30 per person this is more than you will pay for admittance to most tourist attractions in Europe or the USA for example. How they think this is reasonable is beyond me and all that you get is admittance for this fee, nothing more. Locals can enter for free naturally, just like pretty much everywhere else in Sri lanka the main objective seems to be to screw every tourist out of as much of their hard earned money as possible. That aside the attraction itself was very enjoyable, a fun climb up to the top where some astonishing views await.

We had the privilege of an excellent guide and that makes it a very enriching outing for us. I don’t think you can learn much of ‘Kassapa’ and his Lion fort unless you’re a history buff so get a guide to come with you it worth the trip. Bring water with you and don’t get con into buying any trick boxes. There are some drink stalls at the end of the trip but prepare to pay higher than norm.

Even if you are of average fitness, this climb is worth the effort and pain..the steps number 1200 but that starts with the first step right after the ticket booth so dont get scared of..in between there are a lot of landing spaces that you can stop for a breather..It should take an averge of a couple of hours to do the whole walk up and down..I wouldn't suggest during rains as some the steps are not safe and can get quite slippery..and good walking shoes or sneakers.. The best time would be the morning trip before the sun hits its peak and it can get really hot..there are no snack stands around so bring cold water to keep you going.. The view during the climb up is as far as the eye can see and it only gets better the higher you go.. If you are looking for an amazing palace at the site (as the king lived here in historic times), there isnt much to see..but historically the grounds are huge so you can imagine how lavishly the royalty lived..Paintings on the walls are also still visible.. If you are one for pushing yourself to make the effort and see a 360 panoramic view, go for it..you wont regret it definitely Just watch out for the guys hanging around the stairs wanting to help you up..they are tip hunters.. Back down there is a guy who reads palms..Cant stay I really believe it but just for fun as a one time thing..
The views are definitely worth it - amazing just how much of the area is still covered by forest. The ticket only allows one day entry as you could easily spend longer there.

Sigiriya, is one of the seven World Heritage Sites in Sri Lanka, the climb to the top - via the famed cave paintings is not for the faint hearted. The section to the paintings is a spiral stair and the section beyond the lions paws is particulaly exposed. The climb is quite breath- taking and well worth the nerves and excitment.
